Once it is established that it has this meaning in one of the dialects of the Arabs, it is clear in meaning and evident in indication, and is outside the openings of the surahs, whose status as *mutashabih* we have already explained at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The same applies if it has this meaning in one of the non-Arabic languages and the Arabs used it in their speech with that meaning, like the other foreign words that the Arabs used and that are found in the Noble Book; through that usage they became part of the language of the Arabs.

As for the clause *"We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed,"* it is a new sentence (*mustanifah*) brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the hardship he suffered from the polytheists. *Shaqa'* (distress) comes in the sense of hardship. Ibn Kaysan said: "The root meaning of *shaqa'* in the language is hardship and fatigue," and from it is the poet's saying:

*The man of intellect suffers in comfort because of his intellect, while the ignorant one in misery enjoys ease.*

The meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be exhausted by excessive grief over them and their disbelief, and by your anguish that they should believe." It is like His saying, glorified is He: *"Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief"* [al-Kahf: 6]. Al-Nahhas said: "Some grammarians say the *lam* in *li-tashqa* is the *lam* of negation, and some say it is the *lam* of denial (*juhud*)." Ibn Kaysan said: "It is the *lam* of genitive (*khafd*)." This explanation of the verse is according to the view of those who say that *Ta-Ha*, like the other openings of surahs, is a listing of the names of letters. If it is made the name of the surah, then His saying *"We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed"* is a predicate about it, it being in the position of the subject. As for the view of those who say its meaning is "O man," or in the sense of commanding treading the earth, the sentence is new, to turn the Prophet (ﷺ) away from what he was doing of excessive worship.

The accusative of *illa tadhkiratan* (but as a reminder) is as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for *anzalna* (We sent down), like your saying: "I did not strike you for discipline, except out of compassion for you." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is a substitute (*badal*) for *li-tashqa*, meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected this, on the grounds that a reminder is not distress. He said: "It is rather in the accusative of verbal noun (*masdariyyah*): meaning, We sent it down so that you would remind by it a reminder; or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: *We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed* by it; We sent it down only for reminder."

The accusative of *tanzilan mimman khalaqa al-ard wa al-samawat al-'ula* (a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens) is as a verbal noun: meaning, We sent it down as a revelation. It is also said: it is a substitute for *tadhkiratan* (reminder). It is also said: it is in the accusative of praise. It is also said: it is governed by *yakhsha* (fears), meaning: he fears a revelation from Allah, as its object. It is also said: it is in the accusative of state (*hal*), by interpreting it as an active participle. Abu Haywa al-Shami read *tanzilun* (with *raf'*, nominative) on the meaning "this is a revelation." *Mimman khalaqa* (from the One who created) is attached to *tanzilan*, or to an omitted element that is an attribute of it. The specifying of the creation of the earth and the heavens is because they are the greatest of the created things that the servants observe, Mighty and Majestic is He. *Al-'ula* is the plural of *al-'ulya*, meaning the elevated, like the plural of *kubra* and *sughra* as *kubar* and *sughar*. The meaning of the verse is to inform the servants of the perfection of His greatness, glorified is He, and the magnificence of His majesty.

The nominative of *al-Rahman* (The Most Merciful) is as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Akhfash said. It may also be nominative as an object of praise, or as an inceptive subject. It has been read in the genitive; al-Zajjaj said it is a substitute of *mimman* (from the One who). Al-Nahhas allowed that it may be nominative as a substitute of the pronoun in *khalaqa*. The clause *'ala al-'arshi istawa* (settled upon the Throne) is in the position of nominative, as a predicate of an omitted subject, or as the predicate of *al-Rahman* according to whoever makes it a subject.

Ahmad ibn Yahya said: Tha'lab said: "*Al-istiwa'*" means turning toward something. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said the same. It is also said that it is a metaphor for kingship and dominion. The investigation of the verification of this is lengthy, and the discussion of it has already been presented in *al-A'raf*. What Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari held is that He, glorified is He, is settled upon His Throne without limit and without modality, and before him the great majority of the pious early generations held this view, those who transmit the attributes as they came, without distortion and without interpretation.

*"To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"*: that is, He is the owner of everything and its governor, and of what is between them of existing things, and what is beneath the soil. *Al-thara* (soil) in the language is moist dust. That is, whatever is beneath the dust of anything. Al-Wahidi said: "The exegetes say that He, glorified is He, intended the soil beneath the rock on which the bull stands, which is beneath the earth, and none knows what is beneath the soil except Allah, glorified is He."

*"And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden"*: *al-jahr bi-al-qawl* (speaking aloud) is raising the voice with it. *Al-sirr* (the secret) is what a person tells another and confides to him. *Al-akhfa* (what is more hidden than the secret) is what a person speaks to himself and what occurs to his mind.

The meaning is: If you speak aloud in the remembrance and supplication of Allah, know that He is free of need of that, for He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, so there is no need for you to speak aloud. In this there is a sense of prohibiting loud speech, like His saying, glorified is He: *"And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear"* [al-A'raf: 205]. It is also said: *al-sirr* is what a person conceals within himself, and *al-akhfa* than it is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he himself does while not knowing it. It is also said: *al-sirr* is what a person harbors in his soul, and *al-akhfa* than it is what has not yet happened and no one has harbored. It is also said: *al-sirr* is the secret of created beings, and *al-akhfa* than it is the secret of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ibn Jarir denied this and said: "*Al-akhfa* is what is not in the secret of the human being but will be in his soul."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 1–16 (part 2 of 3):

Then He mentioned that the one worshipped in the manner stated is Allah, glorified is He, who is exalted above any partner and who deserves to be named by the Most Beautiful Names. So He said: ﴿Allah! There is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾ Here, *Allah* is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject), meaning: the One described with these perfect attributes is Allah. The clause ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining that divinity belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He; that is, there is no god in existence except Him. Likewise, the clause ﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ explains His entitlement to the Most Beautiful Names, which are the ninety-nine mentioned in the authentic hadith.

Their explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180] in Surah al-A'raf. *Al-husna* is the feminine form of *al-ahsan* (the most beautiful). *Al-asma'* (the names) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *al-husna* is its predicate. It is permissible for *Allah* to be the subject with the sentence following it as its predicate, and it is also permissible for it to be an apposition (*badal*) to the pronoun in *ya'lamu* (He knows).

Then the Exalted set forth the matter of Divine Oneness by mentioning the story of Musa, which contains manifest power and a strange account. So He said: ﴿And has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ The interrogative is for confirmation (*taqrir*), and its meaning is: has not the story of Musa already reached you? It was said its meaning is: the story of Musa has indeed reached you. Al-Kalbi said: the story of Musa had not reached him at that time.

Within the context of this story is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he encounters of the hardships of the duties of prophethood, the bearing of its burdens, and the enduring of its calamities, and that this is the way of the prophets before him. The meaning of *al-hadith* (the story) here is the account of what happened to Musa. ﴿When he saw a fire﴾ is an adverbial clause of time (*zarf*) related to *al-hadith*. It was said that its governing element is an implied verb: that is, "Mention," and it was said that it is implied afterward: that is, when he saw a fire, such-and-such happened. His seeing the fire took place on a dark night when he set out traveling to his mother after asking permission from Shu'ayb. ﴿When he saw it, he said to his family, "Stay here.">﴾ The word *ahl* (family) here refers to his wife, and the plural form is used either because the word *ahl* is in the plural sense or for emphasis. It was said that it refers to the wife, the child, and the servant. The meaning of *imkuthu* (stay here) is: remain in your place. He used the word *mukth* (staying) rather than *iqamah* (residing), because *iqamah* implies permanence, whereas *mukth* does not.

Hamzah read ﴿li-ahlihi﴾ with a *damma* on the *ha'* (*li-ahlihi*), and likewise in Surah al-Qasas. Al-Nahhas said: this is according to the dialect of those who say *marartu bihu ya rajul* (I passed by him, O man), so he kept it in its original form, and that is permissible. However, Hamzah differed from his usual practice in these two places only.

﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾ means: I have seen. It is said *anastu al-sawt* (I perceived the sound) meaning I heard it, and *anastu al-rajul* (I perceived the man) meaning I saw him. It was said that *al-inas* is clear seeing, and it was said that *al-inas* is specific to seeing what is pleasant to the heart. The sentence is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the command to stay. Since bringing a burning brand (*qabas*) and finding guidance were both expected, he gave the command with hope, so he said: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it﴾, that is, I will come to you from the fire with a brand. *Al-qabas* is a flame from fire, and likewise *al-miqbas*. It is said: *qabistu minhu naran, aqbisu qabsan, fa-aqbasani*, meaning he gave me. Likewise *iqtabastu*.

Al-Yazidi said: *aqbastu al-rajul 'ilman* (I gave the man knowledge) and *qabastuhu naran* (I gave him fire), but if you sought it for him, you say *aqbastuhu*. Al-Kisa'i said: *aqbastuhu naran wa 'ilman* (I gave him fire and knowledge) are the same, and *qabastuhu* is also used for both. ﴿Or find at the fire guidance﴾, that is, a guide who will lead me to the path and show me the way. Al-Farra' said: he meant a guide, but expressed it with the verbal noun (*masdar*) for the sake of intensification, or by omitting a modifier: that is, one who possesses guidance. The word *aw* (or) in both places is for preventing the absence of both, not for combining them. The preposition *'ala* (on/at) indicates that the people of the fire are elevated above the nearest place to it.

﴿So when he came to it﴾ means: when he came to the fire he had perceived, he was called from the tree, as is explicitly stated in Surah al-Qasas, that is, from its direction and side: ﴿O Musa! Indeed, I am your Lord.﴾ That is, he was called and it was said, "O Musa." Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd and al-Yazidi read *anni* (that I) with a *fath* on the *hamza*. The rest read it with a *kasra*, meaning: that I am. ﴿Remove your sandals﴾: Allah commanded him to remove his sandals, because that is more expressive of humility, closer to honour, esteem and good manners. It was said: they were made from the skin of an undressed donkey. It was also said: the meaning of removing the sandals is emptying the heart of family and wealth, and this is one of the innovations in tafsir.

Then the Exalted gave the reason for the command to remove them, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.﴾ *Al-muqaddas* means the purified; *al-qudus* is purity; and a sacred land is a purified land. It was so named because Allah expelled the disbelievers from it and populated it with believers. *Tuwa* is the name of the valley. Al-Jawhari said: *Tuwa* is the name of a place in Syria, with the *ta'* pronounced with a *kasra* or a *damma*; it is declined and not declined. Whoever declines it makes it the name of a valley or place and treats it as indefinite; whoever does not decline it treats it as a town or district and as definite. 'Ikrimah read *Tiwa* with a *kasra* on the *ta'*, and the rest read it with a *damma*. It was said that *Tuwa*, like *thuna* (two by two), is a verbal noun from *tayy* (folding), governing *nudiya* (he was called), or governing *al-muqaddas*: that is, he was called twice, or it was sanctified time after time.

﴿And I have chosen you﴾: the people of Medina, the people of Mecca, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read *wa-ana ikhtartuka* in the singular. Hamzah read ﴿wa-inna ikhtarnaka﴾ in the plural. Al-Nahhas said: the first reading is preferable for two reasons: first, that it corresponds more closely to the written text (*al-khatt*); second, that it better fits the flow of the speech, given His saying: ﴿O Musa, indeed I am your Lord.﴾ The meaning of *ikhtartuka* is: I have chosen you for prophethood and messengership. The *fa'* (so) in His saying ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ is for establishing the order of what follows upon what precedes. *Ma* (what) is either a relative pronoun or a verbal particle (*masdariyyah*): that is, listen to that which is revealed to you, or to the revelation itself. The clause ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to *ma* in *lima yuha* (to what is revealed).

Then the Exalted commanded him to worship, so He said: ﴿So worship Me.﴾ The *fa'* here is like the *fa'* before it, because the exclusivity of divinity to Him, glorified is He, necessitates restricting worship to Him. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾ He singled out prayer for mention, although it falls under the command to worship, because it is the noblest act of obedience and the most excellent worship. He gave the reason for the command to establish prayer with His words ﴿for My remembrance﴾: that is, so that you remember Me, for complete remembrance is only realized within worship and prayer. Or the meaning is: so that you remember Me through them, since they include remembrances (*adhkar*). Or the meaning is: establish prayer whenever you remember that you owe a prayer. It was said that the meaning is: so that I may mention you with praise in the highest place (*'Illiyyin*). On this view, the verbal noun may be read as attached to the subject or to the object.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ is a reason for what precedes of the command: that is, the Hour, which is the time of reckoning and punishment, is coming, so do good deeds, namely worship of Allah and prayer. The meaning of ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ is disputed. Al-Wahidi said: most exegetes said: "I conceal it from Myself," and this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Mubarrad and Qutrub said: this is according to the usage of the Arabs, who say, when they intensify concealing something, "I concealed it even from myself," meaning I did not reveal it to anyone. The meaning of the verse is that Allah intensified the concealment of the Hour, and so He expressed it in the most emphatic manner known to the Arabs.

It has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he read *akhfiha* with a *fath* on the *hamza*, meaning "I reveal it," and likewise Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from al-Kisa'i, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Wafa' ibn Iyas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Nahhas said: this narration has no chain other than this one. Al-Qurtubi said: Ibn al-Anbari also narrated it in his book *al-Radd*, saying: my father narrated to me, Muhammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us, al-Farra' narrated to us, al-Kisa'i narrated to us, and he mentioned it. Al-Nahhas said: a better chain than this is what Yahya al-Qattan narrated from al-Thawri, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he read *ukhfiha* with a *damma* on the *hamza*. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Farra' said: the meaning of the reading with a *fath* is "I almost reveal it," from *khafaytu al-shay'* when I revealed it, and *ukhfihi* (I conceal it). Al-Qurtubi said: some linguists have said it is permissible that *ukhfiha* with a *damma* on the *alif* means "I reveal it," because it is said *khafaytu al-shay'* and *akhfaytuhu*, from words of opposites (*huruf al-adda*), which occur in the sense of both concealing and revealing. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *khafaytu* and *akhfaytu* have the same meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: this is good, and al-Farra' and Sibawayh have recited what indicates that *akhfah* means "revealed," namely the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"If you conceal the disease, we shall not hide it, and if you stir up war, we shall not sit idle."*

That is: if you conceal the disease, we shall not reveal it. Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from Abu al-Khattab that it is with a *damma* on the *nun* in *nukhfih*, and said Imru' al-Qays said:

*"She concealed them from her emerging, as if what concealed them was the rain-drops of a clawed cloud."*

That is: she revealed them. Al-Nahhas rejected this view and said: the meaning is not "I reveal it," especially since *ukhfiha* is an irregular reading, so how could the correct and widespread reading be disregarded. Ibn al-Anbari said: there is another interpretation of the verse, namely that the speech stops at *akad* (I almost), and after it is an implied element: that is, "I almost bring it," and the beginning is with *ukhfiha* (I conceal it) so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives. Similar to this is the saying of 'Umayr ibn Dabi' al-Burjumi:

*"I resolved but did not do it, and I almost did, I wish I had left, over 'Uthman, his wives weeping."*

That is: "and I almost did." Al-Nahhas chose this view. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is from the category of negation (*salb*), not of opposites: the meaning of *ukhfiha* is "I remove its concealment from it," that is, its covering, and from this comes the expression *ashkaytuhu*, meaning I removed his complaint. Abu Hatim narrated from al-Akhfash that *akad* is superfluous for emphasis, and said: similar to it is His saying ﴿when he extends his hand, he can hardly see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. Similar is the saying of the poet:

*"Swift to battle, bearing his weapons, so that his foe can scarcely breathe."*

He said: the meaning of "I almost conceal it" is: I come close to that, because when you say "Zayd almost stood up," it is possible that he stood and possible that he did not stand. And it indicates that He concealed it by means of an indication other than this verse.

His saying ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ is connected either to *ati'ah* (coming) or to *ukhfiha* (I conceal it), and *ma* is a verbal particle: that is, so that every soul may be recompensed for its striving. Although *sa'y* (striving) is apparent in actions, here it includes both actions and abstentions, because it is certain that one who abandons what is obligatory upon him is punished for his abandonment and held accountable for it.

So let not one who does not believe in it, and who follows his own desire, turn you away from it, lest you perish. That is, let them not divert you from belief in the Hour and from affirming it, or from remembering it and being mindful of it, [as those who disbelieve do not believe in it]. Although this prohibition appears on its surface to be addressed to the disbeliever, in reality it is a prohibition addressed to him (ﷺ) against being diverted, or against displaying his religion before the disbelievers. It belongs to the same figure of speech as "Do not let me find you here," as is well known. It has been said that the pronoun in "from it" refers to the prayer, but this is far-fetched. His statement "and who follows his own desire" is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: the one who does not believe. "Who follows his own desire" means who follows his own whims, by immersing himself in sensual, transient pleasures. (p. 906) "Lest you perish" means lest you be ruined, because your being turned away from it by the disbelievers' obstruction of you necessarily entails ruin and follows from it.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) [said]: "When the revelation first came to him, he would stand on the balls of his feet when he prayed, so God revealed: ﴿Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched.﴾" Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, saying: They said, "This man has indeed become wretched with his Lord," so God revealed this verse. Ibn 'Asakir also reported from him, saying: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) rose in the night, he would tie himself with a rope so that he would not sleep, so God revealed this verse." Al-Bazzar reported from 'Ali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would shift his weight between his two feet, standing on each foot in turn, until this was revealed: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched.﴾" Al-Suyuti graded its chain as good (ḥasan). Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him something longer than this. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would sometimes recite the Qur'an while praying, standing on one foot, so God revealed: Ta-Ha, [We did not send down the Qur'an to you] by your two feet to make you wretched." Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him concerning His statement "Ta-Ha," that he said: "O man." Al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ta-Ha" in Nabataean (*al-Nabatiyya*, the language of the Nabataeans), meaning: "Tread, O man." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also, who said: "It is like the saying 'sit down' (*uq'ud*)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, who said: "Ta-Ha" in Nabataean means "O man." Ibn Jarir reported from him, who said: "Ta-Ha" means "O man" in Syriac (*al-Suryaniyya*). Al-Hakim reported from him also, who said: "Ta-Ha is like your saying 'O Muhammad' in the language of Abyssinia." There is disagreement and contradiction in these reports from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have ten names with my Lord." Abu al-Tufayl said: "I memorised eight of them: Muhammad, Ahmad, Abu al-Qasim, al-Fatih, al-Khatim, al-Mahi, al-'Aqib, and al-Hashir." Sayf claimed that Abu Ja'far told him: "The two remaining names are Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin." Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched.﴾ He said: "O man, We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched." He used to stand the night on his two feet. It is a dialect of the tribe of 'Akk: if you say to an 'Akkī, "O man," he does not turn; but when you say "Ta-Ha," he turns to you.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ta-Ha is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of His names."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His statement: ﴿And what is beneath the soil (al-thara)﴾, that he said: "Al-thara is everything that is moist." Abu Ya'la reported from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked, "What is beneath this earth?" He said, "Water." It was said, "What is beneath the water?" He said, "Darkness." It was said, "What is beneath the darkness?" He said, "Air." It was said, "What is beneath the air?" He said, "The soil (al-thara)." It was said, "What is beneath the soil?" He said, "The knowledge of created beings ends at the knowledge of the Creator." Ibn Mardawayh reported something similar from him, but longer.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden﴾, that he said: "The secret (al-sirr) is what the son of Adam conceals within himself, and what is more hidden is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he will do before he knows it. He knows all of that, what has passed of it and what remains. His knowledge is one, and all creatures before Him are like a single soul, as in His statement: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28]." Al-Hakim reported from him in this verse, and graded it authentic (*sahih*), that he said: "The secret is what you yourself know, and what is more hidden is what God casts into your heart of what you do not know." 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi reported it with the wording: "He knows what you conceal in yourself, and He knows what you will do tomorrow." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿Or I may find at the fire a guidance (huda)﴾, that he said: "Someone who will point out the way."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ali concerning His statement: ﴿Take off your two sandals﴾, that he said: "They were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so it was said to him, 'Take them off.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿You are in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾, that he said: "Al-Mubarak said: Tuwa is the name of the valley." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him: "In the sacred valley, Tuwa," meaning the holy land, because he passed through its valley by night and folded it up (*tawa*). It is said: "I folded the valley of such-and-such." Ibn Jarir also reported from him concerning His statement, "Tuwa," that he said: "Tread the valley."

In the two *Sahihs* and elsewhere, from the hadith of Anas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If one of you sleeps through the prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God said: ﴿Establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾" Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God said: ﴿Establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾" Ibn Shihab used to recite it as *lidhikrā* (for the remembrance).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾, that he said: "I do not reveal it to anyone other than Myself." Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I almost conceal it from myself."

(p-٩٠٣)

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan by the consensus of all. Al-Nahhas and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat Ta-Ha was revealed in Mecca." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Darimi, Ibn Khuzayma in *al-Tawhid*, al-'Uqayli in *al-Du'afa'*, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an, they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will be sent down; blessed are the bodies that will carry this; blessed are the tongues that will speak this.'"

Ibn Khuzayma said after narrating it: "It is a *gharib* (unusual, single-channel) hadith, and there is a *nakarah* (irregularity) in it. Ibrahim ibn Muhajir and his teacher have been spoken of," meaning Ibrahim ibn Muhajir ibn Sammar and his teacher 'Umar ibn Hafs ibn Dhakwan, and both are among the transmitters of its chain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which al-An'am is mentioned from the First Reminder (*al-Dhikr al-Awwal*). I was given Surat Ta-Ha and the surahs beginning with *ta-sin* from the tablets of Musa. I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the closings of al-Baqarah from beneath the Throne. I was given al-Mufassal as a supererogatory gift."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every Qur'an will be taken away from the people of Paradise, so they will recite nothing from it except Surat Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin, for they will recite these two in Paradise."

Al-Daraqutni in his *Sunan* narrated from Anas ibn Malik, mentioning the story of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with his sister and Khabbab, and their recitation of Ta-Ha, and that this was the cause of 'Umar's Islam. The story is well known in the books of biography (*al-siyar*).

(p-٩٠٣)
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Ta-Ha﴾ ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed﴾ ﴿but only as a reminder for one who fears﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful settled upon the Throne﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is even more hidden﴾ ﴿Allah — there is no god but Him; His are the most beautiful names﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Musa?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Wait, I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance"﴾ ﴿When he came to it, he was called: "O Musa! ﴿I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire divert you from it, lest you perish﴾.

As for His saying *Ta-Ha*: Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with *imalah* (inclining the vowel toward *i*) of the *ha'* and with a *fath* (open vowel) on the *ta'*. Abu Bakr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash inclined both. Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' read them between the two pronunciations, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read with *tafkhim* (full, emphatic pronunciation). Al-Tha'labi said: "All of them are correct and eloquent dialects." Al-Nahhas said: "There is no basis for *imalah* according to most of the grammarians, for two reasons. The first is that there is no *ya'* or *kasrah* here that would justify *imalah*. The second is that the *ta'* is one of the blockers of *imalah*."

The scholars differed about the meaning of this word, in several opinions:

The first: it is among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses) whose meaning is not understood.

The second: it means "O man" (*ya rajul*) in the dialect of 'Ukl and in the dialect of 'Akk. Al-Kalbi said: "If I said to a man from 'Akk, 'O man!' he would not answer until you said *Ta-Ha*." Ibn Jarir recited in this regard:

*I called "Ta-Ha" in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he was turning away from me.*

Another version reads "*muzayilan*" (departing) instead of "*mu'wilan*" (fleeing). It is also said that in the dialect of 'Akk it means "O my beloved." Qutrub said: "It is likewise in the dialect of Tayy, meaning 'O man.'" So said al-Hasan and 'Ikrima. It is also said that it is so in the Syriac language, related by al-Mahdawi. Ibn Jarir related that it is so in the Nabataean language, and al-Sudi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. Al-Tha'labi related from 'Ikrima that it is so in the Abyssinian language, narrating it from 'Ikrima. There is no obstacle to this word being established with that meaning in all of these languages, if the transmission is sound.

The third opinion: it is a name of Allah, glorified is He.

The fourth opinion: it is a name of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fifth opinion: it is a name of the surah.

The sixth opinion: it is disjointed letters (*huruf muqatta'ah*), each of which indicates a meaning. Then they differed about the meanings these letters indicate, in several opinions, all of which are forced and strained.

The seventh opinion: its meaning is "Blessed is the one who is guided."

The eighth opinion: its meaning is: "Tread the earth, O Muhammad." Ibn al-Anbari said: "That is because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to bear the hardship of prayer until his feet nearly swelled, and he needed to rest. So it was said to him, 'Tread the earth,' meaning: do not exhaust yourself until you need to rest."

Al-Qadi 'Iyad related in *al-Shifa'* from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he stood on one foot and raised the other," so Allah revealed *Ta-Ha*, meaning: "Tread the earth, O Muhammad." It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he read *Taha* on the pattern of *da'* (an imperative meaning "leave"), meaning an imperative to tread, and the original was *ta'* (tread), so the *hamzah* was changed to *ha'*.

Al-Wahidi related from most of the exegetes that this word means "O man," intending the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "This is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of 'Ata', and of al-Kalbi, except that some of them say it is in the language of Abyssinia, Nabataea and Syriac, and al-Kalbi says it is in the dialect of 'Akk." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The dialect of Quraysh agreed with that dialect in this meaning, because Allah, glorified is He, did not address His Prophet in the language of other than Quraysh." End of quotation.

Once it is established that it has this meaning in one of the dialects of the Arabs, it is clear in meaning and evident in indication, and is outside the openings of the surahs, whose status as *mutashabih* we have already explained at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The same applies if it has this meaning in one of the non-Arabic languages and the Arabs used it in their speech with that meaning, like the other foreign words that the Arabs used and that are found in the Noble Book; through that usage they became part of the language of the Arabs.

As for the clause *"We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed,"* it is a new sentence (*mustanifah*) brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the hardship he suffered from the polytheists. *Shaqa'* (distress) comes in the sense of hardship. Ibn Kaysan said: "The root meaning of *shaqa'* in the language is hardship and fatigue," and from it is the poet's saying:

*The man of intellect suffers in comfort because of his intellect, while the ignorant one in misery enjoys ease.*

The meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be exhausted by excessive grief over them and their disbelief, and by your anguish that they should believe." It is like His saying, glorified is He: *"Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief"* [al-Kahf: 6]. Al-Nahhas said: "Some grammarians say the *lam* in *li-tashqa* is the *lam* of negation, and some say it is the *lam* of denial (*juhud*)." Ibn Kaysan said: "It is the *lam* of genitive (*khafd*)." This explanation of the verse is according to the view of those who say that *Ta-Ha*, like the other openings of surahs, is a listing of the names of letters. If it is made the name of the surah, then His saying *"We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed"* is a predicate about it, it being in the position of the subject. As for the view of those who say its meaning is "O man," or in the sense of commanding treading the earth, the sentence is new, to turn the Prophet (ﷺ) away from what he was doing of excessive worship.

The accusative of *illa tadhkiratan* (but as a reminder) is as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for *anzalna* (We sent down), like your saying: "I did not strike you for discipline, except out of compassion for you." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is a substitute (*badal*) for *li-tashqa*, meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected this, on the grounds that a reminder is not distress. He said: "It is rather in the accusative of verbal noun (*masdariyyah*): meaning, We sent it down so that you would remind by it a reminder; or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: *We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed* by it; We sent it down only for reminder."

The accusative of *tanzilan mimman khalaqa al-ard wa al-samawat al-'ula* (a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens) is as a verbal noun: meaning, We sent it down as a revelation. It is also said: it is a substitute for *tadhkiratan* (reminder). It is also said: it is in the accusative of praise. It is also said: it is governed by *yakhsha* (fears), meaning: he fears a revelation from Allah, as its object. It is also said: it is in the accusative of state (*hal*), by interpreting it as an active participle. Abu Haywa al-Shami read *tanzilun* (with *raf'*, nominative) on the meaning "this is a revelation." *Mimman khalaqa* (from the One who created) is attached to *tanzilan*, or to an omitted element that is an attribute of it. The specifying of the creation of the earth and the heavens is because they are the greatest of the created things that the servants observe, Mighty and Majestic is He. *Al-'ula* is the plural of *al-'ulya*, meaning the elevated, like the plural of *kubra* and *sughra* as *kubar* and *sughar*. The meaning of the verse is to inform the servants of the perfection of His greatness, glorified is He, and the magnificence of His majesty.

The nominative of *al-Rahman* (The Most Merciful) is as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Akhfash said. It may also be nominative as an object of praise, or as an inceptive subject. It has been read in the genitive; al-Zajjaj said it is a substitute of *mimman* (from the One who). Al-Nahhas allowed that it may be nominative as a substitute of the pronoun in *khalaqa*. The clause *'ala al-'arshi istawa* (settled upon the Throne) is in the position of nominative, as a predicate of an omitted subject, or as the predicate of *al-Rahman* according to whoever makes it a subject.

Ahmad ibn Yahya said: Tha'lab said: "*Al-istiwa'*" means turning toward something. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said the same. It is also said that it is a metaphor for kingship and dominion. The investigation of the verification of this is lengthy, and the discussion of it has already been presented in *al-A'raf*. What Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari held is that He, glorified is He, is settled upon His Throne without limit and without modality, and before him the great majority of the pious early generations held this view, those who transmit the attributes as they came, without distortion and without interpretation.

*"To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"*: that is, He is the owner of everything and its governor, and of what is between them of existing things, and what is beneath the soil. *Al-thara* (soil) in the language is moist dust. That is, whatever is beneath the dust of anything. Al-Wahidi said: "The exegetes say that He, glorified is He, intended the soil beneath the rock on which the bull stands, which is beneath the earth, and none knows what is beneath the soil except Allah, glorified is He."

*"And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden"*: *al-jahr bi-al-qawl* (speaking aloud) is raising the voice with it. *Al-sirr* (the secret) is what a person tells another and confides to him. *Al-akhfa* (what is more hidden than the secret) is what a person speaks to himself and what occurs to his mind.

The meaning is: If you speak aloud in the remembrance and supplication of Allah, know that He is free of need of that, for He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, so there is no need for you to speak aloud. In this there is a sense of prohibiting loud speech, like His saying, glorified is He: *"And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear"* [al-A'raf: 205]. It is also said: *al-sirr* is what a person conceals within himself, and *al-akhfa* than it is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he himself does while not knowing it. It is also said: *al-sirr* is what a person harbors in his soul, and *al-akhfa* than it is what has not yet happened and no one has harbored. It is also said: *al-sirr* is the secret of created beings, and *al-akhfa* than it is the secret of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ibn Jarir denied this and said: "*Al-akhfa* is what is not in the secret of the human being but will be in his soul."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 1–16 (part 2 of 3):

Then He mentioned that the one worshipped in the manner stated is Allah, glorified is He, who is exalted above any partner and who deserves to be named by the Most Beautiful Names. So He said: ﴿Allah! There is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾ Here, *Allah* is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject), meaning: the One described with these perfect attributes is Allah. The clause ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining that divinity belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He; that is, there is no god in existence except Him. Likewise, the clause ﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ explains His entitlement to the Most Beautiful Names, which are the ninety-nine mentioned in the authentic hadith.

Their explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180] in Surah al-A'raf. *Al-husna* is the feminine form of *al-ahsan* (the most beautiful). *Al-asma'* (the names) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *al-husna* is its predicate. It is permissible for *Allah* to be the subject with the sentence following it as its predicate, and it is also permissible for it to be an apposition (*badal*) to the pronoun in *ya'lamu* (He knows).

Then the Exalted set forth the matter of Divine Oneness by mentioning the story of Musa, which contains manifest power and a strange account. So He said: ﴿And has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ The interrogative is for confirmation (*taqrir*), and its meaning is: has not the story of Musa already reached you? It was said its meaning is: the story of Musa has indeed reached you. Al-Kalbi said: the story of Musa had not reached him at that time.

Within the context of this story is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he encounters of the hardships of the duties of prophethood, the bearing of its burdens, and the enduring of its calamities, and that this is the way of the prophets before him. The meaning of *al-hadith* (the story) here is the account of what happened to Musa. ﴿When he saw a fire﴾ is an adverbial clause of time (*zarf*) related to *al-hadith*. It was said that its governing element is an implied verb: that is, "Mention," and it was said that it is implied afterward: that is, when he saw a fire, such-and-such happened. His seeing the fire took place on a dark night when he set out traveling to his mother after asking permission from Shu'ayb. ﴿When he saw it, he said to his family, "Stay here.">﴾ The word *ahl* (family) here refers to his wife, and the plural form is used either because the word *ahl* is in the plural sense or for emphasis. It was said that it refers to the wife, the child, and the servant. The meaning of *imkuthu* (stay here) is: remain in your place. He used the word *mukth* (staying) rather than *iqamah* (residing), because *iqamah* implies permanence, whereas *mukth* does not.

Hamzah read ﴿li-ahlihi﴾ with a *damma* on the *ha'* (*li-ahlihi*), and likewise in Surah al-Qasas. Al-Nahhas said: this is according to the dialect of those who say *marartu bihu ya rajul* (I passed by him, O man), so he kept it in its original form, and that is permissible. However, Hamzah differed from his usual practice in these two places only.

﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾ means: I have seen. It is said *anastu al-sawt* (I perceived the sound) meaning I heard it, and *anastu al-rajul* (I perceived the man) meaning I saw him. It was said that *al-inas* is clear seeing, and it was said that *al-inas* is specific to seeing what is pleasant to the heart. The sentence is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the command to stay. Since bringing a burning brand (*qabas*) and finding guidance were both expected, he gave the command with hope, so he said: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it﴾, that is, I will come to you from the fire with a brand. *Al-qabas* is a flame from fire, and likewise *al-miqbas*. It is said: *qabistu minhu naran, aqbisu qabsan, fa-aqbasani*, meaning he gave me. Likewise *iqtabastu*.

Al-Yazidi said: *aqbastu al-rajul 'ilman* (I gave the man knowledge) and *qabastuhu naran* (I gave him fire), but if you sought it for him, you say *aqbastuhu*. Al-Kisa'i said: *aqbastuhu naran wa 'ilman* (I gave him fire and knowledge) are the same, and *qabastuhu* is also used for both. ﴿Or find at the fire guidance﴾, that is, a guide who will lead me to the path and show me the way. Al-Farra' said: he meant a guide, but expressed it with the verbal noun (*masdar*) for the sake of intensification, or by omitting a modifier: that is, one who possesses guidance. The word *aw* (or) in both places is for preventing the absence of both, not for combining them. The preposition *'ala* (on/at) indicates that the people of the fire are elevated above the nearest place to it.

﴿So when he came to it﴾ means: when he came to the fire he had perceived, he was called from the tree, as is explicitly stated in Surah al-Qasas, that is, from its direction and side: ﴿O Musa! Indeed, I am your Lord.﴾ That is, he was called and it was said, "O Musa." Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd and al-Yazidi read *anni* (that I) with a *fath* on the *hamza*. The rest read it with a *kasra*, meaning: that I am. ﴿Remove your sandals﴾: Allah commanded him to remove his sandals, because that is more expressive of humility, closer to honour, esteem and good manners. It was said: they were made from the skin of an undressed donkey. It was also said: the meaning of removing the sandals is emptying the heart of family and wealth, and this is one of the innovations in tafsir.

Then the Exalted gave the reason for the command to remove them, so He said: ﴿Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.﴾ *Al-muqaddas* means the purified; *al-qudus* is purity; and a sacred land is a purified land. It was so named because Allah expelled the disbelievers from it and populated it with believers. *Tuwa* is the name of the valley. Al-Jawhari said: *Tuwa* is the name of a place in Syria, with the *ta'* pronounced with a *kasra* or a *damma*; it is declined and not declined. Whoever declines it makes it the name of a valley or place and treats it as indefinite; whoever does not decline it treats it as a town or district and as definite. 'Ikrimah read *Tiwa* with a *kasra* on the *ta'*, and the rest read it with a *damma*. It was said that *Tuwa*, like *thuna* (two by two), is a verbal noun from *tayy* (folding), governing *nudiya* (he was called), or governing *al-muqaddas*: that is, he was called twice, or it was sanctified time after time.

﴿And I have chosen you﴾: the people of Medina, the people of Mecca, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read *wa-ana ikhtartuka* in the singular. Hamzah read ﴿wa-inna ikhtarnaka﴾ in the plural. Al-Nahhas said: the first reading is preferable for two reasons: first, that it corresponds more closely to the written text (*al-khatt*); second, that it better fits the flow of the speech, given His saying: ﴿O Musa, indeed I am your Lord.﴾ The meaning of *ikhtartuka* is: I have chosen you for prophethood and messengership. The *fa'* (so) in His saying ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ is for establishing the order of what follows upon what precedes. *Ma* (what) is either a relative pronoun or a verbal particle (*masdariyyah*): that is, listen to that which is revealed to you, or to the revelation itself. The clause ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to *ma* in *lima yuha* (to what is revealed).

Then the Exalted commanded him to worship, so He said: ﴿So worship Me.﴾ The *fa'* here is like the *fa'* before it, because the exclusivity of divinity to Him, glorified is He, necessitates restricting worship to Him. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾ He singled out prayer for mention, although it falls under the command to worship, because it is the noblest act of obedience and the most excellent worship. He gave the reason for the command to establish prayer with His words ﴿for My remembrance﴾: that is, so that you remember Me, for complete remembrance is only realized within worship and prayer. Or the meaning is: so that you remember Me through them, since they include remembrances (*adhkar*). Or the meaning is: establish prayer whenever you remember that you owe a prayer. It was said that the meaning is: so that I may mention you with praise in the highest place (*'Illiyyin*). On this view, the verbal noun may be read as attached to the subject or to the object.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ is a reason for what precedes of the command: that is, the Hour, which is the time of reckoning and punishment, is coming, so do good deeds, namely worship of Allah and prayer. The meaning of ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ is disputed. Al-Wahidi said: most exegetes said: "I conceal it from Myself," and this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Mubarrad and Qutrub said: this is according to the usage of the Arabs, who say, when they intensify concealing something, "I concealed it even from myself," meaning I did not reveal it to anyone. The meaning of the verse is that Allah intensified the concealment of the Hour, and so He expressed it in the most emphatic manner known to the Arabs.

It has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he read *akhfiha* with a *fath* on the *hamza*, meaning "I reveal it," and likewise Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from al-Kisa'i, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Wafa' ibn Iyas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Nahhas said: this narration has no chain other than this one. Al-Qurtubi said: Ibn al-Anbari also narrated it in his book *al-Radd*, saying: my father narrated to me, Muhammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us, al-Farra' narrated to us, al-Kisa'i narrated to us, and he mentioned it. Al-Nahhas said: a better chain than this is what Yahya al-Qattan narrated from al-Thawri, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he read *ukhfiha* with a *damma* on the *hamza*. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Farra' said: the meaning of the reading with a *fath* is "I almost reveal it," from *khafaytu al-shay'* when I revealed it, and *ukhfihi* (I conceal it). Al-Qurtubi said: some linguists have said it is permissible that *ukhfiha* with a *damma* on the *alif* means "I reveal it," because it is said *khafaytu al-shay'* and *akhfaytuhu*, from words of opposites (*huruf al-adda*), which occur in the sense of both concealing and revealing. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *khafaytu* and *akhfaytu* have the same meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: this is good, and al-Farra' and Sibawayh have recited what indicates that *akhfah* means "revealed," namely the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"If you conceal the disease, we shall not hide it, and if you stir up war, we shall not sit idle."*

That is: if you conceal the disease, we shall not reveal it. Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from Abu al-Khattab that it is with a *damma* on the *nun* in *nukhfih*, and said Imru' al-Qays said:

*"She concealed them from her emerging, as if what concealed them was the rain-drops of a clawed cloud."*

That is: she revealed them. Al-Nahhas rejected this view and said: the meaning is not "I reveal it," especially since *ukhfiha* is an irregular reading, so how could the correct and widespread reading be disregarded. Ibn al-Anbari said: there is another interpretation of the verse, namely that the speech stops at *akad* (I almost), and after it is an implied element: that is, "I almost bring it," and the beginning is with *ukhfiha* (I conceal it) so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives. Similar to this is the saying of 'Umayr ibn Dabi' al-Burjumi:

*"I resolved but did not do it, and I almost did, I wish I had left, over 'Uthman, his wives weeping."*

That is: "and I almost did." Al-Nahhas chose this view. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is from the category of negation (*salb*), not of opposites: the meaning of *ukhfiha* is "I remove its concealment from it," that is, its covering, and from this comes the expression *ashkaytuhu*, meaning I removed his complaint. Abu Hatim narrated from al-Akhfash that *akad* is superfluous for emphasis, and said: similar to it is His saying ﴿when he extends his hand, he can hardly see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. Similar is the saying of the poet:

*"Swift to battle, bearing his weapons, so that his foe can scarcely breathe."*

He said: the meaning of "I almost conceal it" is: I come close to that, because when you say "Zayd almost stood up," it is possible that he stood and possible that he did not stand. And it indicates that He concealed it by means of an indication other than this verse.

His saying ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ is connected either to *ati'ah* (coming) or to *ukhfiha* (I conceal it), and *ma* is a verbal particle: that is, so that every soul may be recompensed for its striving. Although *sa'y* (striving) is apparent in actions, here it includes both actions and abstentions, because it is certain that one who abandons what is obligatory upon him is punished for his abandonment and held accountable for it.

So let not one who does not believe in it, and who follows his own desire, turn you away from it, lest you perish. That is, let them not divert you from belief in the Hour and from affirming it, or from remembering it and being mindful of it, [as those who disbelieve do not believe in it]. Although this prohibition appears on its surface to be addressed to the disbeliever, in reality it is a prohibition addressed to him (ﷺ) against being diverted, or against displaying his religion before the disbelievers. It belongs to the same figure of speech as "Do not let me find you here," as is well known. It has been said that the pronoun in "from it" refers to the prayer, but this is far-fetched. His statement "and who follows his own desire" is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: the one who does not believe. "Who follows his own desire" means who follows his own whims, by immersing himself in sensual, transient pleasures. (p. 906) "Lest you perish" means lest you be ruined, because your being turned away from it by the disbelievers' obstruction of you necessarily entails ruin and follows from it.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) [said]: "When the revelation first came to him, he would stand on the balls of his feet when he prayed, so God revealed: ﴿Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched.﴾" Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, saying: They said, "This man has indeed become wretched with his Lord," so God revealed this verse. Ibn 'Asakir also reported from him, saying: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) rose in the night, he would tie himself with a rope so that he would not sleep, so God revealed this verse." Al-Bazzar reported from 'Ali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would shift his weight between his two feet, standing on each foot in turn, until this was revealed: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched.﴾" Al-Suyuti graded its chain as good (ḥasan). Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him something longer than this. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would sometimes recite the Qur'an while praying, standing on one foot, so God revealed: Ta-Ha, [We did not send down the Qur'an to you] by your two feet to make you wretched." Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him concerning His statement "Ta-Ha," that he said: "O man." Al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ta-Ha" in Nabataean (*al-Nabatiyya*, the language of the Nabataeans), meaning: "Tread, O man." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also, who said: "It is like the saying 'sit down' (*uq'ud*)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, who said: "Ta-Ha" in Nabataean means "O man." Ibn Jarir reported from him, who said: "Ta-Ha" means "O man" in Syriac (*al-Suryaniyya*). Al-Hakim reported from him also, who said: "Ta-Ha is like your saying 'O Muhammad' in the language of Abyssinia." There is disagreement and contradiction in these reports from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have ten names with my Lord." Abu al-Tufayl said: "I memorised eight of them: Muhammad, Ahmad, Abu al-Qasim, al-Fatih, al-Khatim, al-Mahi, al-'Aqib, and al-Hashir." Sayf claimed that Abu Ja'far told him: "The two remaining names are Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin." Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched.﴾ He said: "O man, We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you wretched." He used to stand the night on his two feet. It is a dialect of the tribe of 'Akk: if you say to an 'Akkī, "O man," he does not turn; but when you say "Ta-Ha," he turns to you.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ta-Ha is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of His names."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His statement: ﴿And what is beneath the soil (al-thara)﴾, that he said: "Al-thara is everything that is moist." Abu Ya'la reported from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked, "What is beneath this earth?" He said, "Water." It was said, "What is beneath the water?" He said, "Darkness." It was said, "What is beneath the darkness?" He said, "Air." It was said, "What is beneath the air?" He said, "The soil (al-thara)." It was said, "What is beneath the soil?" He said, "The knowledge of created beings ends at the knowledge of the Creator." Ibn Mardawayh reported something similar from him, but longer.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden﴾, that he said: "The secret (al-sirr) is what the son of Adam conceals within himself, and what is more hidden is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he will do before he knows it. He knows all of that, what has passed of it and what remains. His knowledge is one, and all creatures before Him are like a single soul, as in His statement: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28]." Al-Hakim reported from him in this verse, and graded it authentic (*sahih*), that he said: "The secret is what you yourself know, and what is more hidden is what God casts into your heart of what you do not know." 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi reported it with the wording: "He knows what you conceal in yourself, and He knows what you will do tomorrow." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿Or I may find at the fire a guidance (huda)﴾, that he said: "Someone who will point out the way."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ali concerning His statement: ﴿Take off your two sandals﴾, that he said: "They were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so it was said to him, 'Take them off.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿You are in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾, that he said: "Al-Mubarak said: Tuwa is the name of the valley." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him: "In the sacred valley, Tuwa," meaning the holy land, because he passed through its valley by night and folded it up (*tawa*). It is said: "I folded the valley of such-and-such." Ibn Jarir also reported from him concerning His statement, "Tuwa," that he said: "Tread the valley."

In the two *Sahihs* and elsewhere, from the hadith of Anas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If one of you sleeps through the prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God said: ﴿Establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾" Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God said: ﴿Establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾" Ibn Shihab used to recite it as *lidhikrā* (for the remembrance).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾, that he said: "I do not reveal it to anyone other than Myself." Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I almost conceal it from myself."

(p-٩٠٣)

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan by the consensus of all. Al-Nahhas and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat Ta-Ha was revealed in Mecca." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Darimi, Ibn Khuzayma in *al-Tawhid*, al-'Uqayli in *al-Du'afa'*, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an, they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will be sent down; blessed are the bodies that will carry this; blessed are the tongues that will speak this.'"

Ibn Khuzayma said after narrating it: "It is a *gharib* (unusual, single-channel) hadith, and there is a *nakarah* (irregularity) in it. Ibrahim ibn Muhajir and his teacher have been spoken of," meaning Ibrahim ibn Muhajir ibn Sammar and his teacher 'Umar ibn Hafs ibn Dhakwan, and both are among the transmitters of its chain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which al-An'am is mentioned from the First Reminder (*al-Dhikr al-Awwal*). I was given Surat Ta-Ha and the surahs beginning with *ta-sin* from the tablets of Musa. I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the closings of al-Baqarah from beneath the Throne. I was given al-Mufassal as a supererogatory gift."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every Qur'an will be taken away from the people of Paradise, so they will recite nothing from it except Surat Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin, for they will recite these two in Paradise."

Al-Daraqutni in his *Sunan* narrated from Anas ibn Malik, mentioning the story of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with his sister and Khabbab, and their recitation of Ta-Ha, and that this was the cause of 'Umar's Islam. The story is well known in the books of biography (*al-siyar*).

(p-٩٠٣)
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Ta-Ha﴾ ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed﴾ ﴿but only as a reminder for one who fears﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful settled upon the Throne﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is even more hidden﴾ ﴿Allah — there is no god but Him; His are the most beautiful names﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Musa?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Wait, I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance"﴾ ﴿When he came to it, he was called: "O Musa! ﴿I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire divert you from it, lest you perish﴾.

As for His saying *Ta-Ha*: Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with *imalah* (inclining the vowel toward *i*) of the *ha'* and with a *fath* (open vowel) on the *ta'*. Abu Bakr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash inclined both. Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' read them between the two pronunciations, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read with *tafkhim* (full, emphatic pronunciation). Al-Tha'labi said: "All of them are correct and eloquent dialects." Al-Nahhas said: "There is no basis for *imalah* according to most of the grammarians, for two reasons. The first is that there is no *ya'* or *kasrah* here that would justify *imalah*. The second is that the *ta'* is one of the blockers of *imalah*."

The scholars differed about the meaning of this word, in several opinions:

The first: it is among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses) whose meaning is not understood.

The second: it means "O man" (*ya rajul*) in the dialect of 'Ukl and in the dialect of 'Akk. Al-Kalbi said: "If I said to a man from 'Akk, 'O man!' he would not answer until you said *Ta-Ha*." Ibn Jarir recited in this regard:

*I called "Ta-Ha" in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he was turning away from me.*

Another version reads "*muzayilan*" (departing) instead of "*mu'wilan*" (fleeing). It is also said that in the dialect of 'Akk it means "O my beloved." Qutrub said: "It is likewise in the dialect of Tayy, meaning 'O man.'" So said al-Hasan and 'Ikrima. It is also said that it is so in the Syriac language, related by al-Mahdawi. Ibn Jarir related that it is so in the Nabataean language, and al-Sudi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. Al-Tha'labi related from 'Ikrima that it is so in the Abyssinian language, narrating it from 'Ikrima. There is no obstacle to this word being established with that meaning in all of these languages, if the transmission is sound.

The third opinion: it is a name of Allah, glorified is He.

The fourth opinion: it is a name of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fifth opinion: it is a name of the surah.

The sixth opinion: it is disjointed letters (*huruf muqatta'ah*), each of which indicates a meaning. Then they differed about the meanings these letters indicate, in several opinions, all of which are forced and strained.

The seventh opinion: its meaning is "Blessed is the one who is guided."

The eighth opinion: its meaning is: "Tread the earth, O Muhammad." Ibn al-Anbari said: "That is because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to bear the hardship of prayer until his feet nearly swelled, and he needed to rest. So it was said to him, 'Tread the earth,' meaning: do not exhaust yourself until you need to rest."

Al-Qadi 'Iyad related in *al-Shifa'* from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he stood on one foot and raised the other," so Allah revealed *Ta-Ha*, meaning: "Tread the earth, O Muhammad." It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he read *Taha* on the pattern of *da'* (an imperative meaning "leave"), meaning an imperative to tread, and the original was *ta'* (tread), so the *hamzah* was changed to *ha'*.

Al-Wahidi related from most of the exegetes that this word means "O man," intending the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "This is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of 'Ata', and of al-Kalbi, except that some of them say it is in the language of Abyssinia, Nabataea and Syriac, and al-Kalbi says it is in the dialect of 'Akk." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The dialect of Quraysh agreed with that dialect in this meaning, because Allah, glorified is He, did not address His Prophet in the language of other than Quraysh." End of quotation.

Once it is established that it has this meaning in one of the dialects of the Arabs, it is clear in meaning and evident in indication, and is outside the openings of the surahs, whose status as *mutashabih* we have already explained at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The same applies if it has this meaning in one of the non-Arabic languages and the Arabs used it in their speech with that meaning, like the other foreign words that the Arabs used and that are found in the Noble Book; through that usage they became part of the language of the Arabs.

As for the clause *"We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed,"* it is a new sentence (*mustanifah*) brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the hardship he suffered from the polytheists. *Shaqa'* (distress) comes in the sense of hardship. Ibn Kaysan said: "The root meaning of *shaqa'* in the language is hardship and fatigue," and from it is the poet's saying:

*The man of intellect suffers in comfort because of his intellect, while the ignorant one in misery enjoys ease.*

The meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be exhausted by excessive grief over them and their disbelief, and by your anguish that they should believe." It is like His saying, glorified is He: *"Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief"* [al-Kahf: 6]. Al-Nahhas said: "Some grammarians say the *lam* in *li-tashqa* is the *lam* of negation, and some say it is the *lam* of denial (*juhud*)." Ibn Kaysan said: "It is the *lam* of genitive (*khafd*)." This explanation of the verse is according to the view of those who say that *Ta-Ha*, like the other openings of surahs, is a listing of the names of letters. If it is made the name of the surah, then His saying *"We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed"* is a predicate about it, it being in the position of the subject. As for the view of those who say its meaning is "O man," or in the sense of commanding treading the earth, the sentence is new, to turn the Prophet (ﷺ) away from what he was doing of excessive worship.

The accusative of *illa tadhkiratan* (but as a reminder) is as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for *anzalna* (We sent down), like your saying: "I did not strike you for discipline, except out of compassion for you." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is a substitute (*badal*) for *li-tashqa*, meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected this, on the grounds that a reminder is not distress. He said: "It is rather in the accusative of verbal noun (*masdariyyah*): meaning, We sent it down so that you would remind by it a reminder; or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: *We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would be distressed* by it; We sent it down only for reminder."

The accusative of *tanzilan mimman khalaqa al-ard wa al-samawat al-'ula* (a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens) is as a verbal noun: meaning, We sent it down as a revelation. It is also said: it is a substitute for *tadhkiratan* (reminder). It is also said: it is in the accusative of praise. It is also said: it is governed by *yakhsha* (fears), meaning: he fears a revelation from Allah, as its object. It is also said: it is in the accusative of state (*hal*), by interpreting it as an active participle. Abu Haywa al-Shami read *tanzilun* (with *raf'*, nominative) on the meaning "this is a revelation." *Mimman khalaqa* (from the One who created) is attached to *tanzilan*, or to an omitted element that is an attribute of it. The specifying of the creation of the earth and the heavens is because they are the greatest of the created things that the servants observe, Mighty and Majestic is He. *Al-'ula* is the plural of *al-'ulya*, meaning the elevated, like the plural of *kubra* and *sughra* as *kubar* and *sughar*. The meaning of the verse is to inform the servants of the perfection of His greatness, glorified is He, and the magnificence of His majesty.

The nominative of *al-Rahman* (The Most Merciful) is as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Akhfash said. It may also be nominative as an object of praise, or as an inceptive subject. It has been read in the genitive; al-Zajjaj said it is a substitute of *mimman* (from the One who). Al-Nahhas allowed that it may be nominative as a substitute of the pronoun in *khalaqa*. The clause *'ala al-'arshi istawa* (settled upon the Throne) is in the position of nominative, as a predicate of an omitted subject, or as the predicate of *al-Rahman* according to whoever makes it a subject.

Ahmad ibn Yahya said: Tha'lab said: "*Al-istiwa'*" means turning toward something. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said the same. It is also said that it is a metaphor for kingship and dominion. The investigation of the verification of this is lengthy, and the discussion of it has already been presented in *al-A'raf*. What Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari held is that He, glorified is He, is settled upon His Throne without limit and without modality, and before him the great majority of the pious early generations held this view, those who transmit the attributes as they came, without distortion and without interpretation.

*"To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"*: that is, He is the owner of everything and its governor, and of what is between them of existing things, and what is beneath the soil. *Al-thara* (soil) in the language is moist dust. That is, whatever is beneath the dust of anything. Al-Wahidi said: "The exegetes say that He, glorified is He, intended the soil beneath the rock on which the bull stands, which is beneath the earth, and none knows what is beneath the soil except Allah, glorified is He."

*"And if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is more hidden"*: *al-jahr bi-al-qawl* (speaking aloud) is raising the voice with it. *Al-sirr* (the secret) is what a person tells another and confides to him. *Al-akhfa* (what is more hidden than the secret) is what a person speaks to himself and what occurs to his mind.

The meaning is: If you speak aloud in the remembrance and supplication of Allah, know that He is free of need of that, for He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, so there is no need for you to speak aloud. In this there is a sense of prohibiting loud speech, like His saying, glorified is He: *"And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear"* [al-A'raf: 205]. It is also said: *al-sirr* is what a person conceals within himself, and *al-akhfa* than it is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he himself does while not knowing it. It is also said: *al-sirr* is what a person harbors in his soul, and *al-akhfa* than it is what has not yet happened and no one has harbored. It is also said: *al-sirr* is the secret of created beings, and *al-akhfa* than it is the secret of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ibn Jarir denied this and said: "*Al-akhfa* is what is not in the secret of the human being but will be in his soul."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 1–16 (part 2 of 3):

Then He mentioned that the one worshipped in the manner stated is Allah, glorified is He, who is exalted above any partner and who deserves to be named by the Most Beautiful Names. So He said: ﴿Allah! There is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾ Here, *Allah* is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject), meaning: the One described with these perfect attributes is Allah. The clause ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining that divinity belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He; that is, there is no god in existence except Him. Likewise, the clause ﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ explains His entitlement to the Most Beautiful Names, which are the ninety-nine mentioned in the authentic hadith.

Their explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180] in Surah al-A'raf. *Al-husna* is the feminine form of *al-ahsan* (the most beautiful). *Al-asma'* (the names) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *al-husna* is its predicate. It is permissible for *Allah* to be the subject with the sentence following it as its predicate, and it is also permissible for it to be an apposition (*badal*) to the pronoun in *ya'lamu* (He knows).

Then the Exalted set forth the matter of Divine Oneness by mentioning the story of Musa, which contains manifest power and a strange account. So He said: ﴿And has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ The interrogative is for confirmation (*taqrir*), and its meaning is: has not the story of Musa already reached you? It was said its meaning is: the story of Musa has indeed reached you. Al-Kalbi said: the story of Musa had not reached him at that time.

Within the context of this story is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he encounters of the hardships of the duties of prophethood, the bearing of its burdens, and the enduring of its calamities, and that this is the way of the prophets before him. The meaning of *al-hadith* (the story) here is the account of what happened to Musa. ﴿When he saw a fire﴾ is an adverbial clause of time (*zarf*) related to *al-hadith*. It was said that its governing element is an implied verb: that is, "Mention," and it was said that it is implied afterward: that is, when he saw a fire, such-and-such happened. His seeing the fire took place on a dark night when he set out traveling to his mother after asking permission from Shu'ayb. ﴿When he saw it, he said to his family, "Stay here.">﴾ The word *ahl* (family) here refers to his wife, and the plural form is used either because the word *ahl* is in the plural sense or for emphasis. It was said that it refers to the wife, the child, and the servant. The meaning of *imkuthu* (stay here) is: remain in your place. He used the word *mukth* (staying) rather than *iqamah* (residing), because *iqamah* implies permanence, whereas *mukth* does not.

Hamzah read ﴿li-ahlihi﴾ with a *damma* on the *ha'* (*li-ahlihi*), and likewise in Surah al-Qasas. Al-Nahhas said: this is according to the dialect of those who say *marartu bihu ya rajul* (I passed by him, O man), so he kept it in its original form, and that is permissible. However, Hamzah differed from his usual practice in these two places only.
