He said: ﴿Throw it down, O Musa.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nafa), an answer to an implied question. God commanded him to throw it so that He might show him the manifest miracle He had given him in it.

﴿So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly.﴾ This was by God, glory be to Him, transforming its attributes and accidents until it became a serpent that moves: i.e., walks quickly and nimbly. It was said: it had been a staff with two branches, and the two branches became a mouth, while the rest of it was the body of a serpent that moved from place to place, swallowing stones despite its great bulk and frightful appearance. When he saw it like that, he was frightened, alarmed, and turned away fleeing without looking back.

At that point God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Take hold of it and do not fear; We shall return it to its former state.﴾ Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said: the estimated reading is "ila sirataha," like "wa-ikhtara Musa qawmahu" (al-A'raf 155). He said: it may also be a verbal noun (masdar), since the meaning of "sanu'idu-ha" is "sanusayyiru-ha" (We shall make it move). It may also be a masdar with the meaning of an active participle, i.e., "sa'ira" (going), or with the meaning of a passive participle, i.e., "musayyara" (made to move).

The meaning is: We shall return it, after you have taken it, to its first state, which is staffhood. It was said that when he was told "do not fear," he reached such a degree of fearlessness that he would put his hand into its mouth and take hold of its jaw.

﴿And draw your hand to your side (janah)﴾. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: a person's janah is his upper arm (adud). Qutrub said: a person's janah is his side, and the side is expressed by "janah" because it is in the place of the wing. It was also said: "ila" here means "ma'a" (with), i.e., "with your side." The answer to the command is "it will come out white" (takhruj bayda'), i.e., your hand will come out white. The place of "min ghayri su'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: i.e., being without defect; "su'" means fault, and it is used euphemistically to refer to leprosy: i.e., it will come out white, its light shining, illuminating by night and day like the light of the sun, without leprosy. The accusative of "ayatan ukhra" is also a circumstantial clause: i.e., a miracle other than the staff.

Al-Akhfash said: "ayatan" is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) of "bayda'." Al-Nahhas said: this is a good opinion. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "We have given you," or "We shall give you, an ayah other," because when He said "it will come out white," this indicated that He had already given him another sign.

Then God explained this by His saying: ﴿So that We may show you of Our greatest signs.﴾ It was said that the estimated reading is: "We did that so that We might show you." "Min ayatina" is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause, and "al-kubra" means "the greatest," an attribute of an omitted noun. The estimated reading is: "so that We may show you of Our greatest signs," i.e., so that with these two signs, the hand and the staff, We may show you some of Our greatest signs. It does not follow that the hand alone is the greatest sign, so that it would be greater than the staff. This is refuted by the fact that the hand only had a change of colour, whereas the staff, along with the change in colour, had an increase in size, the creation of life, and the power over extraordinary matters.

Al-Nakha'i read "ahussu" with an unpointed sin, meaning driving the sheep; likewise Ikrima read it. It may also be a masdar with the meaning of an active participle, i.e., "sa'ira" (going), or with the meaning of a passive participle, i.e., "musayyara" (made to move).

The meaning is: We shall return it, after you have taken it, to its first state, which is staffhood. It was said that when he was told "do not fear," he reached such a degree of fearlessness that he would put his hand into its mouth and take hold of its jaw.

Qutrub said: a person's janah is his side, and the side is expressed by "janah" because it is in the place of the wing. It was also said: "ila" here means "ma'a" (with), i.e., "with your side." The answer to the command is "it will come out white" (takhruj bayda'), i.e., your hand will come out white. The place of "min ghayri su'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: i.e., being without defect; "su'" means fault, and it is used euphemistically to refer to leprosy: i.e., it will come out white, its light shining, illuminating by night and day like the light of the sun, without leprosy. Al-Nahhas said: they made the two verbs in the place of jazm as answers to his saying "aj'al li wazIran." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the ya' of "akhi" with a fatha.

﴿That we may glorify You much﴾ and ﴿remember You much﴾: this glorification and remembrance are the goal of the preceding supplication. The glorification here is intended by the tongue; it was said it refers to prayer. The accusative of "kathiran" in both places is as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, or of an omitted time.

﴿Indeed, You have always been of us Seeing﴾. "Al-Basir" means the one who sees, and "al-Basir" also means the one who knows hidden matters; this is intended here: i.e., indeed You have been knowing of us in our childhood, so You did good to us, so do good to us likewise now.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the staff of Musa that he said: an angel of the angels gave it to him when he set out for Madyan; it used to shine for him at night, and when he struck the earth with it, it brought forth vegetation for him, and he would beat the leaves of the tree with it for his sheep.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ikrima concerning His saying "and I beat down with it for my sheep" that he said: "I strike the tree with it so that its leaves fall upon my sheep." Something similar has been reported from a group of the early generation (salaf). Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported concerning His saying "and I have other uses for it" that he said: "needs." Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid something similar. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi something similar. He also reported from Qatada who said: it used to shine for him at night, and it was the staff of Adam, peace be upon him. He also reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly" that he said: it had not been a serpent before that; it passed by a tree and ate it, and passed by a rock and swallowed it, so Musa heard the sound of the rock within its belly, and he turned away fleeing. He was called: "O Musa, take it," but he did not take it. Then he was called a second time: "Take it and do not fear," and in the third time it was said to him: "You are among those secure," and so he took it. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning "We shall return it to its former state" that he said: its former condition. They also reported from him concerning "without defect" that he said: "without leprosy." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother﴾ that he said: he was older than Musa. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿and make him a partner in my affair﴾ that he said: "Make Harun a prophet at that time, when Musa was made a prophet."

When Moses asked his Lord, glory be to Him, to expand his breast, ease his task, untie the knot from his tongue, and appoint for him a minister from his family, Allah, glory be to Him, informed him that He had answered that supplication. So He said: ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾, meaning you have been given what you asked for. The "request that is requested" (al-su'l al-mas'ul) means the thing sought, as in your saying "khabar" for "makhbur" (the thing told). The phrase "O Moses" is added to honour him with direct address, and also to observe the rhyme endings (fawasil, the verse-final rhyme pattern).

The sentence ﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) intended to strengthen Moses' heart by reminding him of Allah's blessings upon him. "Mann" means kindness and bounty. The meaning is: We were gracious to you at another time before this time, namely Allah's protection of him from the harm of his enemies, as He explains here. "Ukhra" is the feminine form of "akhar," meaning "other."

﴿When We inspired your mother with what was inspired﴾: "idh" is a zarf (adverbial complement) for the inspiration, meaning We bestowed that favour at the time of the inspiration. The inspiration to her may be mere inspiration (ilham) into her heart, or a dream in which she was shown this, or through a prophet, or through an angel, but not in the manner of prophethood, as with the revelation to Mary. Or it may be that the news was conveyed through earlier prophets and reached her. "What was inspired" refers to what would come to her regarding the matter. He first left it vague and then explained it, to magnify its importance.

﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ explains the inspiration, since revelation has the sense of speech. Alternatively, the "an" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the sense "that cast him." "Qadhf" here means throwing, i.e., throw him into the chest. The meaning of "chest" (al-tabut) was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah in the story of Talut. ﴿Then cast him into the sea﴾ means throw him into the river. "Yamm" means the sea or a large river.

Al-Farra' said: this is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: "Cast him, and the sea will cast him onto the shore." The command addressed to the sea is based on treating it as one who understands and discerns, since its casting him onto the shore was a matter bound to happen. The "sahil" is the shore of the sea. It was named sahil because the water wore it away (sahalahu), as said by Ibn Duraid. What is meant here is the part of the sea adjacent to the shore, not the shore itself. All these pronouns refer to Moses, not to the chest, even though the chest was cast along with him, because the intended subject is Moses, and the pronouns before and after this refer to him.

﴿Let him be taken by an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ is the response to the command to cast. The "enemy" is Pharaoh. When his mother cast him into the sea, which is the well-known Nile, a branch flowed from it to Pharaoh's house. Allah carried him along that branch to Pharaoh's house, where he took the chest and found Moses inside it. It was also said that the sea cast him onto the shore, Pharaoh saw him, and ordered someone to take him. And it was said that Pharaoh's daughter found him. The first view is preferable.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ means Allah cast upon Moses a love originating from Him, which He placed in the hearts of His servants, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. It was also said that He placed upon him a radiance of beauty, so that no one among the people who saw him failed to love him.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "I cast My mercy upon you." It was also said that the word "min" (from) is connected to "alqaytu" (I cast), so the meaning is: I cast love from Me upon you, i.e., I loved you, and whom Allah loves, people love.

﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾: i.e., that you be nurtured and fed in My sight. One says "sana'a al-rajul jariyatahu" when he raised his slave-girl, and "sana'a farasahu" when he persisted in feeding his horse and tending to it. The interpretation of "under My eye" as "in My sight" is correct. Al-Nahhas said: this is known in the language, but there is no specialisation of Moses in this, since all things are in Allah's sight. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said the meaning is: to be nourished according to My love and My will. One says "I take the things under my eye," meaning according to my love. Ibn al-Anbari said: the "eye" in this verse is intended to express the sense of intention and choice, from the Arab saying "so-and-so went on my eye," i.e., with my love. It was said the lam (that) is connected to an omitted element: "I did that so that you might be raised." It was also said it is connected to "alqaytu," and it was said to be connected to what follows: "and that you might be raised under My eye, when your sister walked." Ibn al-Qa'qa' read ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ with the lam sukun as an imperative, and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning: that your movement and conduct be by My will, and under My watchful eye.

﴿When your sister walked﴾ is a zarf complement, connected either to "alqaytu" or to "litusna'a." It may also be a badal (substitute) for "idh awhayna" (when We inspired). His sister's name was Maryam, and she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?﴾ That is, she went out seeking news of him and found Pharaoh and his wife Asiya looking for a wet-nurse for him. So she said this to them: "Shall I direct you to someone who will take him into her care and raise him?" They said: "And who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "Yes, the milk of my brother Harun." Harun was a year older than Moses, and it was also said he was more than a year older. So the mother came, and he accepted her breast, for he would not accept the breast of any other nurse. This is the meaning of ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾. In the codex of Ubayy it is "fa-radadnaka." The fa in "fa-radadnaka" is a fa of elucidation (fasiha). ﴿That her eye may be cooled﴾: Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of 'Abd al-Hamid, read "kay taqirra" with a kasra on the qaf, and the rest read it with a fatha.

Al-Jawhari said: "qarartu bihi 'aynan qurratan wa-qururan," and a man is "qarir al-'ayn." "Qarrat 'aynuhu" (his eye was cooled) yaqarru and yaqirru, the opposite of "sakhinat" (it became hot). The meaning of "the coolness of the eye" is joy at her child's return to her, after she had cast him into the sea and his separation had weighed heavily upon her. ﴿And that she may not grieve﴾: i.e., there should not occur to her, for any reason, grief that would disturb that joy. If he had meant grief from the cause whose removal cooled her eye, he would have placed the negation of grief before the coolness of the eye. Therefore this negation of grief is taken to refer to grief arising from a cause that happens afterwards. It may be said that since the waw (and) is for mere conjunction, this interpretation is not obligatory. It was also said the meaning is: "and do not grieve, you, O Moses, over her loss of compassion," but this is a strained interpretation.

﴿And you killed a soul﴾: the "soul" here is the soul of the Copt whom Moses struck, and it was an accidental killing. ﴿Then We delivered you from distress﴾: the distress that resulted from that killing, namely the fear of punishment, whether in the Hereafter, in this world, or both. It was said that "ghamm" (distress) means killing in the dialect of Quraysh, and how far removed this is!

﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾: "fitna" can mean a trial, an affliction, a difficult matter, or whatever a person is tested with. "Futun" may be a verbal noun like "thubur," "shukur," and "kufur," meaning: We tested you with a test and examined you with an examination. It may also be the plural of "fitna," with the feminine ta' disregarded, like "hujur" for "hujra" and "budur" for "badra." Its meaning would then be: We delivered you time after time from the trials you had fallen into, mentioned earlier, before Allah chose him for His message. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning his deliverance from the distress of that cause, and his deliverance from the trials, is to bestow favour upon him through what Allah had done for him, and to strengthen his heart for what would befall him with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel.

﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾. Al-Farra' said: the implied meaning of the sentence is, "We tested you with a testing, so you went out to the people of Madyan and stayed for years there." Such omission is common in the revelation, as it is in Arabic speech, since they omit much when the meaning is known. Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb, eight stages from Egypt. Moses fled there and remained ten years, and this is the fuller of the two terms. It was also said he stayed with Shu'ayb twenty-eight years, of which ten were the bride-price for his wife, Shu'ayb's daughter, and eighteen years he remained with him until a child was born to him. The fa in ﴿then you stayed﴾ indicates that the trials mentioned are those that came before his stay among the people of Madyan.

﴿Then you came upon a destiny, O Moses﴾: i.e., at a time that had preceded in My decree and destiny, that I would speak to you and make you a prophet. Or it means at an appointed measure of time at which revelation comes to the prophets, which is the beginning of forty years. Or it means at an appointment you knew about through Shu'ayb's informing you of it.

The poet said:
He attained the caliphate, for it was a destiny for him,
as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed destiny.

The word "thumma" (then), which indicates a lapse of time, is used to show that his coming was after a period, because of what happened to him, such as losing his way, his flock scattering, and similar things.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾. "Istina'a" means taking something as one's craft (sun'a), and sun'a is the good that one bestows upon a person. The meaning is: I chose you for My revelation and My message, so that you would act according to My will. Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is, "I chose you to establish My proof and made you between Me and My creation, so that by conveying from Me you would occupy the position I would occupy were I to address them and argue with them myself." It was also said this is an image of the great honour Allah bestowed upon him, by bringing him near as a king brings near one of his special intimates.

﴿Go, you and your brother﴾: i.e., let your brother also go. This is a resumed statement, brought to explain the purpose of the choosing. ﴿With My signs﴾ means with My miracles, which I made a sign for you, namely the nine signs. ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾: i.e., do not become weak or relax. One says "wana yuni wanyan" when he became weak.

The poet said:
Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him
what passed and what remains.

Imru' al-Qays said:
He roams, when the swift horses in their slackness
raise dust in al-Kadid al-Mu'akkal.

Al-Farra' said: "fi dhikri" and "'an dhikri" are the same. The meaning is: do not fall short in remembering Me by doing good to you both and bestowing blessings upon you both, for remembering a blessing is giving thanks for it. It was also said the meaning of "la tanya" is: do not delay in conveying the message. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿la tahina fi dhikri﴾ (do not weaken in remembering Me).

﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. This is a command to both of them to go together. Moses is present and Harun is absent, and Moses is given precedence (taghlib), because he is the fundamental one in delivering the message. The reason given for going is ﴿he has transgressed﴾, i.e., he exceeded the limit in disbelief and rebellion. Earlier, He had singled out Moses alone for the command to go, and here He joined them, in order to honour Moses by singling him out, and to emphasise the command to go by repetition. It was said that in this there is evidence that the going of one of them alone is not sufficient. It was also said the first is a command to Moses to go to all the people, and the second is a command to both of them to go to Pharaoh.

Then Allah commanded them to speak to him gently, because of its effect on his acceptance, for harshness at the outset is among the greatest causes of aversion and obstinacy in disbelief. "Gentle speech" (al-qawl al-layyin) is speech in which there is no harshness, and one says "layyin" (gentle) for something that is soft. The meaning is to leave the harshness aside for the sake of admonition, like their saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ (79:18). It was said that gentle speech means addressing him by his kunya (teknonym). It was also said it means promising him the pleasures of this world if he responds.

Then He gave the reason for the command to speak gently to him: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾, i.e., engage with him in the manner of one who hopes and aspires. So the hope is attributed to both of them, as a group of grammarians said, including Sibawayh and others. Its detailed investigation has been mentioned in more than one place. Al-Zajjaj said: "la'alla" (perhaps) is a word of expectation and hope, and He addressed them in terms they understand. It was also said that "la'alla" here has the sense of a question: "Look and see whether he is reminded or fears." And it was said it has the sense of "kay" (so that).

"Reminded" means considering what they conveyed of the reminder and reflecting deeply upon it, so that this becomes a cause of acceptance. "Fear" is fear of the punishment of Allah that was promised through their two tongues. The word "aw" (or) is used to prevent the absence of both, not to combine them.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿Cast him into the river﴾, that he said: "It is the Nile."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾, that he said: "Everyone who saw him had love for him placed upon them from Him."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: "I made you beloved to My servants."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Imran al-Jawni, regarding His saying ﴿And that you may be reared under My eye﴾, that he said: "You are nurtured under the eye of Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse, that he said: "So that you may be nourished under My eye."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij regarding the verse, that he said: "He says: 'You are under My eye when your mother placed you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walked [after you].'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib reported from Ibn Umar: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Musa only killed the man who was from the people of Pharaoh by mistake.'" Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress﴾, he said: "From the killing of the soul." And ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, he said: "We purified you with purification."

Said ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, that he said: "We tested you with a test."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: "We examined you with an examination."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas a lengthy athar (report) in explanation of the verse. Whoever wishes to take it in full, let him consult it in the book of tafsir (commentary on the Qur'an) in al-Nasa'i's Sunan.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Then you came upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed time."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid and Qatadah regarding ﴿upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed date."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and do not slacken﴾, that he said: "Do not be slow."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali regarding His saying ﴿a gentle word﴾, that he said: "Kunnah him" (i.e., address him by a kunya).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They addressed him by his kunya."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding His saying ﴿perhaps he may remember or fear﴾, that he said: "Will he remember?"

﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾. Al-Farra' said: the implied meaning of the sentence is, "We tested you with a testing, so you went out to the people of Madyan and stayed for years there." Such omission is common in the revelation, as it is in Arabic speech, since they omit much when the meaning is known. Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb, eight stages from Egypt. Moses fled there and remained ten years, and this is the fuller of the two terms. It was also said he stayed with Shu'ayb twenty-eight years, of which ten were the bride-price for his wife, Shu'ayb's daughter, and eighteen years he remained with him until a child was born to him. The fa in ﴿then you stayed﴾ indicates that the trials mentioned are those that came before his stay among the people of Madyan.

﴿Then you came upon a destiny, O Moses﴾: i.e., at a time that had preceded in My decree and destiny, that I would speak to you and make you a prophet. Or it means at an appointed measure of time at which revelation comes to the prophets, which is the beginning of forty years. Or it means at an appointment you knew about through Shu'ayb's informing you of it.

The poet said:
He attained the caliphate, for it was a destiny for him,
as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed destiny.

The word "thumma" (then), which indicates a lapse of time, is used to show that his coming was after a period, because of what happened to him, such as losing his way, his flock scattering, and similar things.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾. "Istina'a" means taking something as one's craft (sun'a), and sun'a is the good that one bestows upon a person. The meaning is: I chose you for My revelation and My message, so that you would act according to My will. Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is, "I chose you to establish My proof and made you between Me and My creation, so that by conveying from Me you would occupy the position I would occupy were I to address them and argue with them myself." It was also said this is an image of the great honour Allah bestowed upon him, by bringing him near as a king brings near one of his special intimates.

﴿Go, you and your brother﴾: i.e., let your brother also go. This is a resumed statement, brought to explain the purpose of the choosing. ﴿With My signs﴾ means with My miracles, which I made a sign for you, namely the nine signs. ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾: i.e., do not become weak or relax. One says "wana yuni wanyan" when he became weak.

The poet said:
Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him
what passed and what remains.

Imru' al-Qays said:
He roams, when the swift horses in their slackness
raise dust in al-Kadid al-Mu'akkal.

Al-Farra' said: "fi dhikri" and "'an dhikri" are the same. The meaning is: do not fall short in remembering Me by doing good to you both and bestowing blessings upon you both, for remembering a blessing is giving thanks for it. It was also said the meaning of "la tanya" is: do not delay in conveying the message. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿la tahina fi dhikri﴾ (do not weaken in remembering Me).

﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. This is a command to both of them to go together. Moses is present and Harun is absent, and Moses is given precedence (taghlib), because he is the fundamental one in delivering the message. The reason given for going is ﴿he has transgressed﴾, i.e., he exceeded the limit in disbelief and rebellion. Earlier, He had singled out Moses alone for the command to go, and here He joined them, in order to honour Moses by singling him out, and to emphasise the command to go by repetition. It was said that in this there is evidence that the going of one of them alone is not sufficient. It was also said the first is a command to Moses to go to all the people, and the second is a command to both of them to go to Pharaoh.

Then Allah commanded them to speak to him gently, because of its effect on his acceptance, for harshness at the outset is among the greatest causes of aversion and obstinacy in disbelief. "Gentle speech" (al-qawl al-layyin) is speech in which there is no harshness, and one says "layyin" (gentle) for something that is soft. The meaning is to leave the harshness aside for the sake of admonition, like their saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ (79:18). It was said that gentle speech means addressing him by his kunya (teknonym). It was also said it means promising him the pleasures of this world if he responds.

Then He gave the reason for the command to speak gently to him: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾, i.e., engage with him in the manner of one who hopes and aspires. So the hope is attributed to both of them, as a group of grammarians said, including Sibawayh and others. Its detailed investigation has been mentioned in more than one place. Al-Zajjaj said: "la'alla" (perhaps) is a word of expectation and hope, and He addressed them in terms they understand. It was also said that "la'alla" here has the sense of a question: "Look and see whether he is reminded or fears." And it was said it has the sense of "kay" (so that).

"Reminded" means considering what they conveyed of the reminder and reflecting deeply upon it, so that this becomes a cause of acceptance. "Fear" is fear of the punishment of Allah that was promised through their two tongues. The word "aw" (or) is used to prevent the absence of both, not to combine them.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿Cast him into the river﴾, that he said: "It is the Nile."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾, that he said: "Everyone who saw him had love for him placed upon them from Him."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: "I made you beloved to My servants."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Imran al-Jawni, regarding His saying ﴿And that you may be reared under My eye﴾, that he said: "You are nurtured under the eye of Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse, that he said: "So that you may be nourished under My eye."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij regarding the verse, that he said: "He says: 'You are under My eye when your mother placed you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walked [after you].'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib reported from Ibn Umar: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Musa only killed the man who was from the people of Pharaoh by mistake.'" Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress﴾, he said: "From the killing of the soul." And ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, he said: "We purified you with purification."

Said ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, that he said: "We tested you with a test."

When Moses asked his Lord, glory be to Him, to expand his breast, ease his task, untie the knot from his tongue, and appoint for him a minister from his family, Allah, glory be to Him, informed him that He had answered that supplication. So He said: ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾, meaning you have been given what you asked for. The "request that is requested" (al-su'l al-mas'ul) means the thing sought, as in your saying "khabar" for "makhbur" (the thing told). The phrase "O Moses" is added to honour him with direct address, and also to observe the rhyme endings (fawasil, the verse-final rhyme pattern).

The sentence ﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) intended to strengthen Moses' heart by reminding him of Allah's blessings upon him. "Mann" means kindness and bounty. The meaning is: We were gracious to you at another time before this time, namely Allah's protection of him from the harm of his enemies, as He explains here. "Ukhra" is the feminine form of "akhar," meaning "other."

﴿When We inspired your mother with what was inspired﴾: "idh" is a zarf (adverbial complement) for the inspiration, meaning We bestowed that favour at the time of the inspiration. The inspiration to her may be mere inspiration (ilham) into her heart, or a dream in which she was shown this, or through a prophet, or through an angel, but not in the manner of prophethood, as with the revelation to Mary. Or it may be that the news was conveyed through earlier prophets and reached her. "What was inspired" refers to what would come to her regarding the matter. He first left it vague and then explained it, to magnify its importance.

﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ explains the inspiration, since revelation has the sense of speech. Alternatively, the "an" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the sense "that cast him." "Qadhf" here means throwing, i.e., throw him into the chest. The meaning of "chest" (al-tabut) was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah in the story of Talut. ﴿Then cast him into the sea﴾ means throw him into the river. "Yamm" means the sea or a large river.

Al-Farra' said: this is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: "Cast him, and the sea will cast him onto the shore." The command addressed to the sea is based on treating it as one who understands and discerns, since its casting him onto the shore was a matter bound to happen. The "sahil" is the shore of the sea. It was named sahil because the water wore it away (sahalahu), as said by Ibn Duraid. What is meant here is the part of the sea adjacent to the shore, not the shore itself. All these pronouns refer to Moses, not to the chest, even though the chest was cast along with him, because the intended subject is Moses, and the pronouns before and after this refer to him.

﴿Let him be taken by an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ is the response to the command to cast. The "enemy" is Pharaoh. When his mother cast him into the sea, which is the well-known Nile, a branch flowed from it to Pharaoh's house. Allah carried him along that branch to Pharaoh's house, where he took the chest and found Moses inside it. It was also said that the sea cast him onto the shore, Pharaoh saw him, and ordered someone to take him. And it was said that Pharaoh's daughter found him. The first view is preferable.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ means Allah cast upon Moses a love originating from Him, which He placed in the hearts of His servants, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. It was also said that He placed upon him a radiance of beauty, so that no one among the people who saw him failed to love him.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "I cast My mercy upon you." It was also said that the word "min" (from) is connected to "alqaytu" (I cast), so the meaning is: I cast love from Me upon you, i.e., I loved you, and whom Allah loves, people love.

﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾: i.e., that you be nurtured and fed in My sight. One says "sana'a al-rajul jariyatahu" when he raised his slave-girl, and "sana'a farasahu" when he persisted in feeding his horse and tending to it. The interpretation of "under My eye" as "in My sight" is correct. Al-Nahhas said: this is known in the language, but there is no specialisation of Moses in this, since all things are in Allah's sight. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said the meaning is: to be nourished according to My love and My will. One says "I take the things under my eye," meaning according to my love. Ibn al-Anbari said: the "eye" in this verse is intended to express the sense of intention and choice, from the Arab saying "so-and-so went on my eye," i.e., with my love. It was said the lam (that) is connected to an omitted element: "I did that so that you might be raised." It was also said it is connected to "alqaytu," and it was said to be connected to what follows: "and that you might be raised under My eye, when your sister walked." Ibn al-Qa'qa' read ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ with the lam sukun as an imperative, and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning: that your movement and conduct be by My will, and under My watchful eye.

﴿When your sister walked﴾ is a zarf complement, connected either to "alqaytu" or to "litusna'a." It may also be a badal (substitute) for "idh awhayna" (when We inspired). His sister's name was Maryam, and she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?﴾ That is, she went out seeking news of him and found Pharaoh and his wife Asiya looking for a wet-nurse for him. So she said this to them: "Shall I direct you to someone who will take him into her care and raise him?" They said: "And who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "Yes, the milk of my brother Harun." Harun was a year older than Moses, and it was also said he was more than a year older. So the mother came, and he accepted her breast, for he would not accept the breast of any other nurse. This is the meaning of ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾. In the codex of Ubayy it is "fa-radadnaka." The fa in "fa-radadnaka" is a fa of elucidation (fasiha). ﴿That her eye may be cooled﴾: Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of 'Abd al-Hamid, read "kay taqirra" with a kasra on the qaf, and the rest read it with a fatha.

Al-Jawhari said: "qarartu bihi 'aynan qurratan wa-qururan," and a man is "qarir al-'ayn." "Qarrat 'aynuhu" (his eye was cooled) yaqarru and yaqirru, the opposite of "sakhinat" (it became hot). The meaning of "the coolness of the eye" is joy at her child's return to her, after she had cast him into the sea and his separation had weighed heavily upon her. ﴿And that she may not grieve﴾: i.e., there should not occur to her, for any reason, grief that would disturb that joy. If he had meant grief from the cause whose removal cooled her eye, he would have placed the negation of grief before the coolness of the eye. Therefore this negation of grief is taken to refer to grief arising from a cause that happens afterwards. It may be said that since the waw (and) is for mere conjunction, this interpretation is not obligatory. It was also said the meaning is: "and do not grieve, you, O Moses, over her loss of compassion," but this is a strained interpretation.

﴿And you killed a soul﴾: the "soul" here is the soul of the Copt whom Moses struck, and it was an accidental killing. ﴿Then We delivered you from distress﴾: the distress that resulted from that killing, namely the fear of punishment, whether in the Hereafter, in this world, or both. It was said that "ghamm" (distress) means killing in the dialect of Quraysh, and how far removed this is!

﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾: "fitna" can mean a trial, an affliction, a difficult matter, or whatever a person is tested with. "Futun" may be a verbal noun like "thubur," "shukur," and "kufur," meaning: We tested you with a test and examined you with an examination. It may also be the plural of "fitna," with the feminine ta' disregarded, like "hujur" for "hujra" and "budur" for "badra." Its meaning would then be: We delivered you time after time from the trials you had fallen into, mentioned earlier, before Allah chose him for His message. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning his deliverance from the distress of that cause, and his deliverance from the trials, is to bestow favour upon him through what Allah had done for him, and to strengthen his heart for what would befall him with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel.

﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾. Al-Farra' said: the implied meaning of the sentence is, "We tested you with a testing, so you went out to the people of Madyan and stayed for years there." Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him

It was also said that He placed upon him a radiance of beauty, so that no one among the people who saw him failed to love him.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "I cast My mercy upon you." It was also said that the word "min" (from) is connected to "alqaytu" (I cast), so the meaning is: I cast love from Me upon you, i.e., I loved you, and whom Allah loves, people love.

﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾: i.e., that you be nurtured and fed in My sight. One says "sana'a al-rajul jariyatahu" when he raised his slave-girl, and "sana'a farasahu" when he persisted in feeding his horse and tending to it. The interpretation of "under My eye" as "in My sight" is correct. Al-Nahhas said: this is known in the language, but there is no specialisation of Moses in this, since all things are in Allah's sight. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said the meaning is: to be nourished according to My love and My will. One says "I take the things under my eye," meaning according to my love. Ibn al-Anbari said: the "eye" in this verse is intended to express the sense of intention and choice, from the Arab saying "so-and-so went on my eye," i.e., with my love. It was said the lam (that) is connected to an omitted element: "I did that so that you might be raised." It was also said it is connected to "alqaytu," and it was said to be connected to what follows: "and that you might be raised under My eye, when your sister walked." Ibn al-Qa'qa' read ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ with the lam sukun as an imperative, and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning: that your movement and conduct be by My will, and under My watchful eye.

﴿When your sister walked﴾ is a zarf complement, connected either to "alqaytu" or to "litusna'a." It may also be a badal (substitute) for "idh awhayna" (when We inspired). His sister's name was Maryam, and she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?﴾ That is, she went out seeking news of him and found Pharaoh and his wife Asiya looking for a wet-nurse for him. So she said this to them: "Shall I direct you to someone who will take him into her care and raise him?" They said: "And who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "Yes, the milk of my brother Harun." Harun was a year older than Moses, and it was also said he was more than a year older. So the mother came, and he accepted her breast, for he would not accept the breast of any other nurse. This is the meaning of ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾. In the codex of Ubayy it is "fa-radadnaka." The fa in "fa-radadnaka" is a fa of elucidation (fasiha). ﴿That her eye may be cooled﴾: Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of 'Abd al-Hamid, read "kay taqirra" with a kasra on the qaf, and the rest read it with a fatha.

Al-Jawhari said: "qarartu bihi 'aynan qurratan wa-qururan," and a man is "qarir al-'ayn." "Qarrat 'aynuhu" (his eye was cooled) yaqarru and yaqirru, the opposite of "sakhinat" (it became hot). The meaning of "the coolness of the eye" is joy at her child's return to her, after she had cast him into the sea and his separation had weighed heavily upon her. ﴿And that she may not grieve﴾: i.e., there should not occur to her, for any reason, grief that would disturb that joy. If he had meant grief from the cause whose removal cooled her eye, he would have placed the negation of grief before the coolness of the eye. Therefore this negation of grief is taken to refer to grief arising from a cause that happens afterwards. It may be said that since the waw (and) is for mere conjunction, this interpretation is not obligatory. It was also said the meaning is: "and do not grieve, you, O Moses, over her loss of compassion," but this is a strained interpretation.

﴿And you killed a soul﴾: the "soul" here is the soul of the Copt whom Moses struck, and it was an accidental killing. ﴿Then We delivered you from distress﴾: the distress that resulted from that killing, namely the fear of punishment, whether in the Hereafter, in this world, or both. It was said that "ghamm" (distress) means killing in the dialect of Quraysh, and how far removed this is!

﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾: "fitna" can mean a trial, an affliction, a difficult matter, or whatever a person is tested with. "Futun" may be a verbal noun like "thubur," "shukur," and "kufur," meaning: We tested you with a test and examined you with an examination. It may also be the plural of "fitna," with the feminine ta' disregarded, like "hujur" for "hujra" and "budur" for "badra." Its meaning would then be: We delivered you time after time from the trials you had fallen into, mentioned earlier, before Allah chose him for His message. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning his deliverance from the distress of that cause, and his deliverance from the trials, is to bestow favour upon him through what Allah had done for him, and to strengthen his heart for what would befall him with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel.

﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾. Al-Farra' said: the implied meaning of the sentence is, "We tested you with a testing, so you went out to the people of Madyan and stayed for years there." Such omission is common in the revelation, as it is in Arabic speech, since they omit much when the meaning is known. Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb, eight stages from Egypt. Moses fled there and remained ten years, and this is the fuller of the two terms. It was also said he stayed with Shu'ayb twenty-eight years, of which ten were the bride-price for his wife, Shu'ayb's daughter, and eighteen years he remained with him until a child was born to him. The fa in ﴿then you stayed﴾ indicates that the trials mentioned are those that came before his stay among the people of Madyan.

﴿Then you came upon a destiny, O Moses﴾: i.e., at a time that had preceded in My decree and destiny, that I would speak to you and make you a prophet. Or it means at an appointed measure of time at which revelation comes to the prophets, which is the beginning of forty years. Or it means at an appointment you knew about through Shu'ayb's informing you of it.

The poet said:
He attained the caliphate, for it was a destiny for him,
as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed destiny.

The word "thumma" (then), which indicates a lapse of time, is used to show that his coming was after a period, because of what happened to him, such as losing his way, his flock scattering, and similar things.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾. "Istina'a" means taking something as one's craft (sun'a), and sun'a is the good that one bestows upon a person. The meaning is: I chose you for My revelation and My message, so that you would act according to My will. Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is, "I chose you to establish My proof and made you between Me and My creation, so that by conveying from Me you would occupy the position I would occupy were I to address them and argue with them myself." It was also said this is an image of the great honour Allah bestowed upon him, by bringing him near as a king brings near one of his special intimates.

﴿Go, you and your brother﴾: i.e., let your brother also go. This is a resumed statement, brought to explain the purpose of the choosing. ﴿With My signs﴾ means with My miracles, which I made a sign for you, namely the nine signs. ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾: i.e., do not become weak or relax. One says "wana yuni wanyan" when he became weak.

The poet said:
Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him
what passed and what remains.

Imru' al-Qays said:
He roams, when the swift horses in their slackness
raise dust in al-Kadid al-Mu'akkal.

Al-Farra' said: "fi dhikri" and "'an dhikri" are the same. The meaning is: do not fall short in remembering Me by doing good to you both and bestowing blessings upon you both, for remembering a blessing is giving thanks for it. It was also said the meaning of "la tanya" is: do not delay in conveying the message. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿la tahina fi dhikri﴾ (do not weaken in remembering Me).

﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. This is a command to both of them to go together. Moses is present and Harun is absent, and Moses is given precedence (taghlib), because he is the fundamental one in delivering the message. The reason given for going is ﴿he has transgressed﴾, i.e., he exceeded the limit in disbelief and rebellion. Earlier, He had singled out Moses alone for the command to go, and here He joined them, in order to honour Moses by singling him out, and to emphasise the command to go by repetition. It was said that in this there is evidence that the going of one of them alone is not sufficient. It was also said the first is a command to Moses to go to all the people, and the second is a command to both of them to go to Pharaoh.

Then Allah commanded them to speak to him gently, because of its effect on his acceptance, for harshness at the outset is among the greatest causes of aversion and obstinacy in disbelief. "Gentle speech" (al-qawl al-layyin) is speech in which there is no harshness, and one says "layyin" (gentle) for something that is soft. The meaning is to leave the harshness aside for the sake of admonition, like their saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ (79:18). It was said that gentle speech means addressing him by his kunya (teknonym). It was also said it means promising him the pleasures of this world if he responds.

Then He gave the reason for the command to speak gently to him: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾, i.e., engage with him in the manner of one who hopes and aspires. So the hope is attributed to both of them, as a group of grammarians said, including Sibawayh and others. Its detailed investigation has been mentioned in more than one place. Al-Zajjaj said: "la'alla" (perhaps) is a word of expectation and hope, and He addressed them in terms they understand. It was also said that "la'alla" here has the sense of a question: "Look and see whether he is reminded or fears." And it was said it has the sense of "kay" (so that).

"Reminded" means considering what they conveyed of the reminder and reflecting deeply upon it, so that this becomes a cause of acceptance. "Fear" is fear of the punishment of Allah that was promised through their two tongues. The word "aw" (or) is used to prevent the absence of both, not to combine them.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿Cast him into the river﴾, that he said: "It is the Nile."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾, that he said: "Everyone who saw him had love for him placed upon them from Him."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: "I made you beloved to My servants."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Imran al-Jawni, regarding His saying ﴿And that you may be reared under My eye﴾, that he said: "You are nurtured under the eye of Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse, that he said: "So that you may be nourished under My eye."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij regarding the verse, that he said: "He says: 'You are under My eye when your mother placed you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walked [after you].'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib reported from Ibn Umar: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Musa only killed the man who was from the people of Pharaoh by mistake.'" Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress﴾, he said: "From the killing of the soul." And ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, he said: "We purified you with purification."

Said ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, that he said: "We tested you with a test."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: "We examined you with an examination."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas a lengthy athar (report) in explanation of the verse. Whoever wishes to take it in full, let him consult it in the book of tafsir (commentary on the Qur'an) in al-Nasa'i's Sunan.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Then you came upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed time."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid and Qatadah regarding ﴿upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed date."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and do not slacken﴾, that he said: "Do not be slow."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali regarding His saying ﴿a gentle word﴾, that he said: "Kunnah him" (i.e., address him by a kunya).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They addressed him by his kunya."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding His saying ﴿perhaps he may remember or fear﴾, that he said: "Will he remember?"

When Moses asked his Lord, glory be to Him, to expand his breast, ease his task, untie the knot from his tongue, and appoint for him a minister from his family, Allah, glory be to Him, informed him that He had answered that supplication. So He said: ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾, meaning you have been given what you asked for. The "request that is requested" (al-su'l al-mas'ul) means the thing sought, as in your saying "khabar" for "makhbur" (the thing told). The phrase "O Moses" is added to honour him with direct address, and also to observe the rhyme endings (fawasil, the verse-final rhyme pattern).

The sentence ﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) intended to strengthen Moses' heart by reminding him of Allah's blessings upon him. "Mann" means kindness and bounty. The meaning is: We were gracious to you at another time before this time, namely Allah's protection of him from the harm of his enemies, as He explains here. "Ukhra" is the feminine form of "akhar," meaning "other."

﴿When We inspired your mother with what was inspired﴾: "idh" is a zarf (adverbial complement) for the inspiration, meaning We bestowed that favour at the time of the inspiration. The inspiration to her may be mere inspiration (ilham) into her heart, or a dream in which she was shown this, or through a prophet, or through an angel, but not in the manner of prophethood, as with the revelation to Mary. Or it may be that the news was conveyed through earlier prophets and reached her. "What was inspired" refers to what would come to her regarding the matter. He first left it vague and then explained it, to magnify its importance.

﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ explains the inspiration, since revelation has the sense of speech. Alternatively, the "an" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the sense "that cast him." "Qadhf" here means throwing, i.e., throw him into the chest. The meaning of "chest" (al-tabut) was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah in the story of Talut. ﴿Then cast him into the sea﴾ means throw him into the river. "Yamm" means the sea or a large river.

Al-Farra' said: this is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: "Cast him, and the sea will cast him onto the shore." The command addressed to the sea is based on treating it as one who understands and discerns, since its casting him onto the shore was a matter bound to happen. The "sahil" is the shore of the sea. It was named sahil because the water wore it away (sahalahu), as said by Ibn Duraid. What is meant here is the part of the sea adjacent to the shore, not the shore itself. All these pronouns refer to Moses, not to the chest, even though the chest was cast along with him, because the intended subject is Moses, and the pronouns before and after this refer to him.

﴿Let him be taken by an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ is the response to the command to cast. The "enemy" is Pharaoh. When his mother cast him into the sea, which is the well-known Nile, a branch flowed from it to Pharaoh's house. Allah carried him along that branch to Pharaoh's house, where he took the chest and found Moses inside it. It was also said that the sea cast him onto the shore, Pharaoh saw him, and ordered someone to take him. And it was said that Pharaoh's daughter found him. The first view is preferable.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ means Allah cast upon Moses a love originating from Him, which He placed in the hearts of His servants, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. He attained the caliphate, for it was a destiny for him,

One says "wana yuni wanyan" when he became weak.

Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij regarding the verse, that he said: "He says: 'You are under My eye when your mother placed you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walked [after you].'"

Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress﴾, he said: "From the killing of the soul." And ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, he said: "We purified you with purification."

Said ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, that he said: "We tested you with a test."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: "We examined you with an examination."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas a lengthy athar (report) in explanation of the verse. Whoever wishes to take it in full, let him consult it in the book of tafsir (commentary on the Qur'an) in al-Nasa'i's Sunan.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Then you came upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed time."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid and Qatadah regarding ﴿upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed date."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and do not slacken﴾, that he said: "Do not be slow."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali regarding His saying ﴿a gentle word﴾, that he said: "Kunnah him" (i.e., address him by a kunya).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They addressed him by his kunya."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding His saying ﴿perhaps he may remember or fear﴾, that he said: "Will he remember?"

When Moses asked his Lord, glory be to Him, to expand his breast, ease his task, untie the knot from his tongue, and appoint for him a minister from his family, Allah, glory be to Him, informed him that He had answered that supplication. So He said: ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾, meaning you have been given what you asked for. The "request that is requested" (al-su'l al-mas'ul) means the thing sought, as in your saying "khabar" for "makhbur" (the thing told). The phrase "O Moses" is added to honour him with direct address, and also to observe the rhyme endings (fawasil, the verse-final rhyme pattern).

The sentence ﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) intended to strengthen Moses' heart by reminding him of Allah's blessings upon him. "Mann" means kindness and bounty. The meaning is: We were gracious to you at another time before this time, namely Allah's protection of him from the harm of his enemies, as He explains here. "Ukhra" is the feminine form of "akhar," meaning "other."

﴿When We inspired your mother with what was inspired﴾: "idh" is a zarf (adverbial complement) for the inspiration, meaning We bestowed that favour at the time of the inspiration. The inspiration to her may be mere inspiration (ilham) into her heart, or a dream in which she was shown this, or through a prophet, or through an angel, but not in the manner of prophethood, as with the revelation to Mary. Or it may be that the news was conveyed through earlier prophets and reached her. "What was inspired" refers to what would come to her regarding the matter. He first left it vague and then explained it, to magnify its importance.

﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ explains the inspiration, since revelation has the sense of speech. Alternatively, the "an" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the sense "that cast him." "Qadhf" here means throwing, i.e., throw him into the chest. The meaning of "chest" (al-tabut) was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah in the story of Talut. ﴿Then cast him into the sea﴾ means throw him into the river. "Yamm" means the sea or a large river.

Al-Farra' said: this is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: "Cast him, and the sea will cast him onto the shore." The command addressed to the sea is based on treating it as one who understands and discerns, since its casting him onto the shore was a matter bound to happen. The "sahil" is the shore of the sea. It was named sahil because the water wore it away (sahalahu), as said by Ibn Duraid. What is meant here is the part of the sea adjacent to the shore, not the shore itself. All these pronouns refer to Moses, not to the chest, even though the chest was cast along with him, because the intended subject is Moses, and the pronouns before and after this refer to him.

﴿Let him be taken by an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ is the response to the command to cast. The "enemy" is Pharaoh. When his mother cast him into the sea, which is the well-known Nile, a branch flowed from it to Pharaoh's house. Allah carried him along that branch to Pharaoh's house, where he took the chest and found Moses inside it. It was also said that the sea cast him onto the shore, Pharaoh saw him, and ordered someone to take him. And it was said that Pharaoh's daughter found him. The first view is preferable.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ means Allah cast upon Moses a love originating from Him, which He placed in the hearts of His servants, so that no one who saw him failed to love him. It was also said that He placed upon him a radiance of beauty, so that no one among the people who saw him failed to love him.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "I cast My mercy upon you." It was also said that the word "min" (from) is connected to "alqaytu" (I cast), so the meaning is: I cast love from Me upon you, i.e., I loved you, and whom Allah loves, people love.

﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾: i.e., that you be nurtured and fed in My sight. One says "sana'a al-rajul jariyatahu" when he raised his slave-girl, and "sana'a farasahu" when he persisted in feeding his horse and tending to it. The interpretation of "under My eye" as "in My sight" is correct. Al-Nahhas said: this is known in the language, but there is no specialisation of Moses in this, since all things are in Allah's sight. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said the meaning is: to be nourished according to My love and My will. One says "I take the things under my eye," meaning according to my love. Ibn al-Anbari said: the "eye" in this verse is intended to express the sense of intention and choice, from the Arab saying "so-and-so went on my eye," i.e., with my love. It was said the lam (that) is connected to an omitted element: "I did that so that you might be raised." It was also said it is connected to "alqaytu," and it was said to be connected to what follows: "and that you might be raised under My eye, when your sister walked." Ibn al-Qa'qa' read ﴿wa-litusna'a﴾ with the lam sukun as an imperative, and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning: that your movement and conduct be by My will, and under My watchful eye.

﴿When your sister walked﴾ is a zarf complement, connected either to "alqaytu" or to "litusna'a." It may also be a badal (substitute) for "idh awhayna" (when We inspired). His sister's name was Maryam, and she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?﴾ That is, she went out seeking news of him and found Pharaoh and his wife Asiya looking for a wet-nurse for him. So she said this to them: "Shall I direct you to someone who will take him into her care and raise him?" They said: "And who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "Yes, the milk of my brother Harun." Harun was a year older than Moses, and it was also said he was more than a year older. So the mother came, and he accepted her breast, for he would not accept the breast of any other nurse. This is the meaning of ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾. In the codex of Ubayy it is "fa-radadnaka." The fa in "fa-radadnaka" is a fa of elucidation (fasiha). ﴿That her eye may be cooled﴾: Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of 'Abd al-Hamid, read "kay taqirra" with a kasra on the qaf, and the rest read it with a fatha.

Al-Jawhari said: "qarartu bihi 'aynan qurratan wa-qururan," and a man is "qarir al-'ayn." "Qarrat 'aynuhu" (his eye was cooled) yaqarru and yaqirru, the opposite of "sakhinat" (it became hot). The meaning of "the coolness of the eye" is joy at her child's return to her, after she had cast him into the sea and his separation had weighed heavily upon her. ﴿And that she may not grieve﴾: i.e., there should not occur to her, for any reason, grief that would disturb that joy. If he had meant grief from the cause whose removal cooled her eye, he would have placed the negation of grief before the coolness of the eye. Therefore this negation of grief is taken to refer to grief arising from a cause that happens afterwards. It may be said that since the waw (and) is for mere conjunction, this interpretation is not obligatory. It was also said the meaning is: "and do not grieve, you, O Moses, over her loss of compassion," but this is a strained interpretation.

﴿And you killed a soul﴾: the "soul" here is the soul of the Copt whom Moses struck, and it was an accidental killing. ﴿Then We delivered you from distress﴾: the distress that resulted from that killing, namely the fear of punishment, whether in the Hereafter, in this world, or both. It was said that "ghamm" (distress) means killing in the dialect of Quraysh, and how far removed this is!

﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾: "fitna" can mean a trial, an affliction, a difficult matter, or whatever a person is tested with. "Futun" may be a verbal noun like "thubur," "shukur," and "kufur," meaning: We tested you with a test and examined you with an examination. It may also be the plural of "fitna," with the feminine ta' disregarded, like "hujur" for "hujra" and "budur" for "badra." Its meaning would then be: We delivered you time after time from the trials you had fallen into, mentioned earlier, before Allah chose him for His message. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning his deliverance from the distress of that cause, and his deliverance from the trials, is to bestow favour upon him through what Allah had done for him, and to strengthen his heart for what would befall him with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel.

﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾. Al-Farra' said: the implied meaning of the sentence is, "We tested you with a testing, so you went out to the people of Madyan and stayed for years there." Such omission is common in the revelation, as it is in Arabic speech, since they omit much when the meaning is known. Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb, eight stages from Egypt. Moses fled there and remained ten years, and this is the fuller of the two terms. It was also said he stayed with Shu'ayb twenty-eight years, of which ten were the bride-price for his wife, Shu'ayb's daughter, and eighteen years he remained with him until a child was born to him. The fa in ﴿then you stayed﴾ indicates that the trials mentioned are those that came before his stay among the people of Madyan.

﴿Then you came upon a destiny, O Moses﴾: i.e., at a time that had preceded in My decree and destiny, that I would speak to you and make you a prophet. Or it means at an appointed measure of time at which revelation comes to the prophets, which is the beginning of forty years. Or it means at an appointment you knew about through Shu'ayb's informing you of it.

The poet said:
He attained the caliphate, for it was a destiny for him,
as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed destiny.

The word "thumma" (then), which indicates a lapse of time, is used to show that his coming was after a period, because of what happened to him, such as losing his way, his flock scattering, and similar things.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾. "Istina'a" means taking something as one's craft (sun'a), and sun'a is the good that one bestows upon a person. The meaning is: I chose you for My revelation and My message, so that you would act according to My will. Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is, "I chose you to establish My proof and made you between Me and My creation, so that by conveying from Me you would occupy the position I would occupy were I to address them and argue with them myself." It was also said this is an image of the great honour Allah bestowed upon him, by bringing him near as a king brings near one of his special intimates.

﴿Go, you and your brother﴾: i.e., let your brother also go. This is a resumed statement, brought to explain the purpose of the choosing. ﴿With My signs﴾ means with My miracles, which I made a sign for you, namely the nine signs. ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾: i.e., do not become weak or relax. One says "wana yuni wanyan" when he became weak.

The poet said:
Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him
what passed and what remains.

Imru' al-Qays said:
He roams, when the swift horses in their slackness
raise dust in al-Kadid al-Mu'akkal.

Al-Farra' said: "fi dhikri" and "'an dhikri" are the same. The meaning is: do not fall short in remembering Me by doing good to you both and bestowing blessings upon you both, for remembering a blessing is giving thanks for it. It was also said the meaning of "la tanya" is: do not delay in conveying the message. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿la tahina fi dhikri﴾ (do not weaken in remembering Me).

﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. This is a command to both of them to go together. Moses is present and Harun is absent, and Moses is given precedence (taghlib), because he is the fundamental one in delivering the message. The reason given for going is ﴿he has transgressed﴾, i.e., he exceeded the limit in disbelief and rebellion. Earlier, He had singled out Moses alone for the command to go, and here He joined them, in order to honour Moses by singling him out, and to emphasise the command to go by repetition. It was said that in this there is evidence that the going of one of them alone is not sufficient. It was also said the first is a command to Moses to go to all the people, and the second is a command to both of them to go to Pharaoh.

Then Allah commanded them to speak to him gently, because of its effect on his acceptance, for harshness at the outset is among the greatest causes of aversion and obstinacy in disbelief. "Gentle speech" (al-qawl al-layyin) is speech in which there is no harshness, and one says "layyin" (gentle) for something that is soft. The meaning is to leave the harshness aside for the sake of admonition, like their saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ (79:18). It was said that gentle speech means addressing him by his kunya (teknonym). It was also said it means promising him the pleasures of this world if he responds.

Then He gave the reason for the command to speak gently to him: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾, i.e., engage with him in the manner of one who hopes and aspires. So the hope is attributed to both of them, as a group of grammarians said, including Sibawayh and others. Its detailed investigation has been mentioned in more than one place. Al-Zajjaj said: "la'alla" (perhaps) is a word of expectation and hope, and He addressed them in terms they understand. It was also said that "la'alla" here has the sense of a question: "Look and see whether he is reminded or fears." And it was said it has the sense of "kay" (so that).

"Reminded" means considering what they conveyed of the reminder and reflecting deeply upon it, so that this becomes a cause of acceptance. "Fear" is fear of the punishment of Allah that was promised through their two tongues. The word "aw" (or) is used to prevent the absence of both, not to combine them.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse, that he said: "So that you may be nourished under My eye."

The word "thumma" (then), which indicates a lapse of time, is used to show that his coming was after a period, because of what happened to him, such as losing his way, his flock scattering, and similar things.

﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾. "Istina'a" means taking something as one's craft (sun'a), and sun'a is the good that one bestows upon a person. The meaning is: I chose you for My revelation and My message, so that you would act according to My will. Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is, "I chose you to establish My proof and made you between Me and My creation, so that by conveying from Me you would occupy the position I would occupy were I to address them and argue with them myself." It was also said this is an image of the great honour Allah bestowed upon him, by bringing him near as a king brings near one of his special intimates.

﴿Go, you and your brother﴾: i.e., let your brother also go. This is a resumed statement, brought to explain the purpose of the choosing. ﴿With My signs﴾ means with My miracles, which I made a sign for you, namely the nine signs. ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾: i.e., do not become weak or relax. One says "wana yuni wanyan" when he became weak.

The poet said:
Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him
what passed and what remains.

Imru' al-Qays said:
He roams, when the swift horses in their slackness
raise dust in al-Kadid al-Mu'akkal.

Al-Farra' said: "fi dhikri" and "'an dhikri" are the same. The meaning is: do not fall short in remembering Me by doing good to you both and bestowing blessings upon you both, for remembering a blessing is giving thanks for it. It was also said the meaning of "la tanya" is: do not delay in conveying the message. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is ﴿la tahina fi dhikri﴾ (do not weaken in remembering Me).

﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. This is a command to both of them to go together. Moses is present and Harun is absent, and Moses is given precedence (taghlib), because he is the fundamental one in delivering the message. The reason given for going is ﴿he has transgressed﴾, i.e., he exceeded the limit in disbelief and rebellion. Earlier, He had singled out Moses alone for the command to go, and here He joined them, in order to honour Moses by singling him out, and to emphasise the command to go by repetition. It was said that in this there is evidence that the going of one of them alone is not sufficient. It was also said the first is a command to Moses to go to all the people, and the second is a command to both of them to go to Pharaoh.

Then Allah commanded them to speak to him gently, because of its effect on his acceptance, for harshness at the outset is among the greatest causes of aversion and obstinacy in disbelief. "Gentle speech" (al-qawl al-layyin) is speech in which there is no harshness, and one says "layyin" (gentle) for something that is soft. The meaning is to leave the harshness aside for the sake of admonition, like their saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ (79:18). It was said that gentle speech means addressing him by his kunya (teknonym). It was also said it means promising him the pleasures of this world if he responds.

Then He gave the reason for the command to speak gently to him: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾, i.e., engage with him in the manner of one who hopes and aspires. So the hope is attributed to both of them, as a group of grammarians said, including Sibawayh and others. Its detailed investigation has been mentioned in more than one place. Al-Zajjaj said: "la'alla" (perhaps) is a word of expectation and hope, and He addressed them in terms they understand. It was also said that "la'alla" here has the sense of a question: "Look and see whether he is reminded or fears." And it was said it has the sense of "kay" (so that).

"Reminded" means considering what they conveyed of the reminder and reflecting deeply upon it, so that this becomes a cause of acceptance. "Fear" is fear of the punishment of Allah that was promised through their two tongues. The word "aw" (or) is used to prevent the absence of both, not to combine them.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿Cast him into the river﴾, that he said: "It is the Nile."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾, that he said: "Everyone who saw him had love for him placed upon them from Him."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: "I made you beloved to My servants."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Imran al-Jawni, regarding His saying ﴿And that you may be reared under My eye﴾, that he said: "You are nurtured under the eye of Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding the verse, that he said: "So that you may be nourished under My eye."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij regarding the verse, that he said: "He says: 'You are under My eye when your mother placed you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walked [after you].'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib reported from Ibn Umar: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Musa only killed the man who was from the people of Pharaoh by mistake.'" Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress﴾, he said: "From the killing of the soul." And ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, he said: "We purified you with purification."

Said ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We tried you with a trial﴾, that he said: "We tested you with a test."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: "We examined you with an examination."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas a lengthy athar (report) in explanation of the verse. Whoever wishes to take it in full, let him consult it in the book of tafsir (commentary on the Qur'an) in al-Nasa'i's Sunan.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid and Qatadah regarding ﴿upon a measure﴾, that he said: "At an appointed date."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and do not slacken﴾, that he said: "Do not be slow."
