﴿الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهدا﴾ ("He who made the earth a cradle for you"): the relative clause is in the nominative case, as a qualifier of "my Lord" containing additional clarification. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative case by way of praise.

The Kūfans read *mahdan* as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of an implied verb: that is, *mahhadahā mahdan* ("He made it a cradle"), or with an omitted *muḍāf*: that is, *dhāt mahd* ("a thing of cradling"). It is a noun for what is made level, like a bed for what is spread out. The rest read ﴿مهادا﴾ (*mihādan*), and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim chose this reading, saying that the readers agree on ﴿ألم نجعل الأرض مهادا﴾ ("Have We not made the earth a bed?") [al-Naba': 6]. Al-Naḥḥās said: The plural is better than the verbal noun, because this place is not a place for the verbal noun except by omission of the *muḍāf*. It was said that *mihādan* may be singular like *firāsh*, and it may be a plural, and the meaning of *mihād* is a bed. So *mihād* is the plural of *mahd*: that is, He made every part of it a cradle for each one of you.

﴿وسلك لكم فيها سبلا﴾ ("and threaded for you in it roads"). *Al-salk* is inserting one thing into another. The meaning is: He put into the earth, for your sake, paths you may travel and made them easy for you. In the other verse: ﴿الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهدا وجعل لكم فيها سبلا لعلكم تهتدون﴾ ("He who made the earth a cradle for you and made for you in it roads, that perhaps you may be guided") [al-Zukhruf: 10].

Then He, glorified is He, said, bestowing favour upon His servants: ﴿وأنزل من السماء ماء﴾ ("and sent down water from the sky"), which is rainwater. It is said that here ends the speech of Mūsā, and what follows, ﴿فأخرجنا به أزواجا من نبات شتى﴾ ("so We brought forth by it pairs of various plants"), is from the speech of God, glorified is He. It is also said that it is part of the speech reported from Mūsā, coordinated with *anzala* (sent down). The shift to the first person plural (*al-taʿkallum*) was to draw attention to how evident the proof of complete power is in it. This was objected to: this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it entails losing the shift (*iltifāt*) because the speaker is not the same. It is answered that the whole speech is reported from one person, Mūsā, and the one who reports it all is God, glorified is He.

The meaning: We brought forth by that water, through tilling and cultivation, pairs: that is, kinds and sorts of various plants. His words *min nabāt* ("of plants") are a qualifier of *azwājan*, or an explanation of it. Likewise *shattā* ("various") is another qualifier of it, meaning scattered, the plural of *shatīt*. Al-Akhfash said: The implied sense is *azwājan shattā min nabāt* ("pairs, various, of plants"). He said: Plants may be various, so *shattā* may be an adjective of *azwājan* or an adjective of *nabāt*. It is said *amrun shatt* ("a scattered matter") meaning dispersed, and *shatta al-amru shattan wa shatātan* ("the matter scattered") meaning dispersed, and *ishtatta* is similar. *Al-shatīt* is the scattered.

Ru'ba said:
"They came together and lowered their eyes, scattered."

The sentence ﴿كلوا وارعوا﴾ ("Eat and graze") is in the accusative case as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), with an implied verb of saying: that is, saying to them that. The command is for permission. It is said *raʿat al-māshiyah al-kalaʾ* ("the livestock grazed the pasture") and *raʿāhā ṣāḥibuhā riʿāyatan* ("its owner pastured it"): that is, he let it loose and sent it out. It comes intransitive and transitive.

The reference in His words ﴿إن في ذلك لآيات لأولي النهى﴾ ("Indeed in that are signs for people of intellect") is to what has been mentioned in these verses. *Al-nuhā* means intellects, the plural of *nuhyah*. He singled out "people of intellect" because they are the ones to whose opinion one resorts. It is also said that it is because they restrain the self from vile things. All of this from Mūsā is an argument against Pharaoh for establishing the Maker, as an answer to his words: ﴿فمن ربكما يا موسى﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿منها خلقناكم﴾ ("from it We created you") and what follows refers back to the earth mentioned earlier. Al-Zajjāj and others said: That is, Adam was created from the earth and his offspring from him. It is also said the meaning is that every drop of seed created from dust is included within the creation of Adam, because every individual of mankind has a share of his creation. ﴿وفيها﴾ ("and into it") meaning into the earth, ﴿نعيدكم﴾ ("We return you") after death, so you are buried in it and your parts scatter until they become of the substance of the earth. He used *fī* rather than *ilā* ("to") to indicate settling. ﴿ومنها﴾ ("and from it") meaning from the earth ﴿نخرجكم تارة أخرى﴾ ("We bring you forth another time"), that is, by resurrection, rising, assembling of bodies and returning the spirits to them as they were before death. *Tāra* is like *marra* (a time).

﴿ولقد أرينا آياتنا كلها﴾ ("And We certainly showed him all Our signs"): that is, We showed Pharaoh and made him know all Our signs. By "signs" is meant the nine signs mentioned in His words: ﴿ولقد آتينا موسى تسع آيات﴾ ("And We gave Mūsā nine clear signs") [al-Isrāʾ: 101], with the annexation (*iḍāfah*) being to a known reference (*ʿahd*). It is also said: the meaning is all the signs that Mūsā brought, and those that other prophets brought, and that Mūsā had informed him of all his miracles and the miracles of all the other prophets. The first is preferable. It is also said that by "signs" is meant the proofs of God, glorified is He, which indicate His oneness. ﴿فكذب وأبى﴾ ("but he denied and refused"): that is, Pharaoh denied Mūsā and refused to respond to him by accepting faith. This indicates that Pharaoh's disbelief was obstinate disbelief, because he saw the signs and denied them, as in His words: ﴿وجحدوا بها واستيقنتها أنفسهم ظلما وعلوا﴾ ("And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance") [al-Naml: 14].

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 20, verses 45–59 (part 2 of 2)

The clause ﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Musa?"﴾ is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafah*), answering an implied question: it is as if it were said, "What did Pharaoh say after this?" The interrogative hamzah here expresses denial regarding what Musa brought of the signs. The meaning is: "You have come, O Musa, to deceive the people into believing that you are a prophet whom they must follow and whose message they must believe, so that through that deception, which is a branch of magic, you may gain control over our land and drive us out of it." The accursed one mentioned the expulsion from the land only to turn his people away from answering Musa, for once it settled in their minds and was fixed in their understanding that the outcome of responding to Musa would be leaving their homes and homelands, they would be unwilling to listen to his words, to consider his miracles, or to heed what he called them to of good.

﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it﴾. The *fāʾ* (here, "so") indicates that what follows is the result of what precedes it. The *lām* is the preparatory *lām* (*lām al-muwattiʾah*) for an oath. The meaning is: "By Allah, we will surely match you with magic like what you have brought, so that it becomes clear to the people that what you have brought is magic, which a sorcerer can equal." ﴿So set between us and you an appointment﴾. The word *mawʿid* is a verbal noun, meaning a promise; it was also said to be a noun of place, meaning: "Appoint for us a known day, or a known place, that we will not break." Al-Qushayri said: "The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said: 'we will not break it,' i.e., we will not break that promise. *Ikhlāf* means to promise something and not fulfil it." Al-Jawhari said: "*al-mīʿād* is a mutual agreement, and also the time or the place; likewise *al-mawʿid*."

Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Shaybah and al-Aʿraj read ﴿we will not break it﴾ with the jussive (*lā nukhlif-hu*), taking it as an answer to the imperative *ijʿal* ("set"). The rest of the readers read it with the nominative (*lā nukhlifu*), taking it as a qualifier of *mawʿidan* ("an appointment"): i.e., "we will not break that promise." ﴿Neither we nor you﴾. Pharaoh delegated the determination of the appointment to Musa, to demonstrate his complete power to bring the like of what Musa had brought. The accusative of ﴿a place equitable﴾ is either by a verb implied and indicated by the verbal noun, or it is a substitute (*badal*) for *mawʿid*. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read *suwan* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, and the rest read it with a *kasrah*; both are dialectal forms. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred the *kasrah* on the *sīn*, because it is the elevated, eloquent dialect. The meaning intended is "a level place"; it was also said: "an equitable and just place between us and you." Sibawayh said: "It is said *siwan* and *suwan*, i.e., just, meaning just between the two places." Zuhayr said:

*They showed us a plot in which there is no wrong,*
*in which equality makes us equal.*

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Qutaybi said: its meaning is "a middle place between the two groups." Abu ʿUbayda recited, for Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi:

*Indeed our father was settled in a town*
*equitable between Qays, the Qays of Ghaylan, and al-Fazar.*

Al-Fazar is Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

Then Musa made an appointment with them for a known time, and so ﴿He said: "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: that was a festival day on which they adorned themselves. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that was the day of ʿAshura. al-Dahhak said: it was Saturday. (p. 913) It was also said: it was the day of Nayruz, and it was said: the day the canal was broken open. al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, al-Sulami and Hubayrah from Hafs read *yawma l-zīnati* with the accusative, and this reading is also reported from Abu ʿAmr; meaning: "On the day of adornment is the fulfilment of our promise." The rest read it with the nominative, as the predicate of *mawʿiduku-m* ("your appointment"). The appointment was made a time after Pharaoh asked that it be a level place, because "the day of adornment" indicates a well-known place where people gather on that day, or it is by supposing an omitted genitive: i.e., "your appointment is the place of the day of adornment." ﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾. This is conjoined to *yawm al-zīna*, so it is in the nominative place if it is conjoined to *yawm*, or in the genitive place if it is conjoined to *al-zīna*. It means the forenoon of that day. The intended "people" are the people of Egypt. The meaning: they will be gathered for the festival at the time of forenoon, and will look into the matter of Musa and Pharaoh. al-Farraʾ said: the meaning is, "When you see the people gathered from every direction in the forenoon, that is the appointment." He said: "Their custom was to gather people on that day."

The *ḍuḥā* (forenoon): al-Jawhari said: "*ḍaḥwat al-nahār* is the time of the day after sunrise, then after it the *ḍuḥā*, which is when the sun shines. It was specified as the forenoon because it is the beginning of the day; when the matter extends between the two, there is ample room in the day." Ibn Masʿud and al-Jahdari read *wa-an yuḥsha*r with the active voice, meaning: "And that Allah gather the people in the forenoon." It was reported from al-Jahdari that he read *wa-an nuḥshara* with a *nūn*, and some readers read it with a *tāʾ* on top, i.e., *wa-an tuḥshara*, meaning: "that you, O Pharaoh, be gathered." The rest read it with the *yāʾ* from below, with the passive voice.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿Indeed we fear that he will hasten against us﴾, he said: "He will hasten," ﴿or that he will transgress﴾, he said: "He will exceed bounds." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding Allah's words ﴿I hear and I see﴾, he said: "I hear what he says and I see what he answers you with; then it is revealed to you, and you answer him." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "When Allah sent Musa to Pharaoh, he said: 'My Lord, what should I say?' He said: 'Say: *Ahya sharran hayya*.'" al-Aʿshā said: The interpretation of that: "The Living before everything, and the Living after everything." al-Suyuti judged its chain to be sound, and Ibn Kathir had preceded him in judging its chain sound in his *Tafsir*.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding Allah's words ﴿upon whoever denies and turns away﴾, he said: "He denied the Book of Allah and turned away from obedience to Allah." Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmaʾ wa-l-Sifat* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾, he said: "He created for everything its mate," ﴿then guided﴾, he said: "He guided it to its mating, its food, its drink and its dwelling." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿My Lord does not err﴾, he said: "He does not make a mistake." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿of diverse plants﴾, he said: "Varied."

Regarding Allah's words ﴿for people of understanding﴾, he said: "for people of piety." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: ﴿for people of understanding﴾, he said: "for people of intellect and reason." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAta' al-Khurasani, he said: "The angel goes and takes dust from the place where the person will be buried and scatters it upon the drop of semen, so he creates from the dust and from the drop, and that is His saying: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you﴾."

Ahmad and al-Hakim reported from Abu Umamah, he said: "When Umm Kulthum, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was placed in the grave, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once more﴾, in the name of Allah, and in the way of Allah, and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." And in a hadith in the *Sunan*, "that he took a handful of dust and threw it into the grave and said: ﴿From it We created you﴾, then another handful and said: ﴿And into it We will return you﴾, then another and said: ﴿And from it We will bring you out once more﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾, he said: "It is the day of ʿAshura." Ibn al-Mundhir reported something similar from Ibn ʿAmr.

The majority of readers recite ﴿أن يفرط﴾ (*an yafruṭa*, "that he may hasten") with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the rā'. The meaning is: "We fear that he will hurry and rush to punish us." It is said *faraṭa minhu amr*, meaning *badara* (he was hasty in it). From this comes *al-fāriṭ* (the forerunner), who goes ahead of the people to the water, so the sense is: he will punish us like one who goes ahead in sin. This is what al-Mubarrad said. He also said: *faraṭa minhu amr* and *afraṭa* mean "he exceeded the limit" (*asrafa*), and *farraṭa* means "he neglected" (*taraka*).

Ibn Muhayṣin read ﴿يُفرَط﴾ (*yufraṭa*) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the rā', meaning: someone drives him to hasten toward us. A group read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', from *al-ifrāṭ* (excess), meaning he will go beyond bounds in harming us. Among them were Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah.

The reciter (*al-rājiz*) said:
"The barbarian (*al-ʿilj*) has exceeded against us and hastened."

The meaning of ﴿أو أن يطغى﴾ ("or that he will transgress") has been discussed shortly before.

The sentence ﴿قال لا تخافا﴾ ("He said: Do not fear, both of you") is a resumed sentence (*mustaʾnafah*), an answer to a presumed question. It forbids them from the fear that had arisen in them because of Pharaoh. Then he gives the reason in His words ﴿إنني معكما﴾ ("Indeed I am with you both"), meaning: with help for them and support against Pharaoh. The meaning of ﴿أسمع وأرى﴾ ("I hear and I see") is perceiving what passes between them and him, such that nothing of it is hidden from Him, glorified is He, and He is not heedless of them. Then He commanded them to come to Him. This coming is an expression for reaching Him after the command to go to him, so there is no repetition.

﴿فقولا إنا رسولا ربك﴾ ("So say: Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord") ﴿أرسلنا إليك﴾ ("We have been sent to you"). ﴿فأرسل معنا بني إسرائيل﴾ ("So send with us the Children of Israel"), meaning: release them and free them from captivity. ﴿ولا تعذبهم﴾ ("And do not punish them") by keeping them in the state they were in. They were in severe torment at Pharaoh's hands: he slaughtered their sons, spared their women, and burdened them with labour they could not bear.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded them to say to Pharaoh: ﴿قد جئناك بآية من ربك﴾ ("We have come to you with a sign from your Lord"). It is said the sign was the staff and the hand. It is also said that Pharaoh said to them: "And what is it?" So Mūsā put his hand into the opening of his shirt, then brought it out, and it had a light like the light of the sun. Pharaoh was amazed at this. Mūsā did not show him the staff except on the Day of the Festival (*yawm al-zīnah*).

﴿والسلام على من اتبع الهدى﴾ ("And peace be upon him who follows the guidance"): *al-salām* means safety (*al-salāmah*). Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that whoever follows the guidance is safe from the wrath of God, glorified and exalted is He, and from His punishment. It is not a greeting. He said: The evidence for this is that it is not the beginning of a meeting or an address. Al-Farrā' said: "Peace be upon him who follows the guidance" and "for him who follows the guidance" are equivalent.

﴿إنا قد أوحي إلينا﴾ ("Indeed it has been revealed to us") from God, glorified is He, ﴿أن العذاب على من كذب وتولى﴾ ("that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away"). By "punishment" is meant destruction and ruin in this world and eternal abiding in the Fire. By "denial" is meant denying the signs of God and His messengers. By "turning away" is meant refusing to accept them and to believe in them.

﴿قال فمن ربكما يا موسى﴾ ("He said: Then who is your Lord, O Mūsā?"). That is, Pharaoh said to them: "Then who is your Lord?" He attributed the Lord to the two of them and did not attribute Him to himself, because he did not confirm them and because he denied lordship. He singled out Mūsā with the address because he was the principal in the messengership. It is also said this was to match the rhyme-ends of the verses (*ruʾūs al-āy*).

﴿قال ربنا الذي أعطى كل شيء خلقه﴾ ("He said: Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation"). That is, Mūsā said in reply to him. *Rabbunā* is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *alladhī aʿṭā kulla shayʾin khalqahu*. It is also permitted that *rabbunā* be the predicate of an omitted subject, and what follows is its qualifier (*ṣifah*). The majority read *khalqahu* with a sukūn on the lām. Zāʾidah narrated from al-Aʿmash that he read *khalaqahu* with a fatḥah on the lām, as a verb. This is the reading of Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and Nuṣayr narrated it from al-Kisāʾī.

On the first reading, *khalqahu* is the second object (*mafʿūl*) of *aʿṭā*. The meaning is: He gave everything its form and shape which matches the benefit assigned to it, matching it, like the hand for seizing, the foot for walking, the tongue for speech, the eye for sight, and the ear for hearing. This is what al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: He gave everything its good state and guided it to what sets it right. Mujāhid said: The meaning is that He did not create the human form within the form of animals, nor the animals within the form of humans, but He created everything and determined it with a determination. From this is the poet's saying:
"For Him in everything He created, and thus God does what He wills."

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that He created for the man the woman, and for every male what suits him of females. On the first reading it is also permitted that *khalqahu* be the first object of *aʿṭā*: that is, He gave His creation everything they need and benefit from. The meaning of ﴿ثم هدى﴾ ("then guided") is that He, glorified is He, guided them to the ways of benefiting from what He gave them, so they benefited from everything in what it was created for. As for the last reading, the verb is a qualifier either of the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) or of the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the noun governed): that is, He gave everything God created its needs and did not leave it void of His giving. On this reading the second object is omitted: that is, He gave everything He created what it needs. Its meaning then agrees with the meaning of the first reading.

﴿قال فما بال القرون الأولى﴾ ("He said: Then what is the state of the former generations?"). When Pharaoh heard what Mūsā argued by implication in this speech for establishing lordship, as is clear, that creation and guidance are established without dispute, and they must have a creator and a guide, and that creator and guide is God, glorified is He, with no lord besides Him, Pharaoh said: "Then what is the state of the former generations? For they did not acknowledge the Lord to whom you call, O Mūsā, but worshipped idols and similar created things." The word *bāl* means state and condition: that is, what is their state and what is their condition? It is also said that Pharaoh's question about the former generations was a deception directed at Mūsā, when he feared that he would show his people that he had overcome him by argument. That is: what is the state of the past generations, and what happened to them of events?

Mūsā answered him: ﴿قال علمها عند ربي﴾ ("He said: Its knowledge is with my Lord"). That is: this which you ask about is not among what we are concerned with, but is from the knowledge of the unseen, which God has kept to Himself; neither you nor I know it. On the first interpretation, the meaning of ﴿علمها عند ربي﴾ is that the knowledge of those who worshipped idols and the like is preserved with God in His Book, and He will requite them for it. The meaning of its being in a Book is that it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*).

Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning is that their deeds are preserved with God, by which He will requite them. The implied phrase is: the knowledge of their deeds is with my Lord in a Book.

There has been disagreement about the meaning of ﴿لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى﴾ ("My Lord neither errs nor forgets"), in several views.

The first: it is a new statement (*ibtidāʾ kalām*) declaring God exalted above these two attributes. The speech is complete at His words ﴿في كتاب﴾ ("in a Book"). This is what al-Zajjāj said. He said: The meaning of *lā yaḍillu* is "does not perish," from His words ﴿أئذا ضللنا في الأرض﴾ ("When we have strayed in the earth?") [al-Sajdah: 10], and *lā yansā* means He forgets nothing of things. Thus He is declared free from perishing and forgetting.

The second view: the meaning of *lā yaḍillu* is "does not err."

The third view: its meaning is "does not disappear." Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: The root of *ḍalāl* is disappearance.

The fourth view: the meaning is that He has no need of a Book, and no knowledge of any thing escapes Him, and He does not forget what He knows of them. This was also reported from al-Zajjāj. Al-Naḥḥās said: It is the most similar of them to the meaning. It is not hidden that it resembles the view of Ibn al-Aʿrābī.

The fifth view: these two sentences are a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of "a Book," and the meaning is that the writer does not go away from God nor forget Him.

﴿الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهدا﴾ ("He who made the earth a cradle for you"): the relative clause is in the nominative case, as a qualifier of "my Lord" containing additional clarification. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative case by way of praise.

The Kūfans read *mahdan* as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of an implied verb: that is, *mahhadahā mahdan* ("He made it a cradle"), or with an omitted *muḍāf*: that is, *dhāt mahd* ("a thing of cradling"). It is a noun for what is made level, like a bed for what is spread out. The rest read ﴿مهادا﴾ (*mihādan*), and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim chose this reading, saying that the readers agree on ﴿ألم نجعل الأرض مهادا﴾ ("Have We not made the earth a bed?") [al-Naba': 6]. Al-Naḥḥās said: The plural is better than the verbal noun, because this place is not a place for the verbal noun except by omission of the *muḍāf*. It was said that *mihādan* may be singular like *firāsh*, and it may be a plural, and the meaning of *mihād* is a bed. So *mihād* is the plural of *mahd*: that is, He made every part of it a cradle for each one of you.

﴿وسلك لكم فيها سبلا﴾ ("and threaded for you in it roads"). *Al-salk* is inserting one thing into another. The meaning is: He put into the earth, for your sake, paths you may travel and made them easy for you. In the other verse: ﴿الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهدا وجعل لكم فيها سبلا لعلكم تهتدون﴾ ("He who made the earth a cradle for you and made for you in it roads, that perhaps you may be guided") [al-Zukhruf: 10].

Then He, glorified is He, said, bestowing favour upon His servants: ﴿وأنزل من السماء ماء﴾ ("and sent down water from the sky"), which is rainwater. It is said that here ends the speech of Mūsā, and what follows, ﴿فأخرجنا به أزواجا من نبات شتى﴾ ("so We brought forth by it pairs of various plants"), is from the speech of God, glorified is He. It is also said that it is part of the speech reported from Mūsā, coordinated with *anzala* (sent down). The shift to the first person plural (*al-taʿkallum*) was to draw attention to how evident the proof of complete power is in it. This was objected to: this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it entails losing the shift (*iltifāt*) because the speaker is not the same. It is answered that the whole speech is reported from one person, Mūsā, and the one who reports it all is God, glorified is He.

The meaning: We brought forth by that water, through tilling and cultivation, pairs: that is, kinds and sorts of various plants. His words *min nabāt* ("of plants") are a qualifier of *azwājan*, or an explanation of it. Likewise *shattā* ("various") is another qualifier of it, meaning scattered, the plural of *shatīt*. Al-Akhfash said: The implied sense is *azwājan shattā min nabāt* ("pairs, various, of plants"). He said: Plants may be various, so *shattā* may be an adjective of *azwājan* or an adjective of *nabāt*. It is said *amrun shatt* ("a scattered matter") meaning dispersed, and *shatta al-amru shattan wa shatātan* ("the matter scattered") meaning dispersed, and *ishtatta* is similar. *Al-shatīt* is the scattered.

Ru'ba said:
"They came together and lowered their eyes, scattered."

The sentence ﴿كلوا وارعوا﴾ ("Eat and graze") is in the accusative case as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), with an implied verb of saying: that is, saying to them that. The command is for permission. It is said *raʿat al-māshiyah al-kalaʾ* ("the livestock grazed the pasture") and *raʿāhā ṣāḥibuhā riʿāyatan* ("its owner pastured it"): that is, he let it loose and sent it out. It comes intransitive and transitive.

The reference in His words ﴿إن في ذلك لآيات لأولي النهى﴾ ("Indeed in that are signs for people of intellect") is to what has been mentioned in these verses. *Al-nuhā* means intellects, the plural of *nuhyah*. He singled out "people of intellect" because they are the ones to whose opinion one resorts. It is also said that it is because they restrain the self from vile things. All of this from Mūsā is an argument against Pharaoh for establishing the Maker, as an answer to his words: ﴿فمن ربكما يا موسى﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿منها خلقناكم﴾ ("from it We created you") and what follows refers back to the earth mentioned earlier. Al-Zajjāj and others said: That is, Adam was created from the earth and his offspring from him. It is also said the meaning is that every drop of seed created from dust is included within the creation of Adam, because every individual of mankind has a share of his creation. ﴿وفيها﴾ ("and into it") meaning into the earth, ﴿نعيدكم﴾ ("We return you") after death, so you are buried in it and your parts scatter until they become of the substance of the earth. He used *fī* rather than *ilā* ("to") to indicate settling. ﴿ومنها﴾ ("and from it") meaning from the earth ﴿نخرجكم تارة أخرى﴾ ("We bring you forth another time"), that is, by resurrection, rising, assembling of bodies and returning the spirits to them as they were before death. *Tāra* is like *marra* (a time).

﴿ولقد أرينا آياتنا كلها﴾ ("And We certainly showed him all Our signs"): that is, We showed Pharaoh and made him know all Our signs. By "signs" is meant the nine signs mentioned in His words: ﴿ولقد آتينا موسى تسع آيات﴾ ("And We gave Mūsā nine clear signs") [al-Isrāʾ: 101], with the annexation (*iḍāfah*) being to a known reference (*ʿahd*). It is also said: the meaning is all the signs that Mūsā brought, and those that other prophets brought, and that Mūsā had informed him of all his miracles and the miracles of all the other prophets. The first is preferable. It is also said that by "signs" is meant the proofs of God, glorified is He, which indicate His oneness. ﴿فكذب وأبى﴾ ("but he denied and refused"): that is, Pharaoh denied Mūsā and refused to respond to him by accepting faith. This indicates that Pharaoh's disbelief was obstinate disbelief, because he saw the signs and denied them, as in His words: ﴿وجحدوا بها واستيقنتها أنفسهم ظلما وعلوا﴾ ("And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance") [al-Naml: 14].

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 20, verses 45–59 (part 2 of 2)

The clause ﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Musa?"﴾ is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafah*), answering an implied question: it is as if it were said, "What did Pharaoh say after this?" The interrogative hamzah here expresses denial regarding what Musa brought of the signs. The meaning is: "You have come, O Musa, to deceive the people into believing that you are a prophet whom they must follow and whose message they must believe, so that through that deception, which is a branch of magic, you may gain control over our land and drive us out of it." The accursed one mentioned the expulsion from the land only to turn his people away from answering Musa, for once it settled in their minds and was fixed in their understanding that the outcome of responding to Musa would be leaving their homes and homelands, they would be unwilling to listen to his words, to consider his miracles, or to heed what he called them to of good.

﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it﴾. The *fāʾ* (here, "so") indicates that what follows is the result of what precedes it. The *lām* is the preparatory *lām* (*lām al-muwattiʾah*) for an oath. The meaning is: "By Allah, we will surely match you with magic like what you have brought, so that it becomes clear to the people that what you have brought is magic, which a sorcerer can equal." ﴿So set between us and you an appointment﴾. The word *mawʿid* is a verbal noun, meaning a promise; it was also said to be a noun of place, meaning: "Appoint for us a known day, or a known place, that we will not break." Al-Qushayri said: "The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said: 'we will not break it,' i.e., we will not break that promise. *Ikhlāf* means to promise something and not fulfil it." Al-Jawhari said: "*al-mīʿād* is a mutual agreement, and also the time or the place; likewise *al-mawʿid*."

Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Shaybah and al-Aʿraj read ﴿we will not break it﴾ with the jussive (*lā nukhlif-hu*), taking it as an answer to the imperative *ijʿal* ("set"). The rest of the readers read it with the nominative (*lā nukhlifu*), taking it as a qualifier of *mawʿidan* ("an appointment"): i.e., "we will not break that promise." ﴿Neither we nor you﴾. Pharaoh delegated the determination of the appointment to Musa, to demonstrate his complete power to bring the like of what Musa had brought. The accusative of ﴿a place equitable﴾ is either by a verb implied and indicated by the verbal noun, or it is a substitute (*badal*) for *mawʿid*. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read *suwan* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, and the rest read it with a *kasrah*; both are dialectal forms. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred the *kasrah* on the *sīn*, because it is the elevated, eloquent dialect. The meaning intended is "a level place"; it was also said: "an equitable and just place between us and you." Sibawayh said: "It is said *siwan* and *suwan*, i.e., just, meaning just between the two places." Zuhayr said:

*They showed us a plot in which there is no wrong,*
*in which equality makes us equal.*

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Qutaybi said: its meaning is "a middle place between the two groups." Abu ʿUbayda recited, for Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi:

*Indeed our father was settled in a town*
*equitable between Qays, the Qays of Ghaylan, and al-Fazar.*

Al-Fazar is Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

Then Musa made an appointment with them for a known time, and so ﴿He said: "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: that was a festival day on which they adorned themselves. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that was the day of ʿAshura. al-Dahhak said: it was Saturday. (p. 913) It was also said: it was the day of Nayruz, and it was said: the day the canal was broken open. al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, al-Sulami and Hubayrah from Hafs read *yawma l-zīnati* with the accusative, and this reading is also reported from Abu ʿAmr; meaning: "On the day of adornment is the fulfilment of our promise." The rest read it with the nominative, as the predicate of *mawʿiduku-m* ("your appointment"). The appointment was made a time after Pharaoh asked that it be a level place, because "the day of adornment" indicates a well-known place where people gather on that day, or it is by supposing an omitted genitive: i.e., "your appointment is the place of the day of adornment." ﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾. This is conjoined to *yawm al-zīna*, so it is in the nominative place if it is conjoined to *yawm*, or in the genitive place if it is conjoined to *al-zīna*. It means the forenoon of that day. The intended "people" are the people of Egypt. The meaning: they will be gathered for the festival at the time of forenoon, and will look into the matter of Musa and Pharaoh. al-Farraʾ said: the meaning is, "When you see the people gathered from every direction in the forenoon, that is the appointment." He said: "Their custom was to gather people on that day."

The *ḍuḥā* (forenoon): al-Jawhari said: "*ḍaḥwat al-nahār* is the time of the day after sunrise, then after it the *ḍuḥā*, which is when the sun shines. It was specified as the forenoon because it is the beginning of the day; when the matter extends between the two, there is ample room in the day." Ibn Masʿud and al-Jahdari read *wa-an yuḥsha*r with the active voice, meaning: "And that Allah gather the people in the forenoon." It was reported from al-Jahdari that he read *wa-an nuḥshara* with a *nūn*, and some readers read it with a *tāʾ* on top, i.e., *wa-an tuḥshara*, meaning: "that you, O Pharaoh, be gathered." The rest read it with the *yāʾ* from below, with the passive voice.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿Indeed we fear that he will hasten against us﴾, he said: "He will hasten," ﴿or that he will transgress﴾, he said: "He will exceed bounds." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding Allah's words ﴿I hear and I see﴾, he said: "I hear what he says and I see what he answers you with; then it is revealed to you, and you answer him." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "When Allah sent Musa to Pharaoh, he said: 'My Lord, what should I say?' He said: 'Say: *Ahya sharran hayya*.'" al-Aʿshā said: The interpretation of that: "The Living before everything, and the Living after everything." al-Suyuti judged its chain to be sound, and Ibn Kathir had preceded him in judging its chain sound in his *Tafsir*.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding Allah's words ﴿upon whoever denies and turns away﴾, he said: "He denied the Book of Allah and turned away from obedience to Allah." Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmaʾ wa-l-Sifat* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾, he said: "He created for everything its mate," ﴿then guided﴾, he said: "He guided it to its mating, its food, its drink and its dwelling." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿My Lord does not err﴾, he said: "He does not make a mistake." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿of diverse plants﴾, he said: "Varied."

Regarding Allah's words ﴿for people of understanding﴾, he said: "for people of piety." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: ﴿for people of understanding﴾, he said: "for people of intellect and reason." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAta' al-Khurasani, he said: "The angel goes and takes dust from the place where the person will be buried and scatters it upon the drop of semen, so he creates from the dust and from the drop, and that is His saying: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you﴾."

Ahmad and al-Hakim reported from Abu Umamah, he said: "When Umm Kulthum, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was placed in the grave, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once more﴾, in the name of Allah, and in the way of Allah, and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." And in a hadith in the *Sunan*, "that he took a handful of dust and threw it into the grave and said: ﴿From it We created you﴾, then another handful and said: ﴿And into it We will return you﴾, then another and said: ﴿And from it We will bring you out once more﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾, he said: "It is the day of ʿAshura." Ibn al-Mundhir reported something similar from Ibn ʿAmr.

The majority of readers recite ﴿أن يفرط﴾ (*an yafruṭa*, "that he may hasten") with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the rā'. The meaning is: "We fear that he will hurry and rush to punish us." It is said *faraṭa minhu amr*, meaning *badara* (he was hasty in it). From this comes *al-fāriṭ* (the forerunner), who goes ahead of the people to the water, so the sense is: he will punish us like one who goes ahead in sin. This is what al-Mubarrad said. He also said: *faraṭa minhu amr* and *afraṭa* mean "he exceeded the limit" (*asrafa*), and *farraṭa* means "he neglected" (*taraka*).

Ibn Muhayṣin read ﴿يُفرَط﴾ (*yufraṭa*) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the rā', meaning: someone drives him to hasten toward us. A group read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', from *al-ifrāṭ* (excess), meaning he will go beyond bounds in harming us. Among them were Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah.

The reciter (*al-rājiz*) said:
"The barbarian (*al-ʿilj*) has exceeded against us and hastened."

The meaning of ﴿أو أن يطغى﴾ ("or that he will transgress") has been discussed shortly before.

The sentence ﴿قال لا تخافا﴾ ("He said: Do not fear, both of you") is a resumed sentence (*mustaʾnafah*), an answer to a presumed question. It forbids them from the fear that had arisen in them because of Pharaoh. Then he gives the reason in His words ﴿إنني معكما﴾ ("Indeed I am with you both"), meaning: with help for them and support against Pharaoh. The meaning of ﴿أسمع وأرى﴾ ("I hear and I see") is perceiving what passes between them and him, such that nothing of it is hidden from Him, glorified is He, and He is not heedless of them. Then He commanded them to come to Him. This coming is an expression for reaching Him after the command to go to him, so there is no repetition.

﴿فقولا إنا رسولا ربك﴾ ("So say: Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord") ﴿أرسلنا إليك﴾ ("We have been sent to you"). ﴿فأرسل معنا بني إسرائيل﴾ ("So send with us the Children of Israel"), meaning: release them and free them from captivity. ﴿ولا تعذبهم﴾ ("And do not punish them") by keeping them in the state they were in. They were in severe torment at Pharaoh's hands: he slaughtered their sons, spared their women, and burdened them with labour they could not bear.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded them to say to Pharaoh: ﴿قد جئناك بآية من ربك﴾ ("We have come to you with a sign from your Lord"). It is said the sign was the staff and the hand. It is also said that Pharaoh said to them: "And what is it?" So Mūsā put his hand into the opening of his shirt, then brought it out, and it had a light like the light of the sun. Pharaoh was amazed at this. Mūsā did not show him the staff except on the Day of the Festival (*yawm al-zīnah*).

﴿والسلام على من اتبع الهدى﴾ ("And peace be upon him who follows the guidance"): *al-salām* means safety (*al-salāmah*). Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that whoever follows the guidance is safe from the wrath of God, glorified and exalted is He, and from His punishment. It is not a greeting. He said: The evidence for this is that it is not the beginning of a meeting or an address. Al-Farrā' said: "Peace be upon him who follows the guidance" and "for him who follows the guidance" are equivalent.

﴿إنا قد أوحي إلينا﴾ ("Indeed it has been revealed to us") from God, glorified is He, ﴿أن العذاب على من كذب وتولى﴾ ("that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away"). By "punishment" is meant destruction and ruin in this world and eternal abiding in the Fire. By "denial" is meant denying the signs of God and His messengers. By "turning away" is meant refusing to accept them and to believe in them.

﴿قال فمن ربكما يا موسى﴾ ("He said: Then who is your Lord, O Mūsā?"). That is, Pharaoh said to them: "Then who is your Lord?" He attributed the Lord to the two of them and did not attribute Him to himself, because he did not confirm them and because he denied lordship. He singled out Mūsā with the address because he was the principal in the messengership. It is also said this was to match the rhyme-ends of the verses (*ruʾūs al-āy*).

﴿قال ربنا الذي أعطى كل شيء خلقه﴾ ("He said: Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation"). That is, Mūsā said in reply to him. *Rabbunā* is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *alladhī aʿṭā kulla shayʾin khalqahu*. It is also permitted that *rabbunā* be the predicate of an omitted subject, and what follows is its qualifier (*ṣifah*). The majority read *khalqahu* with a sukūn on the lām. Zāʾidah narrated from al-Aʿmash that he read *khalaqahu* with a fatḥah on the lām, as a verb. This is the reading of Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and Nuṣayr narrated it from al-Kisāʾī.

On the first reading, *khalqahu* is the second object (*mafʿūl*) of *aʿṭā*. The meaning is: He gave everything its form and shape which matches the benefit assigned to it, matching it, like the hand for seizing, the foot for walking, the tongue for speech, the eye for sight, and the ear for hearing. This is what al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: He gave everything its good state and guided it to what sets it right. Mujāhid said: The meaning is that He did not create the human form within the form of animals, nor the animals within the form of humans, but He created everything and determined it with a determination. From this is the poet's saying:
"For Him in everything He created, and thus God does what He wills."

Al-Farrā' said: The meaning is that He created for the man the woman, and for every male what suits him of females. On the first reading it is also permitted that *khalqahu* be the first object of *aʿṭā*: that is, He gave His creation everything they need and benefit from. The meaning of ﴿ثم هدى﴾ ("then guided") is that He, glorified is He, guided them to the ways of benefiting from what He gave them, so they benefited from everything in what it was created for. As for the last reading, the verb is a qualifier either of the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) or of the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the noun governed): that is, He gave everything God created its needs and did not leave it void of His giving. On this reading the second object is omitted: that is, He gave everything He created what it needs. Its meaning then agrees with the meaning of the first reading.

﴿قال فما بال القرون الأولى﴾ ("He said: Then what is the state of the former generations?"). When Pharaoh heard what Mūsā argued by implication in this speech for establishing lordship, as is clear, that creation and guidance are established without dispute, and they must have a creator and a guide, and that creator and guide is God, glorified is He, with no lord besides Him, Pharaoh said: "Then what is the state of the former generations? For they did not acknowledge the Lord to whom you call, O Mūsā, but worshipped idols and similar created things." The word *bāl* means state and condition: that is, what is their state and what is their condition? It is also said that Pharaoh's question about the former generations was a deception directed at Mūsā, when he feared that he would show his people that he had overcome him by argument. That is: what is the state of the past generations, and what happened to them of events?

Mūsā answered him: ﴿قال علمها عند ربي﴾ ("He said: Its knowledge is with my Lord"). That is: this which you ask about is not among what we are concerned with, but is from the knowledge of the unseen, which God has kept to Himself; neither you nor I know it. On the first interpretation, the meaning of ﴿علمها عند ربي﴾ is that the knowledge of those who worshipped idols and the like is preserved with God in His Book, and He will requite them for it. The meaning of its being in a Book is that it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*).

Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning is that their deeds are preserved with God, by which He will requite them. The implied phrase is: the knowledge of their deeds is with my Lord in a Book.

There has been disagreement about the meaning of ﴿لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى﴾ ("My Lord neither errs nor forgets"), in several views.

The first: it is a new statement (*ibtidāʾ kalām*) declaring God exalted above these two attributes. The speech is complete at His words ﴿في كتاب﴾ ("in a Book"). This is what al-Zajjāj said. He said: The meaning of *lā yaḍillu* is "does not perish," from His words ﴿أئذا ضللنا في الأرض﴾ ("When we have strayed in the earth?") [al-Sajdah: 10], and *lā yansā* means He forgets nothing of things. Thus He is declared free from perishing and forgetting.

The second view: the meaning of *lā yaḍillu* is "does not err."

The third view: its meaning is "does not disappear." Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: The root of *ḍalāl* is disappearance.

The fourth view: the meaning is that He has no need of a Book, and no knowledge of any thing escapes Him, and He does not forget what He knows of them. This was also reported from al-Zajjāj. Al-Naḥḥās said: It is the most similar of them to the meaning. It is not hidden that it resembles the view of Ibn al-Aʿrābī.

The fifth view: these two sentences are a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of "a Book," and the meaning is that the writer does not go away from God nor forget Him.

﴿الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهدا﴾ ("He who made the earth a cradle for you"): the relative clause is in the nominative case, as a qualifier of "my Lord" containing additional clarification. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative case by way of praise.

The Kūfans read *mahdan* as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of an implied verb: that is, *mahhadahā mahdan* ("He made it a cradle"), or with an omitted *muḍāf*: that is, *dhāt mahd* ("a thing of cradling"). It is a noun for what is made level, like a bed for what is spread out. The rest read ﴿مهادا﴾ (*mihādan*), and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim chose this reading, saying that the readers agree on ﴿ألم نجعل الأرض مهادا﴾ ("Have We not made the earth a bed?") [al-Naba': 6]. Al-Naḥḥās said: The plural is better than the verbal noun, because this place is not a place for the verbal noun except by omission of the *muḍāf*. It was said that *mihādan* may be singular like *firāsh*, and it may be a plural, and the meaning of *mihād* is a bed. So *mihād* is the plural of *mahd*: that is, He made every part of it a cradle for each one of you.

﴿وسلك لكم فيها سبلا﴾ ("and threaded for you in it roads"). *Al-salk* is inserting one thing into another. The meaning is: He put into the earth, for your sake, paths you may travel and made them easy for you. In the other verse: ﴿الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهدا وجعل لكم فيها سبلا لعلكم تهتدون﴾ ("He who made the earth a cradle for you and made for you in it roads, that perhaps you may be guided") [al-Zukhruf: 10].

Then He, glorified is He, said, bestowing favour upon His servants: ﴿وأنزل من السماء ماء﴾ ("and sent down water from the sky"), which is rainwater. It is said that here ends the speech of Mūsā, and what follows, ﴿فأخرجنا به أزواجا من نبات شتى﴾ ("so We brought forth by it pairs of various plants"), is from the speech of God, glorified is He. It is also said that it is part of the speech reported from Mūsā, coordinated with *anzala* (sent down). The shift to the first person plural (*al-taʿkallum*) was to draw attention to how evident the proof of complete power is in it. This was objected to: this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it entails losing the shift (*iltifāt*) because the speaker is not the same. It is answered that the whole speech is reported from one person, Mūsā, and the one who reports it all is God, glorified is He.

The meaning: We brought forth by that water, through tilling and cultivation, pairs: that is, kinds and sorts of various plants. His words *min nabāt* ("of plants") are a qualifier of *azwājan*, or an explanation of it. Likewise *shattā* ("various") is another qualifier of it, meaning scattered, the plural of *shatīt*. Al-Akhfash said: The implied sense is *azwājan shattā min nabāt* ("pairs, various, of plants"). He said: Plants may be various, so *shattā* may be an adjective of *azwājan* or an adjective of *nabāt*. It is said *amrun shatt* ("a scattered matter") meaning dispersed, and *shatta al-amru shattan wa shatātan* ("the matter scattered") meaning dispersed, and *ishtatta* is similar. *Al-shatīt* is the scattered.

Ru'ba said:
"They came together and lowered their eyes, scattered."

The sentence ﴿كلوا وارعوا﴾ ("Eat and graze") is in the accusative case as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), with an implied verb of saying: that is, saying to them that. The command is for permission. It is said *raʿat al-māshiyah al-kalaʾ* ("the livestock grazed the pasture") and *raʿāhā ṣāḥibuhā riʿāyatan* ("its owner pastured it"): that is, he let it loose and sent it out. It comes intransitive and transitive.

The reference in His words ﴿إن في ذلك لآيات لأولي النهى﴾ ("Indeed in that are signs for people of intellect") is to what has been mentioned in these verses. *Al-nuhā* means intellects, the plural of *nuhyah*. He singled out "people of intellect" because they are the ones to whose opinion one resorts. It is also said that it is because they restrain the self from vile things. All of this from Mūsā is an argument against Pharaoh for establishing the Maker, as an answer to his words: ﴿فمن ربكما يا موسى﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿منها خلقناكم﴾ ("from it We created you") and what follows refers back to the earth mentioned earlier. Al-Zajjāj and others said: That is, Adam was created from the earth and his offspring from him. It is also said the meaning is that every drop of seed created from dust is included within the creation of Adam, because every individual of mankind has a share of his creation. ﴿وفيها﴾ ("and into it") meaning into the earth, ﴿نعيدكم﴾ ("We return you") after death, so you are buried in it and your parts scatter until they become of the substance of the earth. He used *fī* rather than *ilā* ("to") to indicate settling. ﴿ومنها﴾ ("and from it") meaning from the earth ﴿نخرجكم تارة أخرى﴾ ("We bring you forth another time"), that is, by resurrection, rising, assembling of bodies and returning the spirits to them as they were before death. *Tāra* is like *marra* (a time).

﴿ولقد أرينا آياتنا كلها﴾ ("And We certainly showed him all Our signs"): that is, We showed Pharaoh and made him know all Our signs. By "signs" is meant the nine signs mentioned in His words: ﴿ولقد آتينا موسى تسع آيات﴾ ("And We gave Mūsā nine clear signs") [al-Isrāʾ: 101], with the annexation (*iḍāfah*) being to a known reference (*ʿahd*). It is also said: the meaning is all the signs that Mūsā brought, and those that other prophets brought, and that Mūsā had informed him of all his miracles and the miracles of all the other prophets. The first is preferable. It is also said that by "signs" is meant the proofs of God, glorified is He, which indicate His oneness. ﴿فكذب وأبى﴾ ("but he denied and refused"): that is, Pharaoh denied Mūsā and refused to respond to him by accepting faith. This indicates that Pharaoh's disbelief was obstinate disbelief, because he saw the signs and denied them, as in His words: ﴿وجحدوا بها واستيقنتها أنفسهم ظلما وعلوا﴾ ("And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance") [al-Naml: 14].

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 20, verses 45–59 (part 2 of 2)

The clause ﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Musa?"﴾ is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafah*), answering an implied question: it is as if it were said, "What did Pharaoh say after this?" The interrogative hamzah here expresses denial regarding what Musa brought of the signs. The meaning is: "You have come, O Musa, to deceive the people into believing that you are a prophet whom they must follow and whose message they must believe, so that through that deception, which is a branch of magic, you may gain control over our land and drive us out of it." The accursed one mentioned the expulsion from the land only to turn his people away from answering Musa, for once it settled in their minds and was fixed in their understanding that the outcome of responding to Musa would be leaving their homes and homelands, they would be unwilling to listen to his words, to consider his miracles, or to heed what he called them to of good.

﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it﴾. The *fāʾ* (here, "so") indicates that what follows is the result of what precedes it. The *lām* is the preparatory *lām* (*lām al-muwattiʾah*) for an oath. The meaning is: "By Allah, we will surely match you with magic like what you have brought, so that it becomes clear to the people that what you have brought is magic, which a sorcerer can equal." ﴿So set between us and you an appointment﴾. The word *mawʿid* is a verbal noun, meaning a promise; it was also said to be a noun of place, meaning: "Appoint for us a known day, or a known place, that we will not break." Al-Qushayri said: "The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun, and for this reason he said: 'we will not break it,' i.e., we will not break that promise. *Ikhlāf* means to promise something and not fulfil it." Al-Jawhari said: "*al-mīʿād* is a mutual agreement, and also the time or the place; likewise *al-mawʿid*."

Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Shaybah and al-Aʿraj read ﴿we will not break it﴾ with the jussive (*lā nukhlif-hu*), taking it as an answer to the imperative *ijʿal* ("set"). The rest of the readers read it with the nominative (*lā nukhlifu*), taking it as a qualifier of *mawʿidan* ("an appointment"): i.e., "we will not break that promise." ﴿Neither we nor you﴾. Pharaoh delegated the determination of the appointment to Musa, to demonstrate his complete power to bring the like of what Musa had brought. The accusative of ﴿a place equitable﴾ is either by a verb implied and indicated by the verbal noun, or it is a substitute (*badal*) for *mawʿid*. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read *suwan* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn*, and the rest read it with a *kasrah*; both are dialectal forms. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred the *kasrah* on the *sīn*, because it is the elevated, eloquent dialect. The meaning intended is "a level place"; it was also said: "an equitable and just place between us and you." Sibawayh said: "It is said *siwan* and *suwan*, i.e., just, meaning just between the two places." Zuhayr said:

*They showed us a plot in which there is no wrong,*
*in which equality makes us equal.*

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Qutaybi said: its meaning is "a middle place between the two groups." Abu ʿUbayda recited, for Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi:

*Indeed our father was settled in a town*
*equitable between Qays, the Qays of Ghaylan, and al-Fazar.*

Al-Fazar is Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

Then Musa made an appointment with them for a known time, and so ﴿He said: "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: that was a festival day on which they adorned themselves. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that was the day of ʿAshura. al-Dahhak said: it was Saturday. (p. 913) It was also said: it was the day of Nayruz, and it was said: the day the canal was broken open. al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, al-Sulami and Hubayrah from Hafs read *yawma l-zīnati* with the accusative, and this reading is also reported from Abu ʿAmr; meaning: "On the day of adornment is the fulfilment of our promise." The rest read it with the nominative, as the predicate of *mawʿiduku-m* ("your appointment"). The appointment was made a time after Pharaoh asked that it be a level place, because "the day of adornment" indicates a well-known place where people gather on that day, or it is by supposing an omitted genitive: i.e., "your appointment is the place of the day of adornment." ﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾. This is conjoined to *yawm al-zīna*, so it is in the nominative place if it is conjoined to *yawm*, or in the genitive place if it is conjoined to *al-zīna*. It means the forenoon of that day. The intended "people" are the people of Egypt. The meaning: they will be gathered for the festival at the time of forenoon, and will look into the matter of Musa and Pharaoh. al-Farraʾ said: the meaning is, "When you see the people gathered from every direction in the forenoon, that is the appointment." He said: "Their custom was to gather people on that day."

The *ḍuḥā* (forenoon): al-Jawhari said: "*ḍaḥwat al-nahār* is the time of the day after sunrise, then after it the *ḍuḥā*, which is when the sun shines. It was specified as the forenoon because it is the beginning of the day; when the matter extends between the two, there is ample room in the day." Ibn Masʿud and al-Jahdari read *wa-an yuḥsha*r with the active voice, meaning: "And that Allah gather the people in the forenoon." It was reported from al-Jahdari that he read *wa-an nuḥshara* with a *nūn*, and some readers read it with a *tāʾ* on top, i.e., *wa-an tuḥshara*, meaning: "that you, O Pharaoh, be gathered." The rest read it with the *yāʾ* from below, with the passive voice.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿Indeed we fear that he will hasten against us﴾, he said: "He will hasten," ﴿or that he will transgress﴾, he said: "He will exceed bounds." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding Allah's words ﴿I hear and I see﴾, he said: "I hear what he says and I see what he answers you with; then it is revealed to you, and you answer him." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "When Allah sent Musa to Pharaoh, he said: 'My Lord, what should I say?' He said: 'Say: *Ahya sharran hayya*.'" al-Aʿshā said: The interpretation of that: "The Living before everything, and the Living after everything." al-Suyuti judged its chain to be sound, and Ibn Kathir had preceded him in judging its chain sound in his *Tafsir*.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding Allah's words ﴿upon whoever denies and turns away﴾, he said: "He denied the Book of Allah and turned away from obedience to Allah." Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmaʾ wa-l-Sifat* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾, he said: "He created for everything its mate," ﴿then guided﴾, he said: "He guided it to its mating, its food, its drink and its dwelling." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿My Lord does not err﴾, he said: "He does not make a mistake." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿of diverse plants﴾, he said: "Varied."

Regarding Allah's words ﴿for people of understanding﴾, he said: "for people of piety." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: ﴿for people of understanding﴾, he said: "for people of intellect and reason." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAta' al-Khurasani, he said: "The angel goes and takes dust from the place where the person will be buried and scatters it upon the drop of semen, so he creates from the dust and from the drop, and that is His saying: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you﴾."

Ahmad and al-Hakim reported from Abu Umamah, he said: "When Umm Kulthum, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was placed in the grave, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once more﴾, in the name of Allah, and in the way of Allah, and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." And in a hadith in the *Sunan*, "that he took a handful of dust and threw it into the grave and said: ﴿From it We created you﴾, then another handful and said: ﴿And into it We will return you﴾, then another and said: ﴿And from it We will bring you out once more﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding Allah's words ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾, he said: "It is the day of ʿAshura." Ibn al-Mundhir reported something similar from Ibn ʿAmr.

﴿فَتَوَلّى فِرْعَوْنُ﴾ means he turned away from that place to prepare what he needed for what they had agreed upon. It was also said that the meaning of "tawallā" is that he turned away from the truth, but the first meaning is preferable. ﴿فَجَمَعَ كَيْدَهُ﴾ means he gathered what he would use to plot, of his magic and his stratagems. The intended meaning is that he gathered the magicians. It was said they were seventy-two, and it was said four hundred, and it was said twelve thousand, and it was said fourteen thousand. Ibn al-Mundhir said they were eighty thousand. ﴿ثُمَّ أتى﴾ means he came to the appointment they had agreed upon, together with the gathering he had assembled. The clause ﴿قالَ لَهم مُوسى﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah), an answer to an assumed question. ﴿ويْلَكم لا تَفْتَرُوا عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا﴾: he invoked woe upon them and forbade them from fabricating lies against God. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is in the accusative governed by an omitted verb, and the implied meaning is that God has imposed woe upon them." He said: "It may also be a vocative, like His words: ﴿يا ويْلَنا مَن بَعَثَنا مِن مَرْقَدِنا﴾ [Yāsīn 36:52]." ﴿فَيُسْحِتَكم بِعَذابٍ﴾: al-suḥt means extermination. It is said saḥta and asḥta with the same meaning, and its original sense is thorough removal of hair. The Kufans, except Shuʿbah, read ﴿فَيُسْحِتَكُمْ﴾ with a dammah on the imperfect prefix, from asḥta, and this is the dialect of Banū Tamīm. The rest read it with a fatḥah, from saḥta, and this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Its accusative case is because it is an answer to the prohibition (jawāb al-nahy). ﴿وقَدْ خابَ مَنِ افْتَرى﴾ means he lost and perished. The meaning is: whoever fabricates against God has lost, whatever lie it may be.

﴿فَتَنازَعُوا أمْرَهم بَيْنَهُمْ﴾: the magicians, when they heard Mūsā's words, debated among themselves, consulted, and tossed the points of the matter back and forth. ﴿وأسَرُّوا النَّجْوى﴾ means they concealed their secret counsel from Mūsā. Their secret counsel was their saying: ﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾. It was said that they whispered among themselves, saying: "If what Mūsā has brought is magic, we will overcome him, and if it is from God, then there will be a matter for him." It was also said that what they concealed was that if he overcame them, they would follow him, as said by al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. It was said too that what they concealed was that, when they heard Mūsā's words, "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against God," they said: "This is not the speech of a magician." (p-914) Al-najwā means private conversation, and it is used both as a noun and as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Abū ʿAmr read ﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ with a shaddah on the particle entering the clause, and with a yāʾ in the demonstrative, treating inna as governing in its familiar way, namely the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. This reading is related from ʿUthmān, ʿĀʾishah, and other Companions. Al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿī, and other Successors also read it this way. ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar also read this way, as al-Naḥḥās reported. This reading agrees with the apparent grammatical case but differs from the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, since it is written with an alif. Al-Zuhrī, al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, al-Mufaḍḍal, Abān, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ibn Kathīr, and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Ḥafṣ from him read ﴿إنْ هَذانِ﴾ with a light inna, taking it as a negative particle. This reading agrees with the orthography of the Muṣḥaf and with the grammatical case. Ibn Kathīr read like them except that he doubled the nūn in hadhāni. The Medinans, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿إنَّ هَذانِ﴾ with a shaddah on inna and with an alif. Thus they agreed with the orthography but differed from the apparent grammar.

A group of scholars have spoken about the justification of the reading of the Medinans, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿĀmir. Ibn al-Anbārī and al-Naḥḥās fully covered this. It was said that it is the dialect of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, and Kinānah, who make the nominative, accusative, and genitive of the dual with an alif. From this is the words of the poet:

*So he lowered his gaze in the manner of the brave, and had he seen an opening for his fangs, the brave one would have been struck silent.*

And the words of another:

*He took from us a blow between his two ears as provision.*

And the words of another:

*Indeed her father and her father's father have both reached the utmost of glory.*

What supports this is the explicit statement of Sībawayh, al-Akhfash, Abū Zayd, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Farrāʾ that this reading is according to the dialect of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb. Abū ʿUbaydah related from Abū al-Khaṭṭāb that it is the dialect of Banū Kinānah, and someone else related that it is the dialect of Khathʿam. It was also said that inna here means "yes," as al-Kisāʾī related from ʿĀṣim, and Sībawayh likewise related it. Al-Naḥḥās said: "I saw al-Zajjāj and al-Akhfash going this way," so the implied meaning is: "Yes, these two are magicians." From this is the words of the poet:

*Would that I knew whether there is a cure for the lover from the anguish of his love for them. Yes, the meeting.*

That is, "Yes, the meeting." Al-Zajjāj said: "The meaning in the verse is: this belongs to both of them, they are two magicians," and then he omitted the subject, which is "they two" (humā). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and Abū al-Fatḥ ibn Jinnī rejected this. It was also said: the alif in hadhā is made similar to the alif in yafʿalāni, so it was not changed. It was also said that there is an implied hāʾ: "indeed it, these two are magicians." Al-Zajjāj related this from early grammarians, and Ibn al-Anbārī likewise related it. Ibn Kaysān said: since hadhā is said with an alif in the nominative, accusative, and genitive in one unchanged form, and the dual does not change the singular, the dual was treated like the singular, so the alif remained in the nominative, accusative, and genitive. These are sayings that include the justification of this reading, a justification by which it is sound and by which it is freed from error. Through this, what was reported from ʿUthmān and ʿĀʾishah, that it was a mistake by the scribe of the Muṣḥaf, is refuted.

﴿يُرِيدانِ أنْ يُخْرِجاكم مِن أرْضِكم﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿بِسِحْرِهِما﴾ that they have displayed, ﴿ويَذْهَبا بِطَرِيقَتِكُمُ المُثْلى﴾. Al-Kisāʾī said: "bi-ṭarīqatikum" means "with your sunnah." Al-Muthlā is an adjective, like your saying: "a great woman" (imraʾah kubrā). The Arabs say: "So-and-so is on the best way (al-ṭarīqah al-muthlā)," meaning on the upright guidance. Al-Farrāʾ said: The Arabs say: "These are the way of their people and the ways of their people," meaning their nobles. Al-muthlā is the feminine of al-amthal, which means the best, and one says: "So-and-so is the best (amthal) of his people," that is, their best, and they are the excellent ones (al-amāthil). The meaning is: if they overcome you by their magic, the leaders and nobles among you will incline towards them, or they will make you go by your way, which is the best of ways.

﴿فَأجْمِعُوا كَيْدَكُمْ﴾: al-ijmāʿ means firm determination, and resolve upon a matter, as al-Farrāʾ said. You say: "I resolved (ajmaʿtu) on the departure," like "azmaʿtu." Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is: let your resolve be all of you together, like a plot agreed upon. The reciters agreed on the hamzah being cut in ajmiʿū, except Abū ʿAmr, who read it with a connecting hamzah and a fatḥah on the mīm from al-jamʿ. Al-Naḥḥās said: "It was related to me from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad that he said: Abū ʿAmr must read against this reading, which is the reading that most people follow." ﴿ثُمَّ ائْتُوا صَفًّا﴾ means lined up in rows, gathered together, so that their affair would be more orderly and their awe greater. This is the saying of the majority of exegetes. Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-ṣaff is the place of gathering, and the place of prayer is called al-ṣaff. Al-Zajjāj said: according to this, the meaning is: "Then come to the place where you gather for your festival and your prayer." It is said "atayt al-ṣaff," meaning "I came to the place of prayer." So according to the first explanation, the accusative of ṣaffan is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and according to Abū ʿUbaydah's explanation, its accusative is as an object. Al-Zajjāj said: it may mean "then come to the people, lined up," and in that case it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative, and for this reason it was not made plural. It was also read with a kasrah on the hamzah after which there is a yāʾ, and whoever drops the hamzah replaces it with an alif. ﴿وقَدْ أفْلَحَ اليَوْمَ مَنِ اسْتَعْلى﴾ means whoever prevails. It is said: "He overcame him" (istaʿlā ʿalayhi) when he overpowered him. All of this is the speech of the magicians to one another. It was also said that it is the speech of Pharaoh to them.

The clause ﴿قالُوا يا مُوسى إمّا أنْ تُلْقِيَ﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did they do after they had said among themselves what they said?" So it was said: ﴿قالُوا يامُوسى إمّا أنْ تُلْقِيَ﴾. Anna with what follows it is in the position of an accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: choose your throwing first or our throwing. It may also be in the position of a nominative, with it and what follows it being the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is your throwing or our throwing. The object of tulqī is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "Either you throw what you throw first." ﴿وإمّا أنْ نَكُونَ﴾, we, ﴿أوَّلَ مَن ألْقى﴾ what he throws, or first to do the throwing. The intended meaning is the throwing of staves upon the ground. The magicians had staves with them, and Mūsā had thrown his staff on the day he entered upon Pharaoh. So when the magicians wanted to oppose him, they said this to him. ﴿بَلْ ألْقُوا﴾ Mūsā said to them: he commanded them to throw first (p-915), so that his miracle would be more manifest when they had thrown what they had and then he threw his staff, and it swallowed that, and as a display of indifference to their magic. ﴿فَإذا حِبالُهم وعِصِيُّهُمْ﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "So they threw, and behold, their ropes." The fāʾ is an explanatory fāʾ (faṣīḥah), and idhā is either for sudden surprise or for time. The meaning is: they threw, and Mūsā was suddenly struck at the time when the movement of their ropes and staves was imagined to him. Al-Ḥasan read ʿuṣiyyuhum with a ḍammah on the ʿayn, which is the dialect of Banū Tamīm. The rest read it with a kasrah, following the kasrah of the ṣād. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Dhakwān, and Rawḥ from Yaʿqūb read tukhayyalu with a yāʾ, because the staves and the ropes are feminine. That was because they had smeared them with mercury, and when the heat of the sun reached them they trembled and moved. It was read nukhayyilu with a nūn, meaning that God, may He be glorified, is the one who makes it appear so. It was read yukhayyilu with a tahtiyyah, in the active voice, meaning that what makes it appear is the plot. It was also said that what makes it appear is that they move, since the particle anna is in the position of a nominative, meaning: their movement is imagined to him. al-Zajjāj mentioned this meaning. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the position of an accusative, meaning "because that," and then he omitted the bāʾ.

Al-Zajjāj said: whoever read with the tāʾ, meaning the upper tāʾ (the feminine form), took anna to be in the position of an accusative, meaning: it is imagined to him that they are possessed of motion. He said: it may also be in the position of a nominative, as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in tukhayyalu, which refers to the ropes and staves, and the substitution here is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl). It is said: "It was made to appear to him" (khuyyila ilayhi) when it was made to resemble something for him and the confusion and doubt were introduced into him.

﴿فَأوْجَسَ في نَفْسِهِ خِيفَةً مُوسى﴾: that is, he sensed. It was said: he found. It was said: he concealed. It was said: he feared. This was because of what arises from human nature when one sees what one fears. It was said: he feared that people would be seduced before he threw his staff. It was said: the cause of his fear was that their magic was of the same kind as what he had shown them in the staff, so he feared that his affair would be confused for the people and they would not believe. Then God, may He be glorified, removed the fear that had come upon him by the good news He gave him in His words: ﴿قُلْنا لا تَخَفْ إنَّكَ أنْتَ الأعْلى﴾, that is, the one who prevails over them by victory and triumph. The clause is a reason for the prohibition against fear.

﴿وألْقِ ما في يَمِينِكَ﴾ means the staff. He left it indefinite out of magnification and glorification. The jussive of ﴿تَلْقَفْ ما صَنَعُوا﴾ is because it is the answer to the command. It was read with a shaddah on the qāf, and the original is tatalaqqafu, and one of the two tāʾs was omitted. It was read talqaf with a kasrah on the lām, from laqifahu, meaning he swallowed it swiftly. It was read talqafu with a ḍammah, on the assumption of fa-innahā tatalaqqafu. The meaning of ﴿ما صَنَعُوا﴾ is what they made of the ropes and staves. Al-Zajjāj said: the reading with the jussive is the answer to the command. The nominative is permitted, in the sense of a circumstantial clause, as if he said: "Throw it swallowing." The clause ﴿إنَّما صَنَعُوا كَيْدُ ساحِرٍ﴾ is a reason for His words "talqaf." The nominative of kayd is because it is the predicate of inna. This is the reading of the Kufans except ʿĀṣim. They read siḥrin with a kasrah on the sīn and a sukūn on the ḥāʾ, and the idāfah of kayd, that is siḥr, is by widening the usage without an implied term, or by an implied "possessor of magic." The rest read kayda sāḥirin.

﴿ولا يُفْلِحُ السّاحِرُ حَيْثُ أتى﴾: that is, the category of magician does not prosper wherever he goes and in whatever direction he turns. This is part of the completion of the reason.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 60–70 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ That is, the matter they had witnessed from Musa and the staff cast the magicians down prostrate before Allah, the Exalted. The verification of this has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf. ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa."﴾ He mentioned Harun before Musa in reporting their words in order to observe the *fawasil al-ayi* (the rhyming endings of the verses) and to attend to the harmony of their final sounds.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿He will destroy you with a punishment﴾, that he said: "He will ruin you."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿He will destroy you﴾ that he said: "He will uproot you."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Salih that he said: "He will slaughter you."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali regarding ﴿and they will take away your best way of life﴾ that he said: "They will turn people's faces towards themselves."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It means your best, and they are the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd and Abd al-Razzaq narrated regarding His words ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, "what they have falsified," from Qatadah, who said: "Musa cast it down, and it turned into a serpent that devoured their ropes and what they had made."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah that the magicians of Pharaoh were nine hundred. They said to Pharaoh: "If these two are magicians, we will overcome them, for there is no one more skilled in magic than us; and if they are from the Lord of the worlds, then we have no power against the Lord of the worlds." So when what happened to them occurred, that they fell down prostrate, Allah showed them, in their prostration, their places to which they would return. Then ﴿they said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us"﴾ up to His words ﴿and Allah is better and more enduring﴾.

﴿فَتَوَلّى فِرْعَوْنُ﴾ means he turned away from that place to prepare what he needed for what they had agreed upon. It was also said that the meaning of "tawallā" is that he turned away from the truth, but the first meaning is preferable. ﴿فَجَمَعَ كَيْدَهُ﴾ means he gathered what he would use to plot, of his magic and his stratagems. The intended meaning is that he gathered the magicians. It was said they were seventy-two, and it was said four hundred, and it was said twelve thousand, and it was said fourteen thousand. Ibn al-Mundhir said they were eighty thousand. ﴿ثُمَّ أتى﴾ means he came to the appointment they had agreed upon, together with the gathering he had assembled.
