**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 60–70 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ That is, the matter they had witnessed from Musa and the staff cast the magicians down prostrate before Allah, the Exalted. The verification of this has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf. ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa."﴾ He mentioned Harun before Musa in reporting their words in order to observe the *fawasil al-ayi* (the rhyming endings of the verses) and to attend to the harmony of their final sounds.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿He will destroy you with a punishment﴾, that he said: "He will ruin you."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿He will destroy you﴾ that he said: "He will uproot you."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Salih that he said: "He will slaughter you."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali regarding ﴿and they will take away your best way of life﴾ that he said: "They will turn people's faces towards themselves."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It means your best, and they are the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd and Abd al-Razzaq narrated regarding His words ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, "what they have falsified," from Qatadah, who said: "Musa cast it down, and it turned into a serpent that devoured their ropes and what they had made."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah that the magicians of Pharaoh were nine hundred. They said to Pharaoh: "If these two are magicians, we will overcome them, for there is no one more skilled in magic than us; and if they are from the Lord of the worlds, then we have no power against the Lord of the worlds." So when what happened to them occurred, that they fell down prostrate, Allah showed them, in their prostration, their places to which they would return. Then ﴿they said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us"﴾ up to His words ﴿and Allah is better and more enduring﴾.

﴿فَتَوَلّى فِرْعَوْنُ﴾ means he turned away from that place to prepare what he needed for what they had agreed upon. It was also said that the meaning of "tawallā" is that he turned away from the truth, but the first meaning is preferable. ﴿فَجَمَعَ كَيْدَهُ﴾ means he gathered what he would use to plot, of his magic and his stratagems. The intended meaning is that he gathered the magicians. It was said they were seventy-two, and it was said four hundred, and it was said twelve thousand, and it was said fourteen thousand. Ibn al-Mundhir said they were eighty thousand. ﴿ثُمَّ أتى﴾ means he came to the appointment they had agreed upon, together with the gathering he had assembled. The clause ﴿قالَ لَهم مُوسى﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah), an answer to an assumed question. ﴿ويْلَكم لا تَفْتَرُوا عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا﴾: he invoked woe upon them and forbade them from fabricating lies against God. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is in the accusative governed by an omitted verb, and the implied meaning is that God has imposed woe upon them." He said: "It may also be a vocative, like His words: ﴿يا ويْلَنا مَن بَعَثَنا مِن مَرْقَدِنا﴾ [Yāsīn 36:52]." ﴿فَيُسْحِتَكم بِعَذابٍ﴾: al-suḥt means extermination. It is said saḥta and asḥta with the same meaning, and its original sense is thorough removal of hair. The Kufans, except Shuʿbah, read ﴿فَيُسْحِتَكُمْ﴾ with a dammah on the imperfect prefix, from asḥta, and this is the dialect of Banū Tamīm. The rest read it with a fatḥah, from saḥta, and this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Its accusative case is because it is an answer to the prohibition (jawāb al-nahy). ﴿وقَدْ خابَ مَنِ افْتَرى﴾ means he lost and perished. The meaning is: whoever fabricates against God has lost, whatever lie it may be.

﴿فَتَنازَعُوا أمْرَهم بَيْنَهُمْ﴾: the magicians, when they heard Mūsā's words, debated among themselves, consulted, and tossed the points of the matter back and forth. ﴿وأسَرُّوا النَّجْوى﴾ means they concealed their secret counsel from Mūsā. Their secret counsel was their saying: ﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾. It was said that they whispered among themselves, saying: "If what Mūsā has brought is magic, we will overcome him, and if it is from God, then there will be a matter for him." It was also said that what they concealed was that if he overcame them, they would follow him, as said by al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. It was said too that what they concealed was that, when they heard Mūsā's words, "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against God," they said: "This is not the speech of a magician." (p-914) Al-najwā means private conversation, and it is used both as a noun and as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Abū ʿAmr read ﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ with a shaddah on the particle entering the clause, and with a yāʾ in the demonstrative, treating inna as governing in its familiar way, namely the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. This reading is related from ʿUthmān, ʿĀʾishah, and other Companions. Al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿī, and other Successors also read it this way. ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar also read this way, as al-Naḥḥās reported. This reading agrees with the apparent grammatical case but differs from the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, since it is written with an alif. Al-Zuhrī, al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, al-Mufaḍḍal, Abān, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ibn Kathīr, and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Ḥafṣ from him read ﴿إنْ هَذانِ﴾ with a light inna, taking it as a negative particle. This reading agrees with the orthography of the Muṣḥaf and with the grammatical case. Ibn Kathīr read like them except that he doubled the nūn in hadhāni. The Medinans, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿إنَّ هَذانِ﴾ with a shaddah on inna and with an alif. Thus they agreed with the orthography but differed from the apparent grammar.

It was said that it is the dialect of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, and Kinānah, who make the nominative, accusative, and genitive of the dual with an alif. From this is the words of the poet:

*So he lowered his gaze in the manner of the brave, and had he seen an opening for his fangs, the brave one would have been struck silent.*

And the words of another:

*He took from us a blow between his two ears as provision.*

And the words of another:

*Indeed her father and her father's father have both reached the utmost of glory.*

What supports this is the explicit statement of Sībawayh, al-Akhfash, Abū Zayd, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Farrāʾ that this reading is according to the dialect of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb. Abū ʿUbaydah related from Abū al-Khaṭṭāb that it is the dialect of Banū Kinānah, and someone else related that it is the dialect of Khathʿam. It was also said that inna here means "yes," as al-Kisāʾī related from ʿĀṣim, and Sībawayh likewise related it. Al-Naḥḥās said: "I saw al-Zajjāj and al-Akhfash going this way," so the implied meaning is: "Yes, these two are magicians." From this is the words of the poet:

*Would that I knew whether there is a cure for the lover from the anguish of his love for them. Yes, the meeting.*

That is, "Yes, the meeting." Al-Zajjāj said: "The meaning in the verse is: this belongs to both of them, they are two magicians," and then he omitted the subject, which is "they two" (humā). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and Abū al-Fatḥ ibn Jinnī rejected this. It was also said: the alif in hadhā is made similar to the alif in yafʿalāni, so it was not changed. It was also said that there is an implied hāʾ: "indeed it, these two are magicians." Al-Zajjāj related this from early grammarians, and Ibn al-Anbārī likewise related it. Ibn Kaysān said: since hadhā is said with an alif in the nominative, accusative, and genitive in one unchanged form, and the dual does not change the singular, the dual was treated like the singular, so the alif remained in the nominative, accusative, and genitive. These are sayings that include the justification of this reading, a justification by which it is sound and by which it is freed from error. Through this, what was reported from ʿUthmān and ʿĀʾishah, that it was a mistake by the scribe of the Muṣḥaf, is refuted.

﴿يُرِيدانِ أنْ يُخْرِجاكم مِن أرْضِكم﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿بِسِحْرِهِما﴾ that they have displayed, ﴿ويَذْهَبا بِطَرِيقَتِكُمُ المُثْلى﴾. Al-Kisāʾī said: "bi-ṭarīqatikum" means "with your sunnah." Al-Muthlā is an adjective, like your saying: "a great woman" (imraʾah kubrā). The Arabs say: "So-and-so is on the best way (al-ṭarīqah al-muthlā)," meaning on the upright guidance. Al-Farrāʾ said: The Arabs say: "These are the way of their people and the ways of their people," meaning their nobles. Al-muthlā is the feminine of al-amthal, which means the best, and one says: "So-and-so is the best (amthal) of his people," that is, their best, and they are the excellent ones (al-amāthil). The meaning is: if they overcome you by their magic, the leaders and nobles among you will incline towards them, or they will make you go by your way, which is the best of ways.

﴿فَأجْمِعُوا كَيْدَكُمْ﴾: al-ijmāʿ means firm determination, and resolve upon a matter, as al-Farrāʾ said. You say: "I resolved (ajmaʿtu) on the departure," like "azmaʿtu." Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is: let your resolve be all of you together, like a plot agreed upon. The reciters agreed on the hamzah being cut in ajmiʿū, except Abū ʿAmr, who read it with a connecting hamzah and a fatḥah on the mīm from al-jamʿ. Al-Naḥḥās said: "It was related to me from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad that he said: Abū ʿAmr must read against this reading, which is the reading that most people follow." ﴿ثُمَّ ائْتُوا صَفًّا﴾ means lined up in rows, gathered together, so that their affair would be more orderly and their awe greater. Al-Zajjāj said: according to this, the meaning is: "Then come to the place where you gather for your festival and your prayer." It is said "atayt al-ṣaff," meaning "I came to the place of prayer." So according to the first explanation, the accusative of ṣaffan is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and according to Abū ʿUbaydah's explanation, its accusative is as an object. Al-Zajjāj said: it may mean "then come to the people, lined up," and in that case it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative, and for this reason it was not made plural. It was also read with a kasrah on the hamzah after which there is a yāʾ, and whoever drops the hamzah replaces it with an alif. ﴿وقَدْ أفْلَحَ اليَوْمَ مَنِ اسْتَعْلى﴾ means whoever prevails. It is said: "He overcame him" (istaʿlā ʿalayhi) when he overpowered him. All of this is the speech of the magicians to one another. It was also said that it is the speech of Pharaoh to them.

The object of tulqī is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "Either you throw what you throw first." ﴿وإمّا أنْ نَكُونَ﴾, we, ﴿أوَّلَ مَن ألْقى﴾ what he throws, or first to do the throwing. He said: "It may also be a vocative, like His words: ﴿يا ويْلَنا مَن بَعَثَنا مِن مَرْقَدِنا﴾ [Yāsīn 36:52]." ﴿فَيُسْحِتَكم بِعَذابٍ﴾: al-suḥt means extermination. It is said saḥta and asḥta with the same meaning, and its original sense is thorough removal of hair. The Kufans, except Shuʿbah, read ﴿فَيُسْحِتَكُمْ﴾ with a dammah on the imperfect prefix, from asḥta, and this is the dialect of Banū Tamīm. The rest read it with a fatḥah, from saḥta, and this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Its accusative case is because it is an answer to the prohibition (jawāb al-nahy). ﴿وقَدْ خابَ مَنِ افْتَرى﴾ means he lost and perished. The meaning is: whoever fabricates against God has lost, whatever lie it may be.

﴿فَتَنازَعُوا أمْرَهم بَيْنَهُمْ﴾: the magicians, when they heard Mūsā's words, debated among themselves, consulted, and tossed the points of the matter back and forth. ﴿وأسَرُّوا النَّجْوى﴾ means they concealed their secret counsel from Mūsā. Their secret counsel was their saying: ﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾. It was said that they whispered among themselves, saying: "If what Mūsā has brought is magic, we will overcome him, and if it is from God, then there will be a matter for him." It was also said that what they concealed was that if he overcame them, they would follow him, as said by al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. It was said too that what they concealed was that, when they heard Mūsā's words, "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against God," they said: "This is not the speech of a magician." (p-914) Al-najwā means private conversation, and it is used both as a noun and as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Abū ʿAmr read ﴿إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ﴾ with a shaddah on the particle entering the clause, and with a yāʾ in the demonstrative, treating inna as governing in its familiar way, namely the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. This reading is related from ʿUthmān, ʿĀʾishah, and other Companions. Al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿī, and other Successors also read it this way. ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar also read this way, as al-Naḥḥās reported. This reading agrees with the apparent grammatical case but differs from the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, since it is written with an alif. Al-Zuhrī, al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, al-Mufaḍḍal, Abān, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ibn Kathīr, and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Ḥafṣ from him read ﴿إنْ هَذانِ﴾ with a light inna, taking it as a negative particle. This reading agrees with the orthography of the Muṣḥaf and with the grammatical case. Ibn Kathīr read like them except that he doubled the nūn in hadhāni. The Medinans, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿إنَّ هَذانِ﴾ with a shaddah on inna and with an alif. Thus they agreed with the orthography but differed from the apparent grammar.

A group of scholars have spoken about the justification of the reading of the Medinans, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿĀmir. Ibn al-Anbārī and al-Naḥḥās fully covered this. It was said that it is the dialect of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, and Kinānah, who make the nominative, accusative, and genitive of the dual with an alif. From this is the words of the poet:

*So he lowered his gaze in the manner of the brave, and had he seen an opening for his fangs, the brave one would have been struck silent.*

And the words of another:

*He took from us a blow between his two ears as provision.*

And the words of another:

*Indeed her father and her father's father have both reached the utmost of glory.*

What supports this is the explicit statement of Sībawayh, al-Akhfash, Abū Zayd, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Farrāʾ that this reading is according to the dialect of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb. Abū ʿUbaydah related from Abū al-Khaṭṭāb that it is the dialect of Banū Kinānah, and someone else related that it is the dialect of Khathʿam. It was also said that inna here means "yes," as al-Kisāʾī related from ʿĀṣim, and Sībawayh likewise related it. Al-Naḥḥās said: "I saw al-Zajjāj and al-Akhfash going this way," so the implied meaning is: "Yes, these two are magicians." From this is the words of the poet:

*Would that I knew whether there is a cure for the lover from the anguish of his love for them. Yes, the meeting.*

That is, "Yes, the meeting." Al-Zajjāj said: "The meaning in the verse is: this belongs to both of them, they are two magicians," and then he omitted the subject, which is "they two" (humā). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and Abū al-Fatḥ ibn Jinnī rejected this. It was also said: the alif in hadhā is made similar to the alif in yafʿalāni, so it was not changed. It was also said that there is an implied hāʾ: "indeed it, these two are magicians." Al-Zajjāj related this from early grammarians, and Ibn al-Anbārī likewise related it. Ibn Kaysān said: since hadhā is said with an alif in the nominative, accusative, and genitive in one unchanged form, and the dual does not change the singular, the dual was treated like the singular, so the alif remained in the nominative, accusative, and genitive. These are sayings that include the justification of this reading, a justification by which it is sound and by which it is freed from error. Through this, what was reported from ʿUthmān and ʿĀʾishah, that it was a mistake by the scribe of the Muṣḥaf, is refuted.

﴿يُرِيدانِ أنْ يُخْرِجاكم مِن أرْضِكم﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿بِسِحْرِهِما﴾ that they have displayed, ﴿ويَذْهَبا بِطَرِيقَتِكُمُ المُثْلى﴾. Al-Kisāʾī said: "bi-ṭarīqatikum" means "with your sunnah." Al-Muthlā is an adjective, like your saying: "a great woman" (imraʾah kubrā). The Arabs say: "So-and-so is on the best way (al-ṭarīqah al-muthlā)," meaning on the upright guidance. Al-Farrāʾ said: The Arabs say: "These are the way of their people and the ways of their people," meaning their nobles. Al-muthlā is the feminine of al-amthal, which means the best, and one says: "So-and-so is the best (amthal) of his people," that is, their best, and they are the excellent ones (al-amāthil). The meaning is: if they overcome you by their magic, the leaders and nobles among you will incline towards them, or they will make you go by your way, which is the best of ways.

﴿فَأجْمِعُوا كَيْدَكُمْ﴾: al-ijmāʿ means firm determination, and resolve upon a matter, as al-Farrāʾ said. You say: "I resolved (ajmaʿtu) on the departure," like "azmaʿtu." Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is: let your resolve be all of you together, like a plot agreed upon. The reciters agreed on the hamzah being cut in ajmiʿū, except Abū ʿAmr, who read it with a connecting hamzah and a fatḥah on the mīm from al-jamʿ. Al-Naḥḥās said: "It was related to me from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad that he said: Abū ʿAmr must read against this reading, which is the reading that most people follow." ﴿ثُمَّ ائْتُوا صَفًّا﴾ means lined up in rows, gathered together, so that their affair would be more orderly and their awe greater. This is the saying of the majority of exegetes. Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-ṣaff is the place of gathering, and the place of prayer is called al-ṣaff. Al-Zajjāj said: according to this, the meaning is: "Then come to the place where you gather for your festival and your prayer." It is said "atayt al-ṣaff," meaning "I came to the place of prayer." So according to the first explanation, the accusative of ṣaffan is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and according to Abū ʿUbaydah's explanation, its accusative is as an object. Al-Zajjāj said: it may mean "then come to the people, lined up," and in that case it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative, and for this reason it was not made plural. It was also read with a kasrah on the hamzah after which there is a yāʾ, and whoever drops the hamzah replaces it with an alif. ﴿وقَدْ أفْلَحَ اليَوْمَ مَنِ اسْتَعْلى﴾ means whoever prevails. It is said: "He overcame him" (istaʿlā ʿalayhi) when he overpowered him. All of this is the speech of the magicians to one another. It was also said that it is the speech of Pharaoh to them.

The clause ﴿قالُوا يا مُوسى إمّا أنْ تُلْقِيَ﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did they do after they had said among themselves what they said?" So it was said: ﴿قالُوا يامُوسى إمّا أنْ تُلْقِيَ﴾. Anna with what follows it is in the position of an accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: choose your throwing first or our throwing. It may also be in the position of a nominative, with it and what follows it being the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is your throwing or our throwing. The object of tulqī is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "Either you throw what you throw first." ﴿وإمّا أنْ نَكُونَ﴾, we, ﴿أوَّلَ مَن ألْقى﴾ what he throws, or first to do the throwing. The intended meaning is the throwing of staves upon the ground. The magicians had staves with them, and Mūsā had thrown his staff on the day he entered upon Pharaoh. So when the magicians wanted to oppose him, they said this to him. ﴿بَلْ ألْقُوا﴾ Mūsā said to them: he commanded them to throw first (p-915), so that his miracle would be more manifest when they had thrown what they had and then he threw his staff, and it swallowed that, and as a display of indifference to their magic. ﴿فَإذا حِبالُهم وعِصِيُّهُمْ﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "So they threw, and behold, their ropes." The fāʾ is an explanatory fāʾ (faṣīḥah), and idhā is either for sudden surprise or for time. The meaning is: they threw, and Mūsā was suddenly struck at the time when the movement of their ropes and staves was imagined to him. Al-Ḥasan read ʿuṣiyyuhum with a ḍammah on the ʿayn, which is the dialect of Banū Tamīm. The rest read it with a kasrah, following the kasrah of the ṣād. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Dhakwān, and Rawḥ from Yaʿqūb read tukhayyalu with a yāʾ, because the staves and the ropes are feminine. That was because they had smeared them with mercury, and when the heat of the sun reached them they trembled and moved. It was read nukhayyilu with a nūn, meaning that God, may He be glorified, is the one who makes it appear so. It was read yukhayyilu with a tahtiyyah, in the active voice, meaning that what makes it appear is the plot. It was also said that what makes it appear is that they move, since the particle anna is in the position of a nominative, meaning: their movement is imagined to him. al-Zajjāj mentioned this meaning. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the position of an accusative, meaning "because that," and then he omitted the bāʾ.

Al-Zajjāj said: whoever read with the tāʾ, meaning the upper tāʾ (the feminine form), took anna to be in the position of an accusative, meaning: it is imagined to him that they are possessed of motion. He said: it may also be in the position of a nominative, as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in tukhayyalu, which refers to the ropes and staves, and the substitution here is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl). It is said: "It was made to appear to him" (khuyyila ilayhi) when it was made to resemble something for him and the confusion and doubt were introduced into him.

﴿فَأوْجَسَ في نَفْسِهِ خِيفَةً مُوسى﴾: that is, he sensed. It was said: he found. It was said: he concealed. It was said: he feared. This was because of what arises from human nature when one sees what one fears. It was said: he feared that people would be seduced before he threw his staff. It was said: the cause of his fear was that their magic was of the same kind as what he had shown them in the staff, so he feared that his affair would be confused for the people and they would not believe. Then God, may He be glorified, removed the fear that had come upon him by the good news He gave him in His words: ﴿قُلْنا لا تَخَفْ إنَّكَ أنْتَ الأعْلى﴾, that is, the one who prevails over them by victory and triumph. The clause is a reason for the prohibition against fear.

﴿وألْقِ ما في يَمِينِكَ﴾ means the staff. He left it indefinite out of magnification and glorification. The jussive of ﴿تَلْقَفْ ما صَنَعُوا﴾ is because it is the answer to the command. It was read with a shaddah on the qāf, and the original is tatalaqqafu, and one of the two tāʾs was omitted. It was read talqaf with a kasrah on the lām, from laqifahu, meaning he swallowed it swiftly. It was read talqafu with a ḍammah, on the assumption of fa-innahā tatalaqqafu. The meaning of ﴿ما صَنَعُوا﴾ is what they made of the ropes and staves. Al-Zajjāj said: the reading with the jussive is the answer to the command. The nominative is permitted, in the sense of a circumstantial clause, as if he said: "Throw it swallowing." The clause ﴿إنَّما صَنَعُوا كَيْدُ ساحِرٍ﴾ is a reason for His words "talqaf." The nominative of kayd is because it is the predicate of inna. This is the reading of the Kufans except ʿĀṣim. They read siḥrin with a kasrah on the sīn and a sukūn on the ḥāʾ, and the idāfah of kayd, that is siḥr, is by widening the usage without an implied term, or by an implied "possessor of magic." The rest read kayda sāḥirin.

﴿ولا يُفْلِحُ السّاحِرُ حَيْثُ أتى﴾: that is, the category of magician does not prosper wherever he goes and in whatever direction he turns. This is part of the completion of the reason.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 60–70 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ That is, the matter they had witnessed from Musa and the staff cast the magicians down prostrate before Allah, the Exalted. The verification of this has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf. ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa."﴾ He mentioned Harun before Musa in reporting their words in order to observe the *fawasil al-ayi* (the rhyming endings of the verses) and to attend to the harmony of their final sounds.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿He will destroy you with a punishment﴾, that he said: "He will ruin you."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿He will destroy you﴾ that he said: "He will uproot you."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Salih that he said: "He will slaughter you."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali regarding ﴿and they will take away your best way of life﴾ that he said: "They will turn people's faces towards themselves."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It means your best, and they are the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd and Abd al-Razzaq narrated regarding His words ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, "what they have falsified," from Qatadah, who said: "Musa cast it down, and it turned into a serpent that devoured their ropes and what they had made."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah that the magicians of Pharaoh were nine hundred. They said to Pharaoh: "If these two are magicians, we will overcome them, for there is no one more skilled in magic than us; and if they are from the Lord of the worlds, then we have no power against the Lord of the worlds." So when what happened to them occurred, that they fell down prostrate, Allah showed them, in their prostration, their places to which they would return. Then ﴿they said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us"﴾ up to His words ﴿and Allah is better and more enduring﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 71–76:

His saying: ﴿He said: "Have you believed in him?"﴾ It is said: āmana lahu and āmana bihi (both mean "to believe in"). Of the first form is His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾, and of the second is His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is also said that the verb here carries the sense of "following" (ittiba'). It was read as a rebuking interrogative, meaning: how did you believe in him without my permission to do so? ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ That is, Moses is your chief, meaning the greatest of you in magic and the highest in rank in the craft of magic, or your teacher and master, as His saying ﴿who taught you magic﴾ indicates. Al-Kisa'i said: "In the Hijaz, when a boy comes from his teacher, he says: I came from my kabir (chief/elder)." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: it means "indeed, he is the great one of magic." Al-Wahidi said: "The kabir in the language is the head, and for this reason the teacher is called the kabir." Pharaoh intended by this statement to introduce doubt among the people so that they would not believe. Otherwise, he knew that they had not learned from Moses, nor was he their chief, nor was there any close relationship between them. ﴿So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides.﴾ That is, by Allah, I will surely do that to you. Cutting off the hands and feet on opposite sides means cutting off the right hand and the left foot, and min (from) indicates the starting point. ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.﴾ That is, upon their trunks, as in His saying: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen?﴾ [al-Tur: 38], meaning "upon it." From this is the verse of Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil:

They crucified al-'Abdi upon a palm trunk,
so let Shayban never sneeze except with a severed nose.

The word fi (in) was chosen to indicate their being firmly fixed upon them, like the firm containment of something within a container. ﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting.﴾ He meant: you will surely know whether I am more severe in punishment for you or Moses. The meaning of abqa is adwam (more enduring). He intended by this speech to mock Moses, because Moses had no part in punishing anyone. It is possible that he meant the punishment with which Moses had threatened them if they did not believe. It was also said that by "Moses" he meant the Lord of Moses, by omitting the mudaf (the noun governed, i.e., "Lord") before it.

﴿They said: "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us."﴾ That is, we will never choose you over what Moses brought us of the clear proofs from Allah, the Exalted, such as the hand and the staff. It was also said that they meant by "the clear proofs" what they saw in their prostration of the dwellings prepared for them in Paradise. ﴿And over He who originated us﴾ is conjoined to "what has come to us," meaning: we will never choose you over what Moses brought of the proofs, and over He who originated us, that is, created us. It was also said that it is an oath: "By Allah who originated us, we will never prefer you, or we do not prefer you." These two interpretations of the verse were mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. ﴿So decide what you will decide.﴾ This is a reply from them to Pharaoh when he said to them: "I will surely cut off..." etc. The meaning: do what you will do, and judge what you will judge. The implied object: what you are going to do to it. ﴿You only decide concerning this worldly life.﴾ That is, your authority over us and the enforcement of your command over us are only in this world, and you have no way over us concerning what comes after it. The demonstrative pronoun is in a position of accusative, either as an adverbial of time or of place, and "ma" is a restrictive particle (kafffa). Al-Farra' permitted the nominative case, by making ma mean alladhi (that which): that which you decide in this worldly life, your judgment and rule are confined to that.

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins﴾ which preceded from us, of disbelief and other things, ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic.﴾ It is conjoined to "our sins": that is, and He may forgive us what you compelled us to do of the work of magic in opposing Moses. So ma is in the accusative position as the object. It was also said that it is a negation particle. Al-Nahhas said: the first is more preferable. It is said that it may also be in the nominative position as the subject of an inchoative sentence, with the predicate omitted: that is, "and what you compelled us to do of magic is removed from us." ﴿And Allah is better and more lasting.﴾ That is, better than you in reward and more lasting than you in punishment. This is the answer to His saying: ﴿and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting.﴾

﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ The criminal (mujrim) is the one who is clothed in disbelief and sins. The meaning of "he will neither die therein nor live" is that he does not die so as to find rest, nor does he live a life that benefits him.

Al-Mubarrad said: he does not die a death that gives relief, nor does he live a life that brings enjoyment. So he suffers as the living suffers, and his state reaches the point of death in what is disliked, except that it does not nullify the sensation of pain. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is neither alive nor dead," when he is not benefiting from his life. Ibn al-Anbari recited in a similar sense:

Is there anyone for a soul that does not die, so that its misery ends,
nor lives a life that has any sweetness?

This verse is among what Allah, the Exalted, relayed of the words of the magicians. It was also said that it is the beginning of a speech, and the pronoun in "indeed, he" in this case refers to the matter (al-sha'n). ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds﴾ That is, whoever comes to his Lord believing in Him, having done righteous deeds: that is, acts of obedience. The modified noun is omitted, and the implied phrase is "the righteous deeds." The clause "has done" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and likewise "believer" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The indication with "those" refers to "whoever," according to its meaning. ﴿For them are the highest ranks﴾ that is, the lofty dwellings whose descriptions fall short of them.

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is an explanation of "the ranks" or a substitute for them. Adn means residence, and its explanation has already been given. The clause ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a circumstantial clause of "gardens," because it is annexed to Eden, and Eden is a proper name for residence, as previously mentioned. The accusative of ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ is a circumstantial state of the pronoun of the group in "for them": that is, remaining and eternal. The indication with "that" refers to what was previously granted to them of reward. It is the subject, and ﴿the recompense of one who purifies himself﴾ is its predicate: that is, the recompense of one who purified himself from disbelief and the sins that necessitate the Fire.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic﴾, that he said: Pharaoh took forty boys from the Children of Israel and ordered that they be taught magic at al-Farama, saying: "Teach them a teaching such that no one on earth will overcome them."

Ibn Abbas said: "They were among those who believed in Moses, and they are the ones who said: 'We have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and what you compelled us to do of magic.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, concerning His saying ﴿And Allah is better and more lasting﴾, that he said: "Better than you if He is obeyed, and more lasting than you in punishment if He is disobeyed."

Ahmad, Muslim, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a sermon and came to this verse: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'As for its people, those who are its people, they will neither die therein nor live. As for those who are not its people, the Fire will cause them to die a death. Then the intercessors will stand and intercede, and they will be brought in bundles upon a river called al-Hayah or al-Hayawan, and they will sprout as the rubbish sprouts in the flood's debris.'"

Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the people of the highest ranks, those beneath them see them as you see the bright star in the horizon of the sky, and indeed Abu Bakr and Umar are among them and they are blessed." In the two Sahihs, with the wording: "Indeed, the people of 'Illiyyin see those above them as you see the setting star in the horizon of the sky."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 71–76:

His saying: ﴿He said: "Have you believed in him?"﴾ It is said: āmana lahu and āmana bihi (both mean "to believe in"). Of the first form is His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾, and of the second is His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is also said that the verb here carries the sense of "following" (ittiba'). It was read as a rebuking interrogative, meaning: how did you believe in him without my permission to do so? ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ That is, Moses is your chief, meaning the greatest of you in magic and the highest in rank in the craft of magic, or your teacher and master, as His saying ﴿who taught you magic﴾ indicates. Al-Kisa'i said: "In the Hijaz, when a boy comes from his teacher, he says: I came from my kabir (chief/elder)." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: it means "indeed, he is the great one of magic." Al-Wahidi said: "The kabir in the language is the head, and for this reason the teacher is called the kabir." The demonstrative pronoun is in a position of accusative, either as an adverbial of time or of place, and "ma" is a restrictive particle (kafffa). Al-Farra' permitted the nominative case, by making ma mean alladhi (that which): that which you decide in this worldly life, your judgment and rule are confined to that.

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins﴾ which preceded from us, of disbelief and other things, ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic.﴾ It is conjoined to "our sins": that is, and He may forgive us what you compelled us to do of the work of magic in opposing Moses. So ma is in the accusative position as the object. It was also said that it is a negation particle. Al-Nahhas said: the first is more preferable. It is said that it may also be in the nominative position as the subject of an inchoative sentence, with the predicate omitted: that is, "and what you compelled us to do of magic is removed from us." ﴿And Allah is better and more lasting.﴾ That is, better than you in reward and more lasting than you in punishment. This is the answer to His saying: ﴿and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting.﴾

﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ The criminal (mujrim) is the one who is clothed in disbelief and sins. The meaning of "he will neither die therein nor live" is that he does not die so as to find rest, nor does he live a life that benefits him.

Al-Mubarrad said: he does not die a death that gives relief, nor does he live a life that brings enjoyment. So he suffers as the living suffers, and his state reaches the point of death in what is disliked, except that it does not nullify the sensation of pain. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is neither alive nor dead," when he is not benefiting from his life. Ibn al-Anbari recited in a similar sense:

Is there anyone for a soul that does not die, so that its misery ends,
nor lives a life that has any sweetness?

This verse is among what Allah, the Exalted, relayed of the words of the magicians. It was also said that it is the beginning of a speech, and the pronoun in "indeed, he" in this case refers to the matter (al-sha'n). ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds﴾ That is, whoever comes to his Lord believing in Him, having done righteous deeds: that is, acts of obedience. The modified noun is omitted, and the implied phrase is "the righteous deeds." The clause "has done" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and likewise "believer" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The indication with "those" refers to "whoever," according to its meaning. ﴿For them are the highest ranks﴾ that is, the lofty dwellings whose descriptions fall short of them.

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is an explanation of "the ranks" or a substitute for them. Adn means residence, and its explanation has already been given. The clause ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a circumstantial clause of "gardens," because it is annexed to Eden, and Eden is a proper name for residence, as previously mentioned. The accusative of ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ is a circumstantial state of the pronoun of the group in "for them": that is, remaining and eternal. The indication with "that" refers to what was previously granted to them of reward. It is the subject, and ﴿the recompense of one who purifies himself﴾ is its predicate: that is, the recompense of one who purified himself from disbelief and the sins that necessitate the Fire.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic﴾, that he said: Pharaoh took forty boys from the Children of Israel and ordered that they be taught magic at al-Farama, saying: "Teach them a teaching such that no one on earth will overcome them."

Ibn Abbas said: "They were among those who believed in Moses, and they are the ones who said: 'We have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and what you compelled us to do of magic.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, concerning His saying ﴿And Allah is better and more lasting﴾, that he said: "Better than you if He is obeyed, and more lasting than you in punishment if He is disobeyed."

Ahmad, Muslim, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a sermon and came to this verse: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'As for its people, those who are its people, they will neither die therein nor live. As for those who are not its people, the Fire will cause them to die a death. Then the intercessors will stand and intercede, and they will be brought in bundles upon a river called al-Hayah or al-Hayawan, and they will sprout as the rubbish sprouts in the flood's debris.'"

Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the people of the highest ranks, those beneath them see them as you see the bright star in the horizon of the sky, and indeed Abu Bakr and Umar are among them and they are blessed." In the two Sahihs, with the wording: "Indeed, the people of 'Illiyyin see those above them as you see the setting star in the horizon of the sky."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verses 71–76:

His saying: ﴿He said: "Have you believed in him?"﴾ It is said: āmana lahu and āmana bihi (both mean "to believe in"). Of the first form is His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾, and of the second is His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is also said that the verb here carries the sense of "following" (ittiba'). It was read as a rebuking interrogative, meaning: how did you believe in him without my permission to do so? ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ That is, Moses is your chief, meaning the greatest of you in magic and the highest in rank in the craft of magic, or your teacher and master, as His saying ﴿who taught you magic﴾ indicates. Al-Kisa'i said: "In the Hijaz, when a boy comes from his teacher, he says: I came from my kabir (chief/elder)." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: it means "indeed, he is the great one of magic." Al-Wahidi said: "The kabir in the language is the head, and for this reason the teacher is called the kabir." Pharaoh intended by this statement to introduce doubt among the people so that they would not believe. Otherwise, he knew that they had not learned from Moses, nor was he their chief, nor was there any close relationship between them. ﴿So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides.﴾ That is, by Allah, I will surely do that to you. Cutting off the hands and feet on opposite sides means cutting off the right hand and the left foot, and min (from) indicates the starting point. ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.﴾ That is, upon their trunks, as in His saying: ﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen?﴾ [al-Tur: 38], meaning "upon it." From this is the verse of Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil:

They crucified al-'Abdi upon a palm trunk,
so let Shayban never sneeze except with a severed nose.

The word fi (in) was chosen to indicate their being firmly fixed upon them, like the firm containment of something within a container. ﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting.﴾ He meant: you will surely know whether I am more severe in punishment for you or Moses. The meaning of abqa is adwam (more enduring). He intended by this speech to mock Moses, because Moses had no part in punishing anyone. It is possible that he meant the punishment with which Moses had threatened them if they did not believe. It was also said that by "Moses" he meant the Lord of Moses, by omitting the mudaf (the noun governed, i.e., "Lord") before it.

﴿They said: "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us."﴾ That is, we will never choose you over what Moses brought us of the clear proofs from Allah, the Exalted, such as the hand and the staff. It was also said that they meant by "the clear proofs" what they saw in their prostration of the dwellings prepared for them in Paradise. ﴿And over He who originated us﴾ is conjoined to "what has come to us," meaning: we will never choose you over what Moses brought of the proofs, and over He who originated us, that is, created us. It was also said that it is an oath: "By Allah who originated us, we will never prefer you, or we do not prefer you." (p. 917) This begins the account of the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the destruction of their enemy. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf and Yunus. The lam in ﴿لَقَدْ﴾ (*laqad*) is the *lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath), and the emphasis it gives is clear. The *an* in ﴿أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي﴾ (*an asri bi-ibadi*) is either *al-mufassirah* (the explanatory *an*), since revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the sense of speech, or *masdariyyah* (the verbal *an*, forming a verbal noun), meaning "[to] travel by night with My servants," that is, to take them out of Egypt. This has already been discussed fully. ﴿فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا﴾ means "Strike for them a path through the sea, dry," that is, make for them a path. *Yabsan* means "dry." It is described with the active participle form as an intensifier, because Allah made that path so dry that there was no water or mud in it. It is also read as *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba', either as a lightened form of *yabasan* with a fatha, or as the plural of *yabis*, like *sahb* for *sahib*. The clause ﴿لَا تَخَافُ دَرَكًا﴾ (*la takhafu darakan*, "you shall not fear being overtaken") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*): "secure from being overtaken by the enemy." Or it is another description of *tariq* (path). *Darak* means catching up with them from Pharaoh and his soldiers. Hamzah read ﴿لَا تَخَفْ﴾ (*la takhaf*) as a jussive response to the command, with the implied sense "if you strike, do not fear." Then ﴿وَلَا تَخْشَى﴾ (*wa la takhsha*, "nor shall you dread") is a new independent clause: "nor shall you dread Pharaoh or the sea." The majority (*al-jumhur*) read ﴿لَا تَخَافُ﴾ (*la takhafu*), which is more preferred, because *takhsha* is not jussive. It is also possible, in the majority reading, that this clause is another description of the path: "you shall not fear it, nor dread it."

﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِ﴾ (*fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu bi-junudih*, "Then Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers"). *Atba'a* here is the causative-reflexive form of *tabi'a*. One says *atba'tuhum* when you follow people who had gone ahead of you and you catch up with them. So the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them, and his soldiers were with him. It was also said that the *ba'* is extra, and the original is *atba'ahum junudah*, meaning he ordered his soldiers to follow Musa and his people. It was read as ﴿فَاتَّبَعَهُمْ﴾ (*fattaba'ahum*), with shaddah, meaning he caught up with them with his soldiers, and he was with them, as one says "the commander rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. The phrase *bi-junudih* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: "leading his soldiers with him."

﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum mina al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*, "Then the sea covered them, covering them as it did"). This means: what overwhelmed them and struck them overwhelmed and struck them. The repetition is for magnification and awe, as in His words ﴿الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ ﴿مَا الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:1–2), "The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality?" It was also said that what overwhelmed them is that whose story has been heard. Ibn al-Anbari said: "What overwhelmed them was a part of what overwhelmed them, because not all the water of the sea covered them; only part of it did." So this expression indicates that what drowned them was only some of the water. The first view is better because of the awe and magnification it conveys. It was read as ﴿فَغَشَّاهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشَّاهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashshahum ... ma ghashshahum*), meaning it covered them with what covered them.

﴿وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَى﴾ (*wa adalla Fir'awnu qawmahu wa ma hada*, "Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them"). That is, he led them away from right guidance, and did not guide them to the ways of salvation, because he assumed that Musa and those with him could not escape him, since they were before him walking on a dry path with the sea ahead of them. The phrase ﴿وَمَا هَدَى﴾ is an emphasis on his leading them astray, because one who misleads may guide the one he misleads in some matters.

﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ﴾ (*ya bani Isra'il, qad anjaynakum min aduwwikum*, "O Children of Israel, We have certainly delivered you from your enemy"). Allah mentioned the favor He bestowed upon the Children of Israel after delivering them. The implied sense is: We said to them after their deliverance, "O Children of Israel." It is also possible that this is addressed to the Jews contemporary with our Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace), because a blessing granted to the forefathers is counted as a blessing granted to their descendants. The enemy here means Pharaoh and his soldiers, destroyed by drowning him and his people in the sea, before the eyes of the Children of Israel. ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنَ﴾ (*wa wa'adnakum janiba al-tur al-ayman*, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Tur"). *Janib* is in the accusative as a direct object, not as an adverb of place, because it is a specific place, not an undefined one. Place nouns are in the accusative as adverbs only when they are indefinite. Makki said: "This is a principle on which there is no disagreement." Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning is that We commanded Musa to order you to go out with him, so that We might speak to him in your presence and you might hear the speech." It was also said that Musa was promised, after the drowning of Pharaoh, that he would come to the side of the mountain, so the promise was to Musa, but they were addressed with it because the promise was made for their sake. Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿وَوَعَدْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*wa 'adnakum*) without an alif, and Abu Ubayda preferred this reading, because the promising (*al-wa'd*) comes only from Allah to Musa specifically, whereas *al-mu'adah* (mutual appointment) can only be between two parties. We have already discussed this meaning in al-Baqarah. *Al-ayman* is in the accusative as an adjective of *janib*. The intended meaning is the right side of the person, because a mountain has no right or left side; so when one says "take the right side of the mountain," it means the right side from your perspective, relative to the mountain. It was also read in the genitive, as an adjective of the noun to which *janib* is attached.

﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَنَّ وَالسَّلْوَى﴾ (*wa nazzalna 'alaykumu al-manna wa al-salwa*, "And We sent down upon you manna and quail"). The explanation of *al-manna* as *al-tarankhabin* (a sweet exudation, like honey-dew) and *al-salwa* as *al-sammani* (quail) was discussed earlier, and we have clarified this fully. The sending down of these was during the wandering (*al-tih*) in the desert.

﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*kulu min tayyibati ma razaqnakum*, "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you"). That is, and We said to them, "Eat." The intended meaning of *al-tayyibat* is the pleasant things. It was also said that it means the lawful (*al-halal*), according to the well-known disagreement on this matter. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read ﴿قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ﴾ and ﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ with the first-person singular *ta'* (of the speaker) in all three places. The rest read with the royal plural *nun* (of majesty) in these places. ﴿وَلَا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ﴾ (*wa la tatghaw fihi*, "and do not transgress therein"). *Al-tughyan* means exceeding limits, that is, do not go beyond what is permissible to what is not permissible. It was also said that the meaning is: do not deny the blessing of Allah, lest you become transgressors. It was also said: do not disbelieve the blessing or forget its thanks. It was also said: do not disobey the Benefactor, that is, do not let ease and well-being lead you into disobedience. There is no obstacle to understanding *al-tughyan* as including all these meanings, since each of them truly counts as transgression.

﴿فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي﴾ (*fa-yahilla 'alaykum ghadabi*, "lest My anger descend upon you"). This is the answer (*jawab*) to the prohibition. That is: My anger will be incumbent upon you and will alight on you. It is derived from *hulul al-dayn* (the falling due of a debt), meaning the arrival of the time of its payment. ﴿وَمَنْ يَحْلِلْ عَلَيْهِ غَضَبِي فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*wa man yahlil 'alayhi ghadabi fa-qad hawa*, "And whoever has My anger descend upon him has certainly perished"). Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فَيَحُلَّ﴾ (*fa-yahulla*) with a damma on the ha', and likewise they read ﴿يَحْلُلْ﴾ (*yahlul*) with a damma on the first lam. The rest read both with a kasra. Both are dialect variants. Al-Farra' said: "The kasra is more beloved to me than the damma, because the damma is from *hulul* in the sense of *wuqu'* (alighting or befalling), whereas *yahill* with a kasra means "must" (*yajibu*). The explanation was given as "must," not as "befall." Abu Ubayda and others mentioned something similar." The meaning of ﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*fa-qad hawa*) is "has certainly perished." Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ means he has gone down into the abyss (*al-hawiyah*), which is the bottom of the Fire, from *hawa yahwi hawyan*, meaning he fell from a height to a low place." *Hawa Fulan* also means he died.

﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba wa amana wa 'amila salihan thumma ihtada*, "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided"). That is, to whoever repents from sins, the greatest of which is associating partners with Allah, and believes in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and does a righteous deed of what the Law has recommended and beautified. ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ means he remains upright in this until he dies. This is what al-Zajjaj and others said. It was also said: he never doubted his faith; it was said: he adhered to the Sunnah and the community (*al-sunnah wa al-jama'ah*); it was said: he learned knowledge in order to be guided by it; it was said: he knew that there is reward for this and punishment for abandoning it. The first view is more preferred than what follows it.

﴿وَمَا أَعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يَا مُوسَى﴾ (*wa ma a'jalaka 'an qawmika ya Musa*, "And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?"). This is a narration of what took place between Allah, glorified is He, and Musa when he came to the appointed meeting. The exegetes said: the appointment was that Musa and a group of the notables of his people would come, so Musa set out with them, then he hastened ahead of them out of longing for his Lord. Allah said to him: "What hastened you?" That is, what made you hasten, so that you left your people and departed from among them. Musa answered this. ﴿قَالَ هُمْ أُولَاءِ عَلَى أَثَرِي﴾ (*qala hum ula'i 'ala athari*, "He said: They are right behind me"). That is, they are close to me, following my track, and will reach me after me. It was also said: he did not mean that they were following behind him, but that they were near him, waiting for his return to them. Then he said, clarifying the reason for what Allah had asked him about: ﴿وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضَى﴾ (*wa 'ajiltu ilayka rabbi li-tarda*, "And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased"). That is, that You may be pleased with me by my hastening to carry out Your command, or that You may increase in being pleased with me by this. Abu Hatim said: Isa ibn Umar said: "The Banu Tamim say *ula* (short form), while the people of the Hijaz say *ula'i* (long form)." Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub read ﴿إِثْرِي﴾ (*ithri*) with a kasra on the hamzah and a sukun on the tha', and the rest read it with a fatha; both are dialect variants. The meaning of ﴿عَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (*'ajiltu ilayka*) is: I hastened to the place where You commanded me to go, so that You might be pleased with me. One says *rajul 'ajil*, *'ajul* and *'ajlan* to mean one who is clearly hasty; *al-'ajalah* is the opposite of slowness.

﴿قَالَ فَإِنَّا قَدْ فَتَنَّا قَوْمَكَ مِنْ بَعْدِكَ﴾ (*qala fa-inna qad fatanna qawmaka min ba'dika*, "He said: Indeed, We have tested your people after you"). This sentence is independent, an answer to an implied question, as though it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" So it is said: He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you," that is, We tried them, examined them, and cast them into trial and affliction. Ibn al-Anbari said: "We made them tested and wretched through worship of the calf after your departure from among them. They were those whom he had left behind with Harun." ﴿وَأَضَلَّهُمُ السَّامِرِيُّ﴾ (*wa adallahumu al-samiri*, "and al-Samiri led them astray"). That is, he called them to error. He was from a people who worshipped cows. He entered the religion of the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was what he had of cow-worship. He was from a tribe known as the Samirah. He said to those with him among the Children of Israel: "Musa has delayed from the appointed meeting between you and him only because of the ornaments that you have with you, and they are forbidden to you." He commanded them to throw them into the fire, and so what happened with the calf happened.

﴿فَرَجَعَ مُوسَى إِلَى قَوْمِهِ غَضْبَانَ أَسِفًا﴾ (*fa-raja'a Musa ila qawmihi ghadban asifan*, "Then Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved"). It was said: the return to his people was after he had completed forty days: Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. *Al-asaf* means intense anger; it was also said: grief. This has already been fully explained in al-A'raf. ﴿قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَلَمْ يَعِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ وَعْدًا حَسَنًا﴾ (*qala ya qawmi alam ya'idkum rabbukum wa'dan hasanan*, "He said: O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"). The interrogative is for rebuke by way of denial. *Al-wa'd al-hasan* (the good promise) is what He promised them: Paradise, if they remain upon His obedience; and He promised that He would make them hear His speech in the Torah through the tongue of Musa, so that they would act by what is in it and thereby deserve the reward for their deeds. It was also said: He promised them victory and triumph. It was also said: it is His words ﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba*), "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents," and so on. ﴿أَفَطَالَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْعَهْدُ﴾ (*afa-tala 'alaykumu al-'ahd*, "Has the time seemed long to you?"). The *fa* connects to an implied clause: "Did He promise you that, so the time has grown long for you, and so you forgot?" ﴿أَمْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ يَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (*am aradtum an yahilla 'alaykum ghadabun min rabbikum*, "Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?"). That is, that it should be incumbent upon you and alight on you. *Al-ghadab* means punishment and vengeance. The meaning is: or did you want to do an act that would be the cause of the descent of Allah's wrath upon you? ﴿فَأَخْلَفْتُمْ مَوْعِدِي﴾ (*fa-akhlaftum mau'idi*, "So you broke your appointment with me"). That is, your appointment with me. The verbal noun is in the genitive as an object-possessive construction (*idafah*) to the object, because they had promised him that they would remain in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he returned to them from Mount Tur. It was also said: they had promised him that they would come after him to the appointed meeting, but they hesitated, and then they refused his summons.

And they said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own power" ﴿ما أخْلَفْنا مَوْعِدَكَ﴾. The word ﴿الَّذِي وعَدْناكَ﴾ refers to the promise we made you. ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā, "by our power") is read with a fatha on the mīm (bi-malkinā) by Nāfi', Abū Ja'far, 'Āṣim and 'Īsā ibn 'Umar. Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr and Ibn 'Āmir read it with a kasra on the mīm (bi-milkinā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because it follows the high, eloquent dialect (al-lughah al-'āliyah al-faṣīḥah). It is the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'a, amlikuhu, milkan" (I possessed the thing). The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with its agent, and its object is omitted: that is, "by our managing our affairs" (bi-milkinā umūranā), or "by our possessing right judgment" (bi-milkinā al-ṣawāb). The meaning is: "Rather, we erred, and we did not have control over ourselves; we were compelled to err." Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿بِمُلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā) with a ḍamma on the mīm, meaning "by our authority" (bi-sulṭāninā): that is, we had no authority by which we could break your promise. It is also said that the fatḥ, kasra and ḍamma in ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ are all dialectal variants of the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'".

﴿ولَكِنّا حُمِّلْنا أوْزارًا مِن زِينَةِ القَوْمِ﴾ "But we were made to carry burdens of the adornments of the people." Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥafṣ, Abū Ja'far and Ruways read ﴿حُمِّلْنا﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a shadda on the mīm (ḥummilnā). The rest read it with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and a light mīm (ḥamalnā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this second reading, because they carried the people's ornaments with them by their own choice, and they were not carried against their will. They had borrowed the ornaments from them when they wanted to leave with Mūsā, and they gave them the impression that they were gathering for a festival or a feast of theirs. It is also said that it refers to what they took from the family of Pharaoh when the sea cast them up onto the shore. They were called ﴿أوْزارًا﴾ (awzāran, "burdens"), meaning sins (āthāman), because it was not lawful for them to take them, and spoils of war were not lawful for them under their law. In the original sense, awzār means "loads" (al-athqāl), as the lexicographers have stated. Here ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾ (al-zīnah, "adornment") means the jewelry (al-ḥilyy). ﴿فَقَذَفْناها﴾ means "so we threw them", that is, we cast them into the fire, seeking deliverance from their sin. It is also said that the meaning is: we threw them to al-Sāmirī so that they would remain with him until Mūsā returned and could decide his opinion about them.

﴿فَكَذَلِكَ ألْقى السّامِرِيُّ﴾ "Thus did al-Sāmirī cast." That is, al-Sāmirī cast them in the same manner of casting. It is said that when the people were slow to notice Mūsā's return, al-Sāmirī said to them: "He has delayed from you only because of the jewelry you have." So they gathered it and handed it over to him. He threw it into the fire and fashioned a calf from it for them. Then he cast upon it a handful (qabḍah) from the trace of the Messenger, who was Jibrīl.

﴿فَصارَ عِجْلًا جَسَدًا لَهُ خُوارٌ﴾ "So it became a calf, a body that had a lowing." (p-919) That is, it lowed as a living calf lows. Al-khuwār is the sound of cattle. It is also said that its lowing was caused by the wind, because it had been made with holes in it; when the wind entered its belly, it lowed, and there was no life in it.

﴿فَقالُوا هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾ "Then they said, 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā, but he forgot.'" That is, al-Sāmirī and those who agreed with him said this statement. ﴿فَنَسِيَ﴾ (fa-nasiya, "but he forgot") means that Mūsā went astray and did not know where his god was, so he set off to seek him at the mountain (al-Ṭūr). It is also said that the meaning is: Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god and your god. It is also said that the one who forgot is al-Sāmirī: that is, al-Sāmirī abandoned what Mūsā had commanded him concerning faith, and went astray. Thus said Ibn al-A'rābī.

﴿أفَلا يَرَوْنَ ألّا يَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِمْ قَوْلًا﴾ "Do they not see that it does not return to them a word?" That is: will they not take heed and reflect that this calf does not return to them any word? That is, it does not answer them, and does not speak to them when they speak to it. So how can they imagine that it is a god when it is incapable of speaking? In ﴿ألّا يَرْجِعُ﴾ the ﴿ألّا﴾ is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy (al-thaqīlah) "anna", and there is an implied pronoun in it that refers to the calf. For this reason the verb after it is in the nominative (irtafa'a). From this is the verse of the poet:

"Among youths from the Indian swords, who know that everyone who goes barefoot and wears sandals is doomed."

That is: that he is doomed. It has also been read with the verb in the accusative, taking it as the governing (nāṣibah) form. The clause ﴿ولا يَمْلِكُ لَهم ضَرًّا ولا نَفْعًا﴾ "and it does not possess for them any harm or benefit" is coordinated with the clause "does not return." That is: do they not see that it has no power to repel harm from them or to bring benefit to them?

﴿ولَقَدْ قالَ لَهم هارُونُ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ "And Hārūn had already said to them before this." The lām here is the preparatory lām (al-muwaṭṭi'ah) for an oath, and the sentence confirms what the preceding sentence contained of denunciation and reproach. That is: Hārūn had said to them, before Mūsā came and returned to them, ﴿ياقَوْمِ إنَّما فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ "O my people, you have only been tested by it." That is: you have fallen into temptation because of the calf, you have been tried by it, and you have gone astray from the path of truth on its account. It is said that the restrictive sense derived from "innamā" (only) is that the calf became a cause of their temptation, not of their guidance; it does not mean that they were tempted by the calf and not by anything else. ﴿وإنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فاتَّبِعُونِي وأطِيعُوا أمْرِي﴾ "Your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." That is: your Lord is the Most Merciful, not the calf, and obey my command, not its command.

﴿قالُوا لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفِينَ حَتّى يَرْجِعَ إلَيْنا مُوسى﴾ "They said, 'We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Mūsā returns to us.'" They answered Hārūn's earlier statement with this reply, which contained their disobedience and their refusal to accept what he called them to of good and his warning them against evil. That is: we will continue to remain upon the worship of this calf until Mūsā returns to us, and he will see whether he will confirm us in its worship or forbid us from it. At that point Hārūn withdrew from them with twelve thousand people who disapproved of what al-Sāmirī had done.

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Ka'b, concerning His words ﴿يَبَسًا﴾ (yabasan, "a dry path"), that he said: "Dry, with no water and no mud in it."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning ﴿لا تَخافُ دَرَكًا﴾ "you will not fear being overtaken" — from the family of Pharaoh — ﴿ولا تَخْشى﴾ "and you will not dread" — from drowning in the sea.

They both also reported from him, concerning ﴿فَقَدْ هَوى﴾ "then he has perished," that it means "wretched" (shaqiya).

They both also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾ "Indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents," that he said: "from shirk, and believes," he said: "he affirms the oneness of Allah"; ﴿وعَمِلَ صالِحًا﴾ "and does righteous deeds," he said: "he performs the obligatory duties"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided," he said: "he does not doubt."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr and al-Firyābī also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾: "whoever repents from sin, believes instead of shirk, and does righteous deeds between himself and his Lord"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided": "he knows that his deed has a reward for which he will be recompensed."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾: "then he goes straight, and holds fast to the Sunnah and the community (al-jamā'ah)."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Bayhaqī in "al-Ba'th" reported by way of 'Amr ibn Maymūn from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Mūsā hastened to his Lord, and Allah said: ﴿وما أعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يامُوسى﴾ "And what hastened you from your people, O Mūsā?" — the verse. He said: "He saw in the shade of the Throne a man, and was amazed by him. He said: 'Who is this, my Lord?' He said: 'I will not tell you who he is, but I will inform you of three things about him: he did not envy people for what Allah had given them of His bounty, he did not disobey his parents, and he did not walk about spreading slander.'"

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, reported from 'Alī, who said: "When Mūsā hastened to his Lord, al-Sāmirī set out, gathered whatever he could of the jewelry of the Children of Israel, and fashioned it into a calf. Then he cast the handful into its belly, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing. Al-Sāmirī said to them: 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā.' Hārūn said to them: 'O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?' When Mūsā returned, he seized his brother by the head, and Hārūn told him what had happened. Mūsā said to al-Sāmirī: 'What is your matter?' He said: ﴿فَقَبَضْتُ قَبْضَةً مِن أثَرِ الرَّسُولِ فَنَبَذْتُها وكَذَلِكَ سَوَّلَتْ لِي نَفْسِي﴾ 'I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger, and I threw it, and thus my soul enticed me.' Mūsā then turned to the calf, put files on it, and ground it down with them while it was on the bank of a river. No one among those who had worshipped that calf drank from that water without his face turning yellow like gold. They said to Mūsā: 'What is our repentance?' He said: 'Let some of you kill others.' So they took knives, and a man began killing his brother, his father and his son, not caring whom he killed, until seventy thousand of them had been killed. Then Allah revealed to Mūsā: 'Command them to raise their hands, for I have forgiven those who were killed and have accepted the repentance of those who remain.'" There are very many accounts of this story.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ "by our power," that he said: "by our command."

'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatādah, concerning ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾, that he said: "by our capacity (ṭāqah)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from al-Suddī.

He also reported from al-Ḥasan, who said: "by our authority (sulṭān)."

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾, that he said: "Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god."

(p. 917) This begins the account of the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the destruction of their enemy. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf and Yunus. The lam in ﴿لَقَدْ﴾ (*laqad*) is the *lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath), and the emphasis it gives is clear. The *an* in ﴿أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي﴾ (*an asri bi-ibadi*) is either *al-mufassirah* (the explanatory *an*), since revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the sense of speech, or *masdariyyah* (the verbal *an*, forming a verbal noun), meaning "[to] travel by night with My servants," that is, to take them out of Egypt. This has already been discussed fully. ﴿فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا﴾ means "Strike for them a path through the sea, dry," that is, make for them a path. *Yabsan* means "dry." It is described with the active participle form as an intensifier, because Allah made that path so dry that there was no water or mud in it. It is also read as *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba', either as a lightened form of *yabasan* with a fatha, or as the plural of *yabis*, like *sahb* for *sahib*. The clause ﴿لَا تَخَافُ دَرَكًا﴾ (*la takhafu darakan*, "you shall not fear being overtaken") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*): "secure from being overtaken by the enemy." Or it is another description of *tariq* (path). *Darak* means catching up with them from Pharaoh and his soldiers. Hamzah read ﴿لَا تَخَفْ﴾ (*la takhaf*) as a jussive response to the command, with the implied sense "if you strike, do not fear." Then ﴿وَلَا تَخْشَى﴾ (*wa la takhsha*, "nor shall you dread") is a new independent clause: "nor shall you dread Pharaoh or the sea." The majority (*al-jumhur*) read ﴿لَا تَخَافُ﴾ (*la takhafu*), which is more preferred, because *takhsha* is not jussive. It is also possible, in the majority reading, that this clause is another description of the path: "you shall not fear it, nor dread it."

﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِ﴾ (*fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu bi-junudih*, "Then Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers"). *Atba'a* here is the causative-reflexive form of *tabi'a*. One says *atba'tuhum* when you follow people who had gone ahead of you and you catch up with them. So the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them, and his soldiers were with him. It was also said that the *ba'* is extra, and the original is *atba'ahum junudah*, meaning he ordered his soldiers to follow Musa and his people. It was read as ﴿فَاتَّبَعَهُمْ﴾ (*fattaba'ahum*), with shaddah, meaning he caught up with them with his soldiers, and he was with them, as one says "the commander rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. The phrase *bi-junudih* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: "leading his soldiers with him."

﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum mina al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*, "Then the sea covered them, covering them as it did"). This means: what overwhelmed them and struck them overwhelmed and struck them. The repetition is for magnification and awe, as in His words ﴿الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ ﴿مَا الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:1–2), "The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality?" It was also said that what overwhelmed them is that whose story has been heard. Ibn al-Anbari said: "What overwhelmed them was a part of what overwhelmed them, because not all the water of the sea covered them; only part of it did." So this expression indicates that what drowned them was only some of the water. The first view is better because of the awe and magnification it conveys. It was read as ﴿فَغَشَّاهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشَّاهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashshahum ... ma ghashshahum*), meaning it covered them with what covered them.

﴿وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَى﴾ (*wa adalla Fir'awnu qawmahu wa ma hada*, "Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them"). That is, he led them away from right guidance, and did not guide them to the ways of salvation, because he assumed that Musa and those with him could not escape him, since they were before him walking on a dry path with the sea ahead of them. The phrase ﴿وَمَا هَدَى﴾ is an emphasis on his leading them astray, because one who misleads may guide the one he misleads in some matters.

﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ﴾ (*ya bani Isra'il, qad anjaynakum min aduwwikum*, "O Children of Israel, We have certainly delivered you from your enemy"). Allah mentioned the favor He bestowed upon the Children of Israel after delivering them. The implied sense is: We said to them after their deliverance, "O Children of Israel." It is also possible that this is addressed to the Jews contemporary with our Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace), because a blessing granted to the forefathers is counted as a blessing granted to their descendants. The enemy here means Pharaoh and his soldiers, destroyed by drowning him and his people in the sea, before the eyes of the Children of Israel. ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنَ﴾ (*wa wa'adnakum janiba al-tur al-ayman*, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Tur"). *Janib* is in the accusative as a direct object, not as an adverb of place, because it is a specific place, not an undefined one. Place nouns are in the accusative as adverbs only when they are indefinite. Makki said: "This is a principle on which there is no disagreement." Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning is that We commanded Musa to order you to go out with him, so that We might speak to him in your presence and you might hear the speech." It was also said that Musa was promised, after the drowning of Pharaoh, that he would come to the side of the mountain, so the promise was to Musa, but they were addressed with it because the promise was made for their sake. Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿وَوَعَدْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*wa 'adnakum*) without an alif, and Abu Ubayda preferred this reading, because the promising (*al-wa'd*) comes only from Allah to Musa specifically, whereas *al-mu'adah* (mutual appointment) can only be between two parties. We have already discussed this meaning in al-Baqarah. *Al-ayman* is in the accusative as an adjective of *janib*. The intended meaning is the right side of the person, because a mountain has no right or left side; so when one says "take the right side of the mountain," it means the right side from your perspective, relative to the mountain. It was also read in the genitive, as an adjective of the noun to which *janib* is attached.

﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَنَّ وَالسَّلْوَى﴾ (*wa nazzalna 'alaykumu al-manna wa al-salwa*, "And We sent down upon you manna and quail"). The explanation of *al-manna* as *al-tarankhabin* (a sweet exudation, like honey-dew) and *al-salwa* as *al-sammani* (quail) was discussed earlier, and we have clarified this fully. The sending down of these was during the wandering (*al-tih*) in the desert.

﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*kulu min tayyibati ma razaqnakum*, "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you"). That is, and We said to them, "Eat." The intended meaning of *al-tayyibat* is the pleasant things. It was also said that it means the lawful (*al-halal*), according to the well-known disagreement on this matter. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read ﴿قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ﴾ and ﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ with the first-person singular *ta'* (of the speaker) in all three places.
