The rest read with the royal plural *nun* (of majesty) in these places. ﴿وَلَا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ﴾ (*wa la tatghaw fihi*, "and do not transgress therein"). *Al-tughyan* means exceeding limits, that is, do not go beyond what is permissible to what is not permissible. It was also said that the meaning is: do not deny the blessing of Allah, lest you become transgressors. It was also said: do not disbelieve the blessing or forget its thanks. It was also said: do not disobey the Benefactor, that is, do not let ease and well-being lead you into disobedience. There is no obstacle to understanding *al-tughyan* as including all these meanings, since each of them truly counts as transgression.

﴿فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي﴾ (*fa-yahilla 'alaykum ghadabi*, "lest My anger descend upon you"). This is the answer (*jawab*) to the prohibition. That is: My anger will be incumbent upon you and will alight on you. It is derived from *hulul al-dayn* (the falling due of a debt), meaning the arrival of the time of its payment. ﴿وَمَنْ يَحْلِلْ عَلَيْهِ غَضَبِي فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*wa man yahlil 'alayhi ghadabi fa-qad hawa*, "And whoever has My anger descend upon him has certainly perished"). Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فَيَحُلَّ﴾ (*fa-yahulla*) with a damma on the ha', and likewise they read ﴿يَحْلُلْ﴾ (*yahlul*) with a damma on the first lam. The rest read both with a kasra. Both are dialect variants. Al-Farra' said: "The kasra is more beloved to me than the damma, because the damma is from *hulul* in the sense of *wuqu'* (alighting or befalling), whereas *yahill* with a kasra means "must" (*yajibu*). The explanation was given as "must," not as "befall." Abu Ubayda and others mentioned something similar." The meaning of ﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*fa-qad hawa*) is "has certainly perished." Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ means he has gone down into the abyss (*al-hawiyah*), which is the bottom of the Fire, from *hawa yahwi hawyan*, meaning he fell from a height to a low place." *Hawa Fulan* also means he died.

﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba wa amana wa 'amila salihan thumma ihtada*, "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided"). That is, to whoever repents from sins, the greatest of which is associating partners with Allah, and believes in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and does a righteous deed of what the Law has recommended and beautified. ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ means he remains upright in this until he dies. This is what al-Zajjaj and others said. It was also said: he never doubted his faith; it was said: he adhered to the Sunnah and the community (*al-sunnah wa al-jama'ah*); it was said: he learned knowledge in order to be guided by it; it was said: he knew that there is reward for this and punishment for abandoning it. The first view is more preferred than what follows it.

﴿وَمَا أَعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يَا مُوسَى﴾ (*wa ma a'jalaka 'an qawmika ya Musa*, "And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?"). This is a narration of what took place between Allah, glorified is He, and Musa when he came to the appointed meeting. The exegetes said: the appointment was that Musa and a group of the notables of his people would come, so Musa set out with them, then he hastened ahead of them out of longing for his Lord. Allah said to him: "What hastened you?" That is, what made you hasten, so that you left your people and departed from among them. Musa answered this. ﴿قَالَ هُمْ أُولَاءِ عَلَى أَثَرِي﴾ (*qala hum ula'i 'ala athari*, "He said: They are right behind me"). That is, they are close to me, following my track, and will reach me after me. It was also said: he did not mean that they were following behind him, but that they were near him, waiting for his return to them. Then he said, clarifying the reason for what Allah had asked him about: ﴿وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضَى﴾ (*wa 'ajiltu ilayka rabbi li-tarda*, "And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased"). That is, that You may be pleased with me by my hastening to carry out Your command, or that You may increase in being pleased with me by this. Abu Hatim said: Isa ibn Umar said: "The Banu Tamim say *ula* (short form), while the people of the Hijaz say *ula'i* (long form)." Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub read ﴿إِثْرِي﴾ (*ithri*) with a kasra on the hamzah and a sukun on the tha', and the rest read it with a fatha; both are dialect variants. The meaning of ﴿عَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (*'ajiltu ilayka*) is: I hastened to the place where You commanded me to go, so that You might be pleased with me. One says *rajul 'ajil*, *'ajul* and *'ajlan* to mean one who is clearly hasty; *al-'ajalah* is the opposite of slowness.

﴿قَالَ فَإِنَّا قَدْ فَتَنَّا قَوْمَكَ مِنْ بَعْدِكَ﴾ (*qala fa-inna qad fatanna qawmaka min ba'dika*, "He said: Indeed, We have tested your people after you"). This sentence is independent, an answer to an implied question, as though it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" So it is said: He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you," that is, We tried them, examined them, and cast them into trial and affliction. Ibn al-Anbari said: "We made them tested and wretched through worship of the calf after your departure from among them. They were those whom he had left behind with Harun." ﴿وَأَضَلَّهُمُ السَّامِرِيُّ﴾ (*wa adallahumu al-samiri*, "and al-Samiri led them astray"). That is, he called them to error. He was from a people who worshipped cows. He entered the religion of the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was what he had of cow-worship. He was from a tribe known as the Samirah. He said to those with him among the Children of Israel: "Musa has delayed from the appointed meeting between you and him only because of the ornaments that you have with you, and they are forbidden to you." He commanded them to throw them into the fire, and so what happened with the calf happened.

﴿فَرَجَعَ مُوسَى إِلَى قَوْمِهِ غَضْبَانَ أَسِفًا﴾ (*fa-raja'a Musa ila qawmihi ghadban asifan*, "Then Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved"). It was said: the return to his people was after he had completed forty days: Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. *Al-asaf* means intense anger; it was also said: grief. This has already been fully explained in al-A'raf. ﴿قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَلَمْ يَعِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ وَعْدًا حَسَنًا﴾ (*qala ya qawmi alam ya'idkum rabbukum wa'dan hasanan*, "He said: O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"). The interrogative is for rebuke by way of denial. *Al-wa'd al-hasan* (the good promise) is what He promised them: Paradise, if they remain upon His obedience; and He promised that He would make them hear His speech in the Torah through the tongue of Musa, so that they would act by what is in it and thereby deserve the reward for their deeds. It was also said: He promised them victory and triumph. It was also said: it is His words ﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba*), "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents," and so on. ﴿أَفَطَالَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْعَهْدُ﴾ (*afa-tala 'alaykumu al-'ahd*, "Has the time seemed long to you?"). The *fa* connects to an implied clause: "Did He promise you that, so the time has grown long for you, and so you forgot?" ﴿أَمْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ يَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (*am aradtum an yahilla 'alaykum ghadabun min rabbikum*, "Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?"). That is, that it should be incumbent upon you and alight on you. *Al-ghadab* means punishment and vengeance. The meaning is: or did you want to do an act that would be the cause of the descent of Allah's wrath upon you? ﴿فَأَخْلَفْتُمْ مَوْعِدِي﴾ (*fa-akhlaftum mau'idi*, "So you broke your appointment with me"). That is, your appointment with me. The verbal noun is in the genitive as an object-possessive construction (*idafah*) to the object, because they had promised him that they would remain in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he returned to them from Mount Tur. It was also said: they had promised him that they would come after him to the appointed meeting, but they hesitated, and then they refused his summons.

And they said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own power" ﴿ما أخْلَفْنا مَوْعِدَكَ﴾. The word ﴿الَّذِي وعَدْناكَ﴾ refers to the promise we made you. ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā, "by our power") is read with a fatha on the mīm (bi-malkinā) by Nāfi', Abū Ja'far, 'Āṣim and 'Īsā ibn 'Umar. Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr and Ibn 'Āmir read it with a kasra on the mīm (bi-milkinā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because it follows the high, eloquent dialect (al-lughah al-'āliyah al-faṣīḥah). It is the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'a, amlikuhu, milkan" (I possessed the thing). The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with its agent, and its object is omitted: that is, "by our managing our affairs" (bi-milkinā umūranā), or "by our possessing right judgment" (bi-milkinā al-ṣawāb). The meaning is: "Rather, we erred, and we did not have control over ourselves; we were compelled to err." Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿بِمُلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā) with a ḍamma on the mīm, meaning "by our authority" (bi-sulṭāninā): that is, we had no authority by which we could break your promise. It is also said that the fatḥ, kasra and ḍamma in ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ are all dialectal variants of the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'".

﴿ولَكِنّا حُمِّلْنا أوْزارًا مِن زِينَةِ القَوْمِ﴾ "But we were made to carry burdens of the adornments of the people." Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥafṣ, Abū Ja'far and Ruways read ﴿حُمِّلْنا﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a shadda on the mīm (ḥummilnā). The rest read it with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and a light mīm (ḥamalnā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this second reading, because they carried the people's ornaments with them by their own choice, and they were not carried against their will. They had borrowed the ornaments from them when they wanted to leave with Mūsā, and they gave them the impression that they were gathering for a festival or a feast of theirs. It is also said that it refers to what they took from the family of Pharaoh when the sea cast them up onto the shore. They were called ﴿أوْزارًا﴾ (awzāran, "burdens"), meaning sins (āthāman), because it was not lawful for them to take them, and spoils of war were not lawful for them under their law. In the original sense, awzār means "loads" (al-athqāl), as the lexicographers have stated. Here ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾ (al-zīnah, "adornment") means the jewelry (al-ḥilyy). ﴿فَقَذَفْناها﴾ means "so we threw them", that is, we cast them into the fire, seeking deliverance from their sin. It is also said that the meaning is: we threw them to al-Sāmirī so that they would remain with him until Mūsā returned and could decide his opinion about them.

﴿فَكَذَلِكَ ألْقى السّامِرِيُّ﴾ "Thus did al-Sāmirī cast." That is, al-Sāmirī cast them in the same manner of casting. It is said that when the people were slow to notice Mūsā's return, al-Sāmirī said to them: "He has delayed from you only because of the jewelry you have." So they gathered it and handed it over to him. He threw it into the fire and fashioned a calf from it for them. Then he cast upon it a handful (qabḍah) from the trace of the Messenger, who was Jibrīl.

﴿فَصارَ عِجْلًا جَسَدًا لَهُ خُوارٌ﴾ "So it became a calf, a body that had a lowing." (p-919) That is, it lowed as a living calf lows. Al-khuwār is the sound of cattle. It is also said that its lowing was caused by the wind, because it had been made with holes in it; when the wind entered its belly, it lowed, and there was no life in it.

﴿فَقالُوا هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾ "Then they said, 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā, but he forgot.'" That is, al-Sāmirī and those who agreed with him said this statement. ﴿فَنَسِيَ﴾ (fa-nasiya, "but he forgot") means that Mūsā went astray and did not know where his god was, so he set off to seek him at the mountain (al-Ṭūr). It is also said that the meaning is: Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god and your god. It is also said that the one who forgot is al-Sāmirī: that is, al-Sāmirī abandoned what Mūsā had commanded him concerning faith, and went astray. Thus said Ibn al-A'rābī.

﴿أفَلا يَرَوْنَ ألّا يَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِمْ قَوْلًا﴾ "Do they not see that it does not return to them a word?" That is: will they not take heed and reflect that this calf does not return to them any word? That is, it does not answer them, and does not speak to them when they speak to it. So how can they imagine that it is a god when it is incapable of speaking? In ﴿ألّا يَرْجِعُ﴾ the ﴿ألّا﴾ is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy (al-thaqīlah) "anna", and there is an implied pronoun in it that refers to the calf. For this reason the verb after it is in the nominative (irtafa'a). From this is the verse of the poet:

"Among youths from the Indian swords, who know that everyone who goes barefoot and wears sandals is doomed."

That is: that he is doomed. It has also been read with the verb in the accusative, taking it as the governing (nāṣibah) form. The clause ﴿ولا يَمْلِكُ لَهم ضَرًّا ولا نَفْعًا﴾ "and it does not possess for them any harm or benefit" is coordinated with the clause "does not return." That is: do they not see that it has no power to repel harm from them or to bring benefit to them?

﴿ولَقَدْ قالَ لَهم هارُونُ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ "And Hārūn had already said to them before this." The lām here is the preparatory lām (al-muwaṭṭi'ah) for an oath, and the sentence confirms what the preceding sentence contained of denunciation and reproach. That is: Hārūn had said to them, before Mūsā came and returned to them, ﴿ياقَوْمِ إنَّما فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ "O my people, you have only been tested by it." That is: you have fallen into temptation because of the calf, you have been tried by it, and you have gone astray from the path of truth on its account. It is said that the restrictive sense derived from "innamā" (only) is that the calf became a cause of their temptation, not of their guidance; it does not mean that they were tempted by the calf and not by anything else. ﴿وإنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فاتَّبِعُونِي وأطِيعُوا أمْرِي﴾ "Your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." That is: your Lord is the Most Merciful, not the calf, and obey my command, not its command.

﴿قالُوا لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفِينَ حَتّى يَرْجِعَ إلَيْنا مُوسى﴾ "They said, 'We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Mūsā returns to us.'" They answered Hārūn's earlier statement with this reply, which contained their disobedience and their refusal to accept what he called them to of good and his warning them against evil. That is: we will continue to remain upon the worship of this calf until Mūsā returns to us, and he will see whether he will confirm us in its worship or forbid us from it. At that point Hārūn withdrew from them with twelve thousand people who disapproved of what al-Sāmirī had done.

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Ka'b, concerning His words ﴿يَبَسًا﴾ (yabasan, "a dry path"), that he said: "Dry, with no water and no mud in it."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning ﴿لا تَخافُ دَرَكًا﴾ "you will not fear being overtaken" — from the family of Pharaoh — ﴿ولا تَخْشى﴾ "and you will not dread" — from drowning in the sea.

They both also reported from him, concerning ﴿فَقَدْ هَوى﴾ "then he has perished," that it means "wretched" (shaqiya).

They both also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾ "Indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents," that he said: "from shirk, and believes," he said: "he affirms the oneness of Allah"; ﴿وعَمِلَ صالِحًا﴾ "and does righteous deeds," he said: "he performs the obligatory duties"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided," he said: "he does not doubt."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr and al-Firyābī also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾: "whoever repents from sin, believes instead of shirk, and does righteous deeds between himself and his Lord"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided": "he knows that his deed has a reward for which he will be recompensed."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾: "then he goes straight, and holds fast to the Sunnah and the community (al-jamā'ah)."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Bayhaqī in "al-Ba'th" reported by way of 'Amr ibn Maymūn from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Mūsā hastened to his Lord, and Allah said: ﴿وما أعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يامُوسى﴾ "And what hastened you from your people, O Mūsā?" — the verse. He said: "He saw in the shade of the Throne a man, and was amazed by him. He said: 'Who is this, my Lord?' He said: 'I will not tell you who he is, but I will inform you of three things about him: he did not envy people for what Allah had given them of His bounty, he did not disobey his parents, and he did not walk about spreading slander.'"

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, reported from 'Alī, who said: "When Mūsā hastened to his Lord, al-Sāmirī set out, gathered whatever he could of the jewelry of the Children of Israel, and fashioned it into a calf. Then he cast the handful into its belly, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing. Al-Sāmirī said to them: 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā.' Hārūn said to them: 'O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?' When Mūsā returned, he seized his brother by the head, and Hārūn told him what had happened. Mūsā said to al-Sāmirī: 'What is your matter?' He said: ﴿فَقَبَضْتُ قَبْضَةً مِن أثَرِ الرَّسُولِ فَنَبَذْتُها وكَذَلِكَ سَوَّلَتْ لِي نَفْسِي﴾ 'I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger, and I threw it, and thus my soul enticed me.' Mūsā then turned to the calf, put files on it, and ground it down with them while it was on the bank of a river. No one among those who had worshipped that calf drank from that water without his face turning yellow like gold. They said to Mūsā: 'What is our repentance?' He said: 'Let some of you kill others.' So they took knives, and a man began killing his brother, his father and his son, not caring whom he killed, until seventy thousand of them had been killed. Then Allah revealed to Mūsā: 'Command them to raise their hands, for I have forgiven those who were killed and have accepted the repentance of those who remain.'" There are very many accounts of this story.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ "by our power," that he said: "by our command."

'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatādah, concerning ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾, that he said: "by our capacity (ṭāqah)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from al-Suddī.

He also reported from al-Ḥasan, who said: "by our authority (sulṭān)."

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾, that he said: "Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god."

(p. 917) This begins the account of the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the destruction of their enemy. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf and Yunus. The lam in ﴿لَقَدْ﴾ (*laqad*) is the *lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath), and the emphasis it gives is clear. The *an* in ﴿أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي﴾ (*an asri bi-ibadi*) is either *al-mufassirah* (the explanatory *an*), since revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the sense of speech, or *masdariyyah* (the verbal *an*, forming a verbal noun), meaning "[to] travel by night with My servants," that is, to take them out of Egypt. This has already been discussed fully. ﴿فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا﴾ means "Strike for them a path through the sea, dry," that is, make for them a path. *Yabsan* means "dry." It is described with the active participle form as an intensifier, because Allah made that path so dry that there was no water or mud in it. It is also read as *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba', either as a lightened form of *yabasan* with a fatha, or as the plural of *yabis*, like *sahb* for *sahib*. The clause ﴿لَا تَخَافُ دَرَكًا﴾ (*la takhafu darakan*, "you shall not fear being overtaken") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*): "secure from being overtaken by the enemy." Or it is another description of *tariq* (path). *Darak* means catching up with them from Pharaoh and his soldiers. Hamzah read ﴿لَا تَخَفْ﴾ (*la takhaf*) as a jussive response to the command, with the implied sense "if you strike, do not fear." Then ﴿وَلَا تَخْشَى﴾ (*wa la takhsha*, "nor shall you dread") is a new independent clause: "nor shall you dread Pharaoh or the sea." The majority (*al-jumhur*) read ﴿لَا تَخَافُ﴾ (*la takhafu*), which is more preferred, because *takhsha* is not jussive. It is also possible, in the majority reading, that this clause is another description of the path: "you shall not fear it, nor dread it."

﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِ﴾ (*fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu bi-junudih*, "Then Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers"). *Atba'a* here is the causative-reflexive form of *tabi'a*. One says *atba'tuhum* when you follow people who had gone ahead of you and you catch up with them. So the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them, and his soldiers were with him. It was also said that the *ba'* is extra, and the original is *atba'ahum junudah*, meaning he ordered his soldiers to follow Musa and his people. It was read as ﴿فَاتَّبَعَهُمْ﴾ (*fattaba'ahum*), with shaddah, meaning he caught up with them with his soldiers, and he was with them, as one says "the commander rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. The phrase *bi-junudih* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: "leading his soldiers with him."

﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum mina al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*, "Then the sea covered them, covering them as it did"). This means: what overwhelmed them and struck them overwhelmed and struck them. The repetition is for magnification and awe, as in His words ﴿الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ ﴿مَا الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:1–2), "The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality?" It was also said that what overwhelmed them is that whose story has been heard. Ibn al-Anbari said: "What overwhelmed them was a part of what overwhelmed them, because not all the water of the sea covered them; only part of it did." So this expression indicates that what drowned them was only some of the water. The first view is better because of the awe and magnification it conveys. It was read as ﴿فَغَشَّاهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشَّاهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashshahum ... ma ghashshahum*), meaning it covered them with what covered them.

﴿وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَى﴾ (*wa adalla Fir'awnu qawmahu wa ma hada*, "Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them"). That is, he led them away from right guidance, and did not guide them to the ways of salvation, because he assumed that Musa and those with him could not escape him, since they were before him walking on a dry path with the sea ahead of them. The phrase ﴿وَمَا هَدَى﴾ is an emphasis on his leading them astray, because one who misleads may guide the one he misleads in some matters.

﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ﴾ (*ya bani Isra'il, qad anjaynakum min aduwwikum*, "O Children of Israel, We have certainly delivered you from your enemy"). Allah mentioned the favor He bestowed upon the Children of Israel after delivering them. The implied sense is: We said to them after their deliverance, "O Children of Israel." It is also possible that this is addressed to the Jews contemporary with our Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace), because a blessing granted to the forefathers is counted as a blessing granted to their descendants. The enemy here means Pharaoh and his soldiers, destroyed by drowning him and his people in the sea, before the eyes of the Children of Israel. ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنَ﴾ (*wa wa'adnakum janiba al-tur al-ayman*, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Tur"). *Janib* is in the accusative as a direct object, not as an adverb of place, because it is a specific place, not an undefined one. Place nouns are in the accusative as adverbs only when they are indefinite. Makki said: "This is a principle on which there is no disagreement." Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning is that We commanded Musa to order you to go out with him, so that We might speak to him in your presence and you might hear the speech." It was also said that Musa was promised, after the drowning of Pharaoh, that he would come to the side of the mountain, so the promise was to Musa, but they were addressed with it because the promise was made for their sake. Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿وَوَعَدْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*wa 'adnakum*) without an alif, and Abu Ubayda preferred this reading, because the promising (*al-wa'd*) comes only from Allah to Musa specifically, whereas *al-mu'adah* (mutual appointment) can only be between two parties. We have already discussed this meaning in al-Baqarah. *Al-ayman* is in the accusative as an adjective of *janib*. The intended meaning is the right side of the person, because a mountain has no right or left side; so when one says "take the right side of the mountain," it means the right side from your perspective, relative to the mountain. It was also read in the genitive, as an adjective of the noun to which *janib* is attached.

﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَنَّ وَالسَّلْوَى﴾ (*wa nazzalna 'alaykumu al-manna wa al-salwa*, "And We sent down upon you manna and quail"). The explanation of *al-manna* as *al-tarankhabin* (a sweet exudation, like honey-dew) and *al-salwa* as *al-sammani* (quail) was discussed earlier, and we have clarified this fully. The sending down of these was during the wandering (*al-tih*) in the desert.

﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*kulu min tayyibati ma razaqnakum*, "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you"). That is, and We said to them, "Eat." The intended meaning of *al-tayyibat* is the pleasant things. It was also said that it means the lawful (*al-halal*), according to the well-known disagreement on this matter. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read ﴿قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ﴾ and ﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ with the first-person singular *ta'* (of the speaker) in all three places. The rest read with the royal plural *nun* (of majesty) in these places. ﴿وَلَا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ﴾ (*wa la tatghaw fihi*, "and do not transgress therein"). *Al-tughyan* means exceeding limits, that is, do not go beyond what is permissible to what is not permissible. It was also said that the meaning is: do not deny the blessing of Allah, lest you become transgressors. It was also said: do not disbelieve the blessing or forget its thanks. It was also said: do not disobey the Benefactor, that is, do not let ease and well-being lead you into disobedience. There is no obstacle to understanding *al-tughyan* as including all these meanings, since each of them truly counts as transgression.

﴿فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي﴾ (*fa-yahilla 'alaykum ghadabi*, "lest My anger descend upon you"). This is the answer (*jawab*) to the prohibition. That is: My anger will be incumbent upon you and will alight on you. It is derived from *hulul al-dayn* (the falling due of a debt), meaning the arrival of the time of its payment. ﴿وَمَنْ يَحْلِلْ عَلَيْهِ غَضَبِي فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*wa man yahlil 'alayhi ghadabi fa-qad hawa*, "And whoever has My anger descend upon him has certainly perished"). Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فَيَحُلَّ﴾ (*fa-yahulla*) with a damma on the ha', and likewise they read ﴿يَحْلُلْ﴾ (*yahlul*) with a damma on the first lam. The rest read both with a kasra. Both are dialect variants. Al-Farra' said: "The kasra is more beloved to me than the damma, because the damma is from *hulul* in the sense of *wuqu'* (alighting or befalling), whereas *yahill* with a kasra means "must" (*yajibu*). The explanation was given as "must," not as "befall." Abu Ubayda and others mentioned something similar." The meaning of ﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*fa-qad hawa*) is "has certainly perished." Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ means he has gone down into the abyss (*al-hawiyah*), which is the bottom of the Fire, from *hawa yahwi hawyan*, meaning he fell from a height to a low place." *Hawa Fulan* also means he died.

﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba wa amana wa 'amila salihan thumma ihtada*, "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided"). That is, to whoever repents from sins, the greatest of which is associating partners with Allah, and believes in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and does a righteous deed of what the Law has recommended and beautified. ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ means he remains upright in this until he dies. This is what al-Zajjaj and others said. It was also said: he never doubted his faith; it was said: he adhered to the Sunnah and the community (*al-sunnah wa al-jama'ah*); it was said: he learned knowledge in order to be guided by it; it was said: he knew that there is reward for this and punishment for abandoning it. The first view is more preferred than what follows it.

﴿وَمَا أَعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يَا مُوسَى﴾ (*wa ma a'jalaka 'an qawmika ya Musa*, "And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?"). This is a narration of what took place between Allah, glorified is He, and Musa when he came to the appointed meeting. The exegetes said: the appointment was that Musa and a group of the notables of his people would come, so Musa set out with them, then he hastened ahead of them out of longing for his Lord. Allah said to him: "What hastened you?" That is, what made you hasten, so that you left your people and departed from among them. Musa answered this. ﴿قَالَ هُمْ أُولَاءِ عَلَى أَثَرِي﴾ (*qala hum ula'i 'ala athari*, "He said: They are right behind me"). That is, they are close to me, following my track, and will reach me after me. It was also said: he did not mean that they were following behind him, but that they were near him, waiting for his return to them. Then he said, clarifying the reason for what Allah had asked him about: ﴿وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضَى﴾ (*wa 'ajiltu ilayka rabbi li-tarda*, "And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased"). That is, that You may be pleased with me by my hastening to carry out Your command, or that You may increase in being pleased with me by this. Abu Hatim said: Isa ibn Umar said: "The Banu Tamim say *ula* (short form), while the people of the Hijaz say *ula'i* (long form)." Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub read ﴿إِثْرِي﴾ (*ithri*) with a kasra on the hamzah and a sukun on the tha', and the rest read it with a fatha; both are dialect variants. The meaning of ﴿عَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (*'ajiltu ilayka*) is: I hastened to the place where You commanded me to go, so that You might be pleased with me. One says *rajul 'ajil*, *'ajul* and *'ajlan* to mean one who is clearly hasty; *al-'ajalah* is the opposite of slowness.

﴿قَالَ فَإِنَّا قَدْ فَتَنَّا قَوْمَكَ مِنْ بَعْدِكَ﴾ (*qala fa-inna qad fatanna qawmaka min ba'dika*, "He said: Indeed, We have tested your people after you"). This sentence is independent, an answer to an implied question, as though it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" So it is said: He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you," that is, We tried them, examined them, and cast them into trial and affliction. Ibn al-Anbari said: "We made them tested and wretched through worship of the calf after your departure from among them. They were those whom he had left behind with Harun." ﴿وَأَضَلَّهُمُ السَّامِرِيُّ﴾ (*wa adallahumu al-samiri*, "and al-Samiri led them astray"). That is, he called them to error. He was from a people who worshipped cows. He entered the religion of the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was what he had of cow-worship. He was from a tribe known as the Samirah. He said to those with him among the Children of Israel: "Musa has delayed from the appointed meeting between you and him only because of the ornaments that you have with you, and they are forbidden to you." He commanded them to throw them into the fire, and so what happened with the calf happened.

﴿فَرَجَعَ مُوسَى إِلَى قَوْمِهِ غَضْبَانَ أَسِفًا﴾ (*fa-raja'a Musa ila qawmihi ghadban asifan*, "Then Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved"). It was said: the return to his people was after he had completed forty days: Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. *Al-asaf* means intense anger; it was also said: grief. This has already been fully explained in al-A'raf. ﴿قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَلَمْ يَعِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ وَعْدًا حَسَنًا﴾ (*qala ya qawmi alam ya'idkum rabbukum wa'dan hasanan*, "He said: O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"). The interrogative is for rebuke by way of denial. *Al-wa'd al-hasan* (the good promise) is what He promised them: Paradise, if they remain upon His obedience; and He promised that He would make them hear His speech in the Torah through the tongue of Musa, so that they would act by what is in it and thereby deserve the reward for their deeds. It was also said: He promised them victory and triumph. It was also said: it is His words ﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba*), "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents," and so on. ﴿أَفَطَالَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْعَهْدُ﴾ (*afa-tala 'alaykumu al-'ahd*, "Has the time seemed long to you?"). The *fa* connects to an implied clause: "Did He promise you that, so the time has grown long for you, and so you forgot?" ﴿أَمْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ يَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (*am aradtum an yahilla 'alaykum ghadabun min rabbikum*, "Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?"). That is, that it should be incumbent upon you and alight on you. *Al-ghadab* means punishment and vengeance. The meaning is: or did you want to do an act that would be the cause of the descent of Allah's wrath upon you? ﴿فَأَخْلَفْتُمْ مَوْعِدِي﴾ (*fa-akhlaftum mau'idi*, "So you broke your appointment with me"). That is, your appointment with me. The verbal noun is in the genitive as an object-possessive construction (*idafah*) to the object, because they had promised him that they would remain in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he returned to them from Mount Tur. It was also said: they had promised him that they would come after him to the appointed meeting, but they hesitated, and then they refused his summons.

And they said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own power" ﴿ما أخْلَفْنا مَوْعِدَكَ﴾. The word ﴿الَّذِي وعَدْناكَ﴾ refers to the promise we made you. ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā, "by our power") is read with a fatha on the mīm (bi-malkinā) by Nāfi', Abū Ja'far, 'Āṣim and 'Īsā ibn 'Umar. Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr and Ibn 'Āmir read it with a kasra on the mīm (bi-milkinā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because it follows the high, eloquent dialect (al-lughah al-'āliyah al-faṣīḥah). It is the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'a, amlikuhu, milkan" (I possessed the thing). The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with its agent, and its object is omitted: that is, "by our managing our affairs" (bi-milkinā umūranā), or "by our possessing right judgment" (bi-milkinā al-ṣawāb). The meaning is: "Rather, we erred, and we did not have control over ourselves; we were compelled to err." Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿بِمُلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā) with a ḍamma on the mīm, meaning "by our authority" (bi-sulṭāninā): that is, we had no authority by which we could break your promise. It is also said that the fatḥ, kasra and ḍamma in ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ are all dialectal variants of the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'".

﴿ولَكِنّا حُمِّلْنا أوْزارًا مِن زِينَةِ القَوْمِ﴾ "But we were made to carry burdens of the adornments of the people." Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥafṣ, Abū Ja'far and Ruways read ﴿حُمِّلْنا﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a shadda on the mīm (ḥummilnā). The rest read it with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and a light mīm (ḥamalnā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this second reading, because they carried the people's ornaments with them by their own choice, and they were not carried against their will. They had borrowed the ornaments from them when they wanted to leave with Mūsā, and they gave them the impression that they were gathering for a festival or a feast of theirs. It is also said that it refers to what they took from the family of Pharaoh when the sea cast them up onto the shore. They were called ﴿أوْزارًا﴾ (awzāran, "burdens"), meaning sins (āthāman), because it was not lawful for them to take them, and spoils of war were not lawful for them under their law. In the original sense, awzār means "loads" (al-athqāl), as the lexicographers have stated. Here ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾ (al-zīnah, "adornment") means the jewelry (al-ḥilyy). ﴿فَقَذَفْناها﴾ means "so we threw them", that is, we cast them into the fire, seeking deliverance from their sin. It is also said that the meaning is: we threw them to al-Sāmirī so that they would remain with him until Mūsā returned and could decide his opinion about them.

﴿فَكَذَلِكَ ألْقى السّامِرِيُّ﴾ "Thus did al-Sāmirī cast." That is, al-Sāmirī cast them in the same manner of casting. It is said that when the people were slow to notice Mūsā's return, al-Sāmirī said to them: "He has delayed from you only because of the jewelry you have." So they gathered it and handed it over to him. He threw it into the fire and fashioned a calf from it for them. Then he cast upon it a handful (qabḍah) from the trace of the Messenger, who was Jibrīl.

﴿فَصارَ عِجْلًا جَسَدًا لَهُ خُوارٌ﴾ "So it became a calf, a body that had a lowing." (p-919) That is, it lowed as a living calf lows. Al-khuwār is the sound of cattle. It is also said that its lowing was caused by the wind, because it had been made with holes in it; when the wind entered its belly, it lowed, and there was no life in it.

﴿فَقالُوا هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾ "Then they said, 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā, but he forgot.'" That is, al-Sāmirī and those who agreed with him said this statement. ﴿فَنَسِيَ﴾ (fa-nasiya, "but he forgot") means that Mūsā went astray and did not know where his god was, so he set off to seek him at the mountain (al-Ṭūr). It is also said that the meaning is: Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god and your god. It is also said that the one who forgot is al-Sāmirī: that is, al-Sāmirī abandoned what Mūsā had commanded him concerning faith, and went astray. Thus said Ibn al-A'rābī.

﴿أفَلا يَرَوْنَ ألّا يَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِمْ قَوْلًا﴾ "Do they not see that it does not return to them a word?" That is: will they not take heed and reflect that this calf does not return to them any word? That is, it does not answer them, and does not speak to them when they speak to it. So how can they imagine that it is a god when it is incapable of speaking? In ﴿ألّا يَرْجِعُ﴾ the ﴿ألّا﴾ is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy (al-thaqīlah) "anna", and there is an implied pronoun in it that refers to the calf. For this reason the verb after it is in the nominative (irtafa'a). From this is the verse of the poet:

"Among youths from the Indian swords, who know that everyone who goes barefoot and wears sandals is doomed."

That is: that he is doomed. It has also been read with the verb in the accusative, taking it as the governing (nāṣibah) form. The clause ﴿ولا يَمْلِكُ لَهم ضَرًّا ولا نَفْعًا﴾ "and it does not possess for them any harm or benefit" is coordinated with the clause "does not return." That is: do they not see that it has no power to repel harm from them or to bring benefit to them?

﴿ولَقَدْ قالَ لَهم هارُونُ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ "And Hārūn had already said to them before this." The lām here is the preparatory lām (al-muwaṭṭi'ah) for an oath, and the sentence confirms what the preceding sentence contained of denunciation and reproach. That is: Hārūn had said to them, before Mūsā came and returned to them, ﴿ياقَوْمِ إنَّما فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ "O my people, you have only been tested by it." That is: you have fallen into temptation because of the calf, you have been tried by it, and you have gone astray from the path of truth on its account. It is said that the restrictive sense derived from "innamā" (only) is that the calf became a cause of their temptation, not of their guidance; it does not mean that they were tempted by the calf and not by anything else. ﴿وإنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فاتَّبِعُونِي وأطِيعُوا أمْرِي﴾ "Your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." That is: your Lord is the Most Merciful, not the calf, and obey my command, not its command.

﴿قالُوا لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفِينَ حَتّى يَرْجِعَ إلَيْنا مُوسى﴾ "They said, 'We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Mūsā returns to us.'" They answered Hārūn's earlier statement with this reply, which contained their disobedience and their refusal to accept what he called them to of good and his warning them against evil. That is: we will continue to remain upon the worship of this calf until Mūsā returns to us, and he will see whether he will confirm us in its worship or forbid us from it. At that point Hārūn withdrew from them with twelve thousand people who disapproved of what al-Sāmirī had done.

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Ka'b, concerning His words ﴿يَبَسًا﴾ (yabasan, "a dry path"), that he said: "Dry, with no water and no mud in it."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning ﴿لا تَخافُ دَرَكًا﴾ "you will not fear being overtaken" — from the family of Pharaoh — ﴿ولا تَخْشى﴾ "and you will not dread" — from drowning in the sea.

They both also reported from him, concerning ﴿فَقَدْ هَوى﴾ "then he has perished," that it means "wretched" (shaqiya).

They both also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾ "Indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents," that he said: "from shirk, and believes," he said: "he affirms the oneness of Allah"; ﴿وعَمِلَ صالِحًا﴾ "and does righteous deeds," he said: "he performs the obligatory duties"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided," he said: "he does not doubt."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr and al-Firyābī also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾: "whoever repents from sin, believes instead of shirk, and does righteous deeds between himself and his Lord"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided": "he knows that his deed has a reward for which he will be recompensed."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾: "then he goes straight, and holds fast to the Sunnah and the community (al-jamā'ah)."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Bayhaqī in "al-Ba'th" reported by way of 'Amr ibn Maymūn from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Mūsā hastened to his Lord, and Allah said: ﴿وما أعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يامُوسى﴾ "And what hastened you from your people, O Mūsā?" — the verse. He said: "He saw in the shade of the Throne a man, and was amazed by him. He said: 'Who is this, my Lord?' He said: 'I will not tell you who he is, but I will inform you of three things about him: he did not envy people for what Allah had given them of His bounty, he did not disobey his parents, and he did not walk about spreading slander.'"

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, reported from 'Alī, who said: "When Mūsā hastened to his Lord, al-Sāmirī set out, gathered whatever he could of the jewelry of the Children of Israel, and fashioned it into a calf. Then he cast the handful into its belly, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing. Al-Sāmirī said to them: 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā.' Hārūn said to them: 'O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?' When Mūsā returned, he seized his brother by the head, and Hārūn told him what had happened. Mūsā said to al-Sāmirī: 'What is your matter?' He said: ﴿فَقَبَضْتُ قَبْضَةً مِن أثَرِ الرَّسُولِ فَنَبَذْتُها وكَذَلِكَ سَوَّلَتْ لِي نَفْسِي﴾ 'I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger, and I threw it, and thus my soul enticed me.' Mūsā then turned to the calf, put files on it, and ground it down with them while it was on the bank of a river. No one among those who had worshipped that calf drank from that water without his face turning yellow like gold. They said to Mūsā: 'What is our repentance?' He said: 'Let some of you kill others.' So they took knives, and a man began killing his brother, his father and his son, not caring whom he killed, until seventy thousand of them had been killed. Then Allah revealed to Mūsā: 'Command them to raise their hands, for I have forgiven those who were killed and have accepted the repentance of those who remain.'" There are very many accounts of this story.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ "by our power," that he said: "by our command."

'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatādah, concerning ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾, that he said: "by our capacity (ṭāqah)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from al-Suddī.

He also reported from al-Ḥasan, who said: "by our authority (sulṭān)."

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾, that he said: "Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god."

(p. 917) This begins the account of the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the destruction of their enemy. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf and Yunus. The lam in ﴿لَقَدْ﴾ (*laqad*) is the *lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath), and the emphasis it gives is clear. The *an* in ﴿أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي﴾ (*an asri bi-ibadi*) is either *al-mufassirah* (the explanatory *an*), since revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the sense of speech, or *masdariyyah* (the verbal *an*, forming a verbal noun), meaning "[to] travel by night with My servants," that is, to take them out of Egypt. This has already been discussed fully. ﴿فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا﴾ means "Strike for them a path through the sea, dry," that is, make for them a path. *Yabsan* means "dry." It is described with the active participle form as an intensifier, because Allah made that path so dry that there was no water or mud in it. It is also read as *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba', either as a lightened form of *yabasan* with a fatha, or as the plural of *yabis*, like *sahb* for *sahib*. The clause ﴿لَا تَخَافُ دَرَكًا﴾ (*la takhafu darakan*, "you shall not fear being overtaken") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*): "secure from being overtaken by the enemy." Or it is another description of *tariq* (path). *Darak* means catching up with them from Pharaoh and his soldiers. Hamzah read ﴿لَا تَخَفْ﴾ (*la takhaf*) as a jussive response to the command, with the implied sense "if you strike, do not fear." Then ﴿وَلَا تَخْشَى﴾ (*wa la takhsha*, "nor shall you dread") is a new independent clause: "nor shall you dread Pharaoh or the sea." The majority (*al-jumhur*) read ﴿لَا تَخَافُ﴾ (*la takhafu*), which is more preferred, because *takhsha* is not jussive. It is also possible, in the majority reading, that this clause is another description of the path: "you shall not fear it, nor dread it."

﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِ﴾ (*fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu bi-junudih*, "Then Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers"). *Atba'a* here is the causative-reflexive form of *tabi'a*. One says *atba'tuhum* when you follow people who had gone ahead of you and you catch up with them. So the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them, and his soldiers were with him. It was also said that the *ba'* is extra, and the original is *atba'ahum junudah*, meaning he ordered his soldiers to follow Musa and his people. It was read as ﴿فَاتَّبَعَهُمْ﴾ (*fattaba'ahum*), with shaddah, meaning he caught up with them with his soldiers, and he was with them, as one says "the commander rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. The phrase *bi-junudih* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: "leading his soldiers with him."

﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum mina al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*, "Then the sea covered them, covering them as it did"). This means: what overwhelmed them and struck them overwhelmed and struck them. The repetition is for magnification and awe, as in His words ﴿الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ ﴿مَا الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:1–2), "The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality?" It was also said that what overwhelmed them is that whose story has been heard. Ibn al-Anbari said: "What overwhelmed them was a part of what overwhelmed them, because not all the water of the sea covered them; only part of it did." So this expression indicates that what drowned them was only some of the water. The first view is better because of the awe and magnification it conveys. It was read as ﴿فَغَشَّاهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشَّاهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashshahum ... ma ghashshahum*), meaning it covered them with what covered them.

﴿وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَى﴾ (*wa adalla Fir'awnu qawmahu wa ma hada*, "Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them"). That is, he led them away from right guidance, and did not guide them to the ways of salvation, because he assumed that Musa and those with him could not escape him, since they were before him walking on a dry path with the sea ahead of them. The phrase ﴿وَمَا هَدَى﴾ is an emphasis on his leading them astray, because one who misleads may guide the one he misleads in some matters.

﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ﴾ (*ya bani Isra'il, qad anjaynakum min aduwwikum*, "O Children of Israel, We have certainly delivered you from your enemy"). Allah mentioned the favor He bestowed upon the Children of Israel after delivering them. The implied sense is: We said to them after their deliverance, "O Children of Israel." It is also possible that this is addressed to the Jews contemporary with our Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace), because a blessing granted to the forefathers is counted as a blessing granted to their descendants. The enemy here means Pharaoh and his soldiers, destroyed by drowning him and his people in the sea, before the eyes of the Children of Israel. ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنَ﴾ (*wa wa'adnakum janiba al-tur al-ayman*, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Tur"). *Janib* is in the accusative as a direct object, not as an adverb of place, because it is a specific place, not an undefined one. Place nouns are in the accusative as adverbs only when they are indefinite. Makki said: "This is a principle on which there is no disagreement." Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning is that We commanded Musa to order you to go out with him, so that We might speak to him in your presence and you might hear the speech." It was also said that Musa was promised, after the drowning of Pharaoh, that he would come to the side of the mountain, so the promise was to Musa, but they were addressed with it because the promise was made for their sake. Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿وَوَعَدْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*wa 'adnakum*) without an alif, and Abu Ubayda preferred this reading, because the promising (*al-wa'd*) comes only from Allah to Musa specifically, whereas *al-mu'adah* (mutual appointment) can only be between two parties. We have already discussed this meaning in al-Baqarah. *Al-ayman* is in the accusative as an adjective of *janib*. The intended meaning is the right side of the person, because a mountain has no right or left side; so when one says "take the right side of the mountain," it means the right side from your perspective, relative to the mountain. It was also read in the genitive, as an adjective of the noun to which *janib* is attached.

﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَنَّ وَالسَّلْوَى﴾ (*wa nazzalna 'alaykumu al-manna wa al-salwa*, "And We sent down upon you manna and quail"). The explanation of *al-manna* as *al-tarankhabin* (a sweet exudation, like honey-dew) and *al-salwa* as *al-sammani* (quail) was discussed earlier, and we have clarified this fully. The sending down of these was during the wandering (*al-tih*) in the desert.

﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*kulu min tayyibati ma razaqnakum*, "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you"). That is, and We said to them, "Eat." The intended meaning of *al-tayyibat* is the pleasant things. It was also said that it means the lawful (*al-halal*), according to the well-known disagreement on this matter. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read ﴿قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ﴾ and ﴿كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ with the first-person singular *ta'* (of the speaker) in all three places. The rest read with the royal plural *nun* (of majesty) in these places. ﴿وَلَا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ﴾ (*wa la tatghaw fihi*, "and do not transgress therein"). *Al-tughyan* means exceeding limits, that is, do not go beyond what is permissible to what is not permissible. It was also said that the meaning is: do not deny the blessing of Allah, lest you become transgressors. It was also said: do not disbelieve the blessing or forget its thanks. It was also said: do not disobey the Benefactor, that is, do not let ease and well-being lead you into disobedience. There is no obstacle to understanding *al-tughyan* as including all these meanings, since each of them truly counts as transgression.

﴿فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي﴾ (*fa-yahilla 'alaykum ghadabi*, "lest My anger descend upon you"). This is the answer (*jawab*) to the prohibition. That is: My anger will be incumbent upon you and will alight on you. It is derived from *hulul al-dayn* (the falling due of a debt), meaning the arrival of the time of its payment. ﴿وَمَنْ يَحْلِلْ عَلَيْهِ غَضَبِي فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*wa man yahlil 'alayhi ghadabi fa-qad hawa*, "And whoever has My anger descend upon him has certainly perished"). Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فَيَحُلَّ﴾ (*fa-yahulla*) with a damma on the ha', and likewise they read ﴿يَحْلُلْ﴾ (*yahlul*) with a damma on the first lam. The rest read both with a kasra. Both are dialect variants. Al-Farra' said: "The kasra is more beloved to me than the damma, because the damma is from *hulul* in the sense of *wuqu'* (alighting or befalling), whereas *yahill* with a kasra means "must" (*yajibu*). The explanation was given as "must," not as "befall." Abu Ubayda and others mentioned something similar." The meaning of ﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (*fa-qad hawa*) is "has certainly perished." Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ means he has gone down into the abyss (*al-hawiyah*), which is the bottom of the Fire, from *hawa yahwi hawyan*, meaning he fell from a height to a low place." *Hawa Fulan* also means he died.

﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba wa amana wa 'amila salihan thumma ihtada*, "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided"). That is, to whoever repents from sins, the greatest of which is associating partners with Allah, and believes in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and does a righteous deed of what the Law has recommended and beautified. ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدَى﴾ means he remains upright in this until he dies. This is what al-Zajjaj and others said. It was also said: he never doubted his faith; it was said: he adhered to the Sunnah and the community (*al-sunnah wa al-jama'ah*); it was said: he learned knowledge in order to be guided by it; it was said: he knew that there is reward for this and punishment for abandoning it. The first view is more preferred than what follows it.

﴿وَمَا أَعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يَا مُوسَى﴾ (*wa ma a'jalaka 'an qawmika ya Musa*, "And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?"). This is a narration of what took place between Allah, glorified is He, and Musa when he came to the appointed meeting. The exegetes said: the appointment was that Musa and a group of the notables of his people would come, so Musa set out with them, then he hastened ahead of them out of longing for his Lord. Allah said to him: "What hastened you?" That is, what made you hasten, so that you left your people and departed from among them. Musa answered this. ﴿قَالَ هُمْ أُولَاءِ عَلَى أَثَرِي﴾ (*qala hum ula'i 'ala athari*, "He said: They are right behind me"). That is, they are close to me, following my track, and will reach me after me. It was also said: he did not mean that they were following behind him, but that they were near him, waiting for his return to them. Then he said, clarifying the reason for what Allah had asked him about: ﴿وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضَى﴾ (*wa 'ajiltu ilayka rabbi li-tarda*, "And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased"). That is, that You may be pleased with me by my hastening to carry out Your command, or that You may increase in being pleased with me by this. Abu Hatim said: Isa ibn Umar said: "The Banu Tamim say *ula* (short form), while the people of the Hijaz say *ula'i* (long form)." Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub read ﴿إِثْرِي﴾ (*ithri*) with a kasra on the hamzah and a sukun on the tha', and the rest read it with a fatha; both are dialect variants. The meaning of ﴿عَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (*'ajiltu ilayka*) is: I hastened to the place where You commanded me to go, so that You might be pleased with me. One says *rajul 'ajil*, *'ajul* and *'ajlan* to mean one who is clearly hasty; *al-'ajalah* is the opposite of slowness.

﴿قَالَ فَإِنَّا قَدْ فَتَنَّا قَوْمَكَ مِنْ بَعْدِكَ﴾ (*qala fa-inna qad fatanna qawmaka min ba'dika*, "He said: Indeed, We have tested your people after you"). This sentence is independent, an answer to an implied question, as though it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" So it is said: He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you," that is, We tried them, examined them, and cast them into trial and affliction. Ibn al-Anbari said: "We made them tested and wretched through worship of the calf after your departure from among them. They were those whom he had left behind with Harun." ﴿وَأَضَلَّهُمُ السَّامِرِيُّ﴾ (*wa adallahumu al-samiri*, "and al-Samiri led them astray"). That is, he called them to error. He was from a people who worshipped cows. He entered the religion of the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was what he had of cow-worship. He was from a tribe known as the Samirah. He said to those with him among the Children of Israel: "Musa has delayed from the appointed meeting between you and him only because of the ornaments that you have with you, and they are forbidden to you." He commanded them to throw them into the fire, and so what happened with the calf happened.

﴿فَرَجَعَ مُوسَى إِلَى قَوْمِهِ غَضْبَانَ أَسِفًا﴾ (*fa-raja'a Musa ila qawmihi ghadban asifan*, "Then Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved"). It was said: the return to his people was after he had completed forty days: Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. *Al-asaf* means intense anger; it was also said: grief. This has already been fully explained in al-A'raf. ﴿قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَلَمْ يَعِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ وَعْدًا حَسَنًا﴾ (*qala ya qawmi alam ya'idkum rabbukum wa'dan hasanan*, "He said: O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"). The interrogative is for rebuke by way of denial. *Al-wa'd al-hasan* (the good promise) is what He promised them: Paradise, if they remain upon His obedience; and He promised that He would make them hear His speech in the Torah through the tongue of Musa, so that they would act by what is in it and thereby deserve the reward for their deeds. It was also said: He promised them victory and triumph. It was also said: it is His words ﴿وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ﴾ (*wa inni la-ghaffarun liman taba*), "And indeed I am truly Forgiving toward whoever repents," and so on. ﴿أَفَطَالَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْعَهْدُ﴾ (*afa-tala 'alaykumu al-'ahd*, "Has the time seemed long to you?"). The *fa* connects to an implied clause: "Did He promise you that, so the time has grown long for you, and so you forgot?" ﴿أَمْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ يَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (*am aradtum an yahilla 'alaykum ghadabun min rabbikum*, "Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?"). That is, that it should be incumbent upon you and alight on you. *Al-ghadab* means punishment and vengeance. The meaning is: or did you want to do an act that would be the cause of the descent of Allah's wrath upon you? ﴿فَأَخْلَفْتُمْ مَوْعِدِي﴾ (*fa-akhlaftum mau'idi*, "So you broke your appointment with me"). That is, your appointment with me. The verbal noun is in the genitive as an object-possessive construction (*idafah*) to the object, because they had promised him that they would remain in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he returned to them from Mount Tur. It was also said: they had promised him that they would come after him to the appointed meeting, but they hesitated, and then they refused his summons.

And they said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own power" ﴿ما أخْلَفْنا مَوْعِدَكَ﴾. The word ﴿الَّذِي وعَدْناكَ﴾ refers to the promise we made you. ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā, "by our power") is read with a fatha on the mīm (bi-malkinā) by Nāfi', Abū Ja'far, 'Āṣim and 'Īsā ibn 'Umar. Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr and Ibn 'Āmir read it with a kasra on the mīm (bi-milkinā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because it follows the high, eloquent dialect (al-lughah al-'āliyah al-faṣīḥah). It is the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'a, amlikuhu, milkan" (I possessed the thing). The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with its agent, and its object is omitted: that is, "by our managing our affairs" (bi-milkinā umūranā), or "by our possessing right judgment" (bi-milkinā al-ṣawāb). The meaning is: "Rather, we erred, and we did not have control over ourselves; we were compelled to err." Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿بِمُلْكِنا﴾ (bi-mulkinā) with a ḍamma on the mīm, meaning "by our authority" (bi-sulṭāninā): that is, we had no authority by which we could break your promise. It is also said that the fatḥ, kasra and ḍamma in ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ are all dialectal variants of the verbal noun of "malaktu al-shay'".

﴿ولَكِنّا حُمِّلْنا أوْزارًا مِن زِينَةِ القَوْمِ﴾ "But we were made to carry burdens of the adornments of the people." Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥafṣ, Abū Ja'far and Ruways read ﴿حُمِّلْنا﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a shadda on the mīm (ḥummilnā). The rest read it with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and a light mīm (ḥamalnā). Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this second reading, because they carried the people's ornaments with them by their own choice, and they were not carried against their will. They had borrowed the ornaments from them when they wanted to leave with Mūsā, and they gave them the impression that they were gathering for a festival or a feast of theirs. It is also said that it refers to what they took from the family of Pharaoh when the sea cast them up onto the shore. They were called ﴿أوْزارًا﴾ (awzāran, "burdens"), meaning sins (āthāman), because it was not lawful for them to take them, and spoils of war were not lawful for them under their law. In the original sense, awzār means "loads" (al-athqāl), as the lexicographers have stated. Here ﴿الزِّينَةِ﴾ (al-zīnah, "adornment") means the jewelry (al-ḥilyy). ﴿فَقَذَفْناها﴾ means "so we threw them", that is, we cast them into the fire, seeking deliverance from their sin. It is also said that the meaning is: we threw them to al-Sāmirī so that they would remain with him until Mūsā returned and could decide his opinion about them.

﴿فَكَذَلِكَ ألْقى السّامِرِيُّ﴾ "Thus did al-Sāmirī cast." That is, al-Sāmirī cast them in the same manner of casting. It is said that when the people were slow to notice Mūsā's return, al-Sāmirī said to them: "He has delayed from you only because of the jewelry you have." So they gathered it and handed it over to him. He threw it into the fire and fashioned a calf from it for them. Then he cast upon it a handful (qabḍah) from the trace of the Messenger, who was Jibrīl.

﴿فَصارَ عِجْلًا جَسَدًا لَهُ خُوارٌ﴾ "So it became a calf, a body that had a lowing." (p-919) That is, it lowed as a living calf lows. Al-khuwār is the sound of cattle. It is also said that its lowing was caused by the wind, because it had been made with holes in it; when the wind entered its belly, it lowed, and there was no life in it.

﴿فَقالُوا هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾ "Then they said, 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā, but he forgot.'" That is, al-Sāmirī and those who agreed with him said this statement. ﴿فَنَسِيَ﴾ (fa-nasiya, "but he forgot") means that Mūsā went astray and did not know where his god was, so he set off to seek him at the mountain (al-Ṭūr). It is also said that the meaning is: Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god and your god. It is also said that the one who forgot is al-Sāmirī: that is, al-Sāmirī abandoned what Mūsā had commanded him concerning faith, and went astray. Thus said Ibn al-A'rābī.

﴿أفَلا يَرَوْنَ ألّا يَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِمْ قَوْلًا﴾ "Do they not see that it does not return to them a word?" That is: will they not take heed and reflect that this calf does not return to them any word? That is, it does not answer them, and does not speak to them when they speak to it. So how can they imagine that it is a god when it is incapable of speaking? In ﴿ألّا يَرْجِعُ﴾ the ﴿ألّا﴾ is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy (al-thaqīlah) "anna", and there is an implied pronoun in it that refers to the calf. For this reason the verb after it is in the nominative (irtafa'a). From this is the verse of the poet:

"Among youths from the Indian swords, who know that everyone who goes barefoot and wears sandals is doomed."

That is: that he is doomed. It has also been read with the verb in the accusative, taking it as the governing (nāṣibah) form. The clause ﴿ولا يَمْلِكُ لَهم ضَرًّا ولا نَفْعًا﴾ "and it does not possess for them any harm or benefit" is coordinated with the clause "does not return." That is: do they not see that it has no power to repel harm from them or to bring benefit to them?

﴿ولَقَدْ قالَ لَهم هارُونُ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ "And Hārūn had already said to them before this." The lām here is the preparatory lām (al-muwaṭṭi'ah) for an oath, and the sentence confirms what the preceding sentence contained of denunciation and reproach. That is: Hārūn had said to them, before Mūsā came and returned to them, ﴿ياقَوْمِ إنَّما فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ "O my people, you have only been tested by it." That is: you have fallen into temptation because of the calf, you have been tried by it, and you have gone astray from the path of truth on its account. It is said that the restrictive sense derived from "innamā" (only) is that the calf became a cause of their temptation, not of their guidance; it does not mean that they were tempted by the calf and not by anything else. ﴿وإنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فاتَّبِعُونِي وأطِيعُوا أمْرِي﴾ "Your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." That is: your Lord is the Most Merciful, not the calf, and obey my command, not its command.

﴿قالُوا لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفِينَ حَتّى يَرْجِعَ إلَيْنا مُوسى﴾ "They said, 'We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Mūsā returns to us.'" They answered Hārūn's earlier statement with this reply, which contained their disobedience and their refusal to accept what he called them to of good and his warning them against evil. That is: we will continue to remain upon the worship of this calf until Mūsā returns to us, and he will see whether he will confirm us in its worship or forbid us from it. At that point Hārūn withdrew from them with twelve thousand people who disapproved of what al-Sāmirī had done.

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Ka'b, concerning His words ﴿يَبَسًا﴾ (yabasan, "a dry path"), that he said: "Dry, with no water and no mud in it."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning ﴿لا تَخافُ دَرَكًا﴾ "you will not fear being overtaken" — from the family of Pharaoh — ﴿ولا تَخْشى﴾ "and you will not dread" — from drowning in the sea.

They both also reported from him, concerning ﴿فَقَدْ هَوى﴾ "then he has perished," that it means "wretched" (shaqiya).

They both also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾ "Indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents," that he said: "from shirk, and believes," he said: "he affirms the oneness of Allah"; ﴿وعَمِلَ صالِحًا﴾ "and does righteous deeds," he said: "he performs the obligatory duties"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided," he said: "he does not doubt."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr and al-Firyābī also reported from him concerning ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾: "whoever repents from sin, believes instead of shirk, and does righteous deeds between himself and his Lord"; ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾ "then is guided": "he knows that his deed has a reward for which he will be recompensed."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿ثُمَّ اهْتَدى﴾: "then he goes straight, and holds fast to the Sunnah and the community (al-jamā'ah)."

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Bayhaqī in "al-Ba'th" reported by way of 'Amr ibn Maymūn from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Mūsā hastened to his Lord, and Allah said: ﴿وما أعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يامُوسى﴾ "And what hastened you from your people, O Mūsā?" — the verse. He said: "He saw in the shade of the Throne a man, and was amazed by him. He said: 'Who is this, my Lord?' He said: 'I will not tell you who he is, but I will inform you of three things about him: he did not envy people for what Allah had given them of His bounty, he did not disobey his parents, and he did not walk about spreading slander.'"

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, reported from 'Alī, who said: "When Mūsā hastened to his Lord, al-Sāmirī set out, gathered whatever he could of the jewelry of the Children of Israel, and fashioned it into a calf. Then he cast the handful into its belly, and it became a calf, a body with a lowing. Al-Sāmirī said to them: 'This is your god and the god of Mūsā.' Hārūn said to them: 'O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?' When Mūsā returned, he seized his brother by the head, and Hārūn told him what had happened. Mūsā said to al-Sāmirī: 'What is your matter?' He said: ﴿فَقَبَضْتُ قَبْضَةً مِن أثَرِ الرَّسُولِ فَنَبَذْتُها وكَذَلِكَ سَوَّلَتْ لِي نَفْسِي﴾ 'I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger, and I threw it, and thus my soul enticed me.' Mūsā then turned to the calf, put files on it, and ground it down with them while it was on the bank of a river. No one among those who had worshipped that calf drank from that water without his face turning yellow like gold. They said to Mūsā: 'What is our repentance?' He said: 'Let some of you kill others.' So they took knives, and a man began killing his brother, his father and his son, not caring whom he killed, until seventy thousand of them had been killed. Then Allah revealed to Mūsā: 'Command them to raise their hands, for I have forgiven those who were killed and have accepted the repentance of those who remain.'" There are very many accounts of this story.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾ "by our power," that he said: "by our command."

'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatādah, concerning ﴿بِمَلْكِنا﴾, that he said: "by our capacity (ṭāqah)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from al-Suddī.

He also reported from al-Ḥasan, who said: "by our authority (sulṭān)."

al-Firyābī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His words ﴿هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ﴾, that he said: "Mūsā forgot to tell you that this was his god."

(p. 917) This begins the account of the deliverance of the Children of Israel and the destruction of their enemy. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf and Yunus. The lam in ﴿لَقَدْ﴾ (*laqad*) is the *lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath), and the emphasis it gives is clear. The *an* in ﴿أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي﴾ (*an asri bi-ibadi*) is either *al-mufassirah* (the explanatory *an*), since revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the sense of speech, or *masdariyyah* (the verbal *an*, forming a verbal noun), meaning "[to] travel by night with My servants," that is, to take them out of Egypt. This has already been discussed fully. ﴿فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا﴾ means "Strike for them a path through the sea, dry," that is, make for them a path. *Yabsan* means "dry." It is described with the active participle form as an intensifier, because Allah made that path so dry that there was no water or mud in it. It is also read as *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba', either as a lightened form of *yabasan* with a fatha, or as the plural of *yabis*, like *sahb* for *sahib*. The clause ﴿لَا تَخَافُ دَرَكًا﴾ (*la takhafu darakan*, "you shall not fear being overtaken") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*): "secure from being overtaken by the enemy." Or it is another description of *tariq* (path). *Darak* means catching up with them from Pharaoh and his soldiers. Hamzah read ﴿لَا تَخَفْ﴾ (*la takhaf*) as a jussive response to the command, with the implied sense "if you strike, do not fear." Then ﴿وَلَا تَخْشَى﴾ (*wa la takhsha*, "nor shall you dread") is a new independent clause: "nor shall you dread Pharaoh or the sea." The majority (*al-jumhur*) read ﴿لَا تَخَافُ﴾ (*la takhafu*), which is more preferred, because *takhsha* is not jussive. It is also possible, in the majority reading, that this clause is another description of the path: "you shall not fear it, nor dread it."

﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِ﴾ (*fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu bi-junudih*, "Then Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers"). *Atba'a* here is the causative-reflexive form of *tabi'a*. One says *atba'tuhum* when you follow people who had gone ahead of you and you catch up with them. So the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them, and his soldiers were with him. It was also said that the *ba'* is extra, and the original is *atba'ahum junudah*, meaning he ordered his soldiers to follow Musa and his people. It was read as ﴿فَاتَّبَعَهُمْ﴾ (*fattaba'ahum*), with shaddah, meaning he caught up with them with his soldiers, and he was with them, as one says "the commander rode with his sword," meaning his sword was with him. The phrase *bi-junudih* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: "leading his soldiers with him."

﴿فَغَشِيَهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum mina al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*, "Then the sea covered them, covering them as it did"). This means: what overwhelmed them and struck them overwhelmed and struck them. The repetition is for magnification and awe, as in His words ﴿الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ ﴿مَا الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:1–2), "The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality?" It was also said that what overwhelmed them is that whose story has been heard. Ibn al-Anbari said: "What overwhelmed them was a part of what overwhelmed them, because not all the water of the sea covered them; only part of it did." So this expression indicates that what drowned them was only some of the water. The first view is better because of the awe and magnification it conveys. It was read as ﴿فَغَشَّاهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشَّاهُمْ﴾ (*fa-ghashshahum ... ma ghashshahum*), meaning it covered them with what covered them.

﴿وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَى﴾ (*wa adalla Fir'awnu qawmahu wa ma hada*, "Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them"). That is, he led them away from right guidance, and did not guide them to the ways of salvation, because he assumed that Musa and those with him could not escape him, since they were before him walking on a dry path with the sea ahead of them. The phrase ﴿وَمَا هَدَى﴾ is an emphasis on his leading them astray, because one who misleads may guide the one he misleads in some matters.

﴿يَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ قَدْ أَنْجَيْنَاكُمْ مِنْ عَدُوِّكُمْ﴾ (*ya bani Isra'il, qad anjaynakum min aduwwikum*, "O Children of Israel, We have certainly delivered you from your enemy"). Allah mentioned the favor He bestowed upon the Children of Israel after delivering them. The implied sense is: We said to them after their deliverance, "O Children of Israel." It is also possible that this is addressed to the Jews contemporary with our Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace), because a blessing granted to the forefathers is counted as a blessing granted to their descendants. The enemy here means Pharaoh and his soldiers, destroyed by drowning him and his people in the sea, before the eyes of the Children of Israel. ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنَ﴾ (*wa wa'adnakum janiba al-tur al-ayman*, "And We appointed for you the right side of Mount Tur"). *Janib* is in the accusative as a direct object, not as an adverb of place, because it is a specific place, not an undefined one. Place nouns are in the accusative as adverbs only when they are indefinite. Makki said: "This is a principle on which there is no disagreement." Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning is that We commanded Musa to order you to go out with him, so that We might speak to him in your presence and you might hear the speech." It was also said that Musa was promised, after the drowning of Pharaoh, that he would come to the side of the mountain, so the promise was to Musa, but they were addressed with it because the promise was made for their sake. Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿وَوَعَدْنَاكُمْ﴾ (*wa 'adnakum*) without an alif, and Abu Ubayda preferred this reading, because the promising (*al-wa'd*) comes only from Allah to Musa specifically, whereas *al-mu'adah* (mutual appointment) can only be between two parties. We have already discussed this meaning in al-Baqarah. *Al-ayman* is in the accusative as an adjective of *janib*. The intended meaning is the right side of the person, because a mountain has no right or left side; so when one says "take the right side of the mountain," it means the right side from your perspective, relative to the mountain. It was also read in the genitive, as an adjective of the noun to which *janib* is attached.
