Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him that he said: "al-yamm" is the sea.

He also related from ʿAli that he said: "al-yamm" is the river.

He also related from Qatada concerning His saying, ﴿He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, that he said: He filled [everything]. He also related from Ibn Zayd concerning His saying, ﴿a reminder from Us﴾, that he said: it is the Qur'an. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning "wizran" (a burden) that he said: it means sin. The meaning of the *fatḥa* form is one act of grasping; then it was applied to what is grasped, which is the meaning of *qubḍah* with a *ḍamma*. The meaning of *"min athari l-Rasūl"* (from the trace of the Messenger) is: from the place on which the hoof of Gabriel's horse had stepped. The meaning of *"fa-nabadhtuhā"* (so I threw it) is: I cast it into the molten jewelry cast in the shape of the calf. *"Wa-kadhālika sawwalat lī nafsī"* (And thus my soul enticed me). When Musa heard this from him, *"Qāla fa-idhhab fa-inna laka fī l-ḥayāti an taqūla lā misās"* (He said, "Go, for it is yours in life to say, 'No touching!'"). That is: go away from among us and leave us; for it is yours in life, that is, as long as you are alive, and the longest of your life is that you will say, "No touching!"

*Al-misās* is derived from *al-mumāssa* (touching): that is, no one will touch you and you will not touch anyone, but not by your own choice; rather, by necessity that compels you to it. For God, glorified is He, commanded Musa to banish the Samiri from his people, and commanded the Children of Israel not to mix with him, nor approach him, nor speak to him, as a punishment for him.

It is said that when Musa said this to him, he fled and began to wander in the wilderness with the beasts of prey and the wild animals, finding no one among people to touch him, until he became like one who says "No touching!", because he was far from people and people were far from him. As the poet said:

*A bearer of banners, sluggish among them, until the Azd say: "No touching!"*

Sibawayh said: *lā misāsa* is built on the *kasra* (indeclinable, with a *kasra* ending). Al-Zajjaj said: the *sīn* was given a *kasra* because the *kasra* is a sign of the feminine. Al-Jawhari said in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: as for the Arabs' saying *lā misās*, like *qiṭām*, it is built on the *kasra* only because it is a derivative of the verbal noun, which is *al-mass* (touching).

Al-Nahhas said: I heard ʿAli ibn Sulayman say: I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad say: when a word is defective (*iʿtallat*) in three respects, it must be built (indeclinable); when it is defective in two respects, it must be non-declinable, since after non-declension there is only building. So *misās* (in this phrase) is defective in three respects: it is a derivative (*maʿdūl*), it is feminine, and it is definite. When building became necessary for it, and the *alif* before the *sīn* was quiescent, the *sīn* was given a *kasra* to avoid the meeting of two quiescent letters. I have seen Abu Ishaq (that is, al-Zajjaj) hold that this statement is wrong, and he held Abu al-ʿAbbas (al-Mubarrad) responsible for saying that if a woman is named Firʿawn, one must build it; and no one says this. Abu Haywah read *misāsa* with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm*, while the rest read it with a *kasra*.

The summary of what has been said about the meaning of *lā misās* is three opinions. The first is that he was forbidden to touch people, and whenever anyone touched him, the toucher and the touched would have a fever. Therefore he would shout whenever he saw someone, "No touching!" The second is that the meaning is preventing people from mixing with him; it was objected that when a man has been shunned, he does not say "No touching!" about himself, but it is said to him. It was answered that the intention is reporting: that is, I make you, O Samiri, such that when you report your condition you say, "No touching!" The third opinion is that the meaning is the cutting off of his offspring, and that he would be unable to touch a woman; this was said by Abu Muslim, and it is very weak.

Then God mentioned his condition in the Hereafter, saying: *"And indeed, for you there is an appointment that you will not be able to escape"* (*wa-inna laka mawʿidan lan tukhlafahu*). That is, God will not fail you in that appointment, which is the Day of Resurrection. *Al-mawʿid* is a verbal noun: that is, indeed for you is a promise for your punishment, and it will certainly happen. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, God will requite you for what you did on the Day of Resurrection, and God does not fail in His promise.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Yazidi and al-Hasan read *"lan tukhlifahu"* (you will not find it failing) with a *kasra* on the *lām*. According to this reading there are two meanings. One is: it will come to you, and you will not find it to be false, just as you say "I praised him" (*aḥmadtuhu*), meaning I found him praiseworthy. The second, as a threat: that is, you must inevitably arrive at it. Ibn Masʿud read *"lan nukhlifahu"* (we will not fail it) with *nūn*, meaning: God will not fail it. The rest read it with a *fatḥa* on the *lām* and with the *tāʾ* (second person) in the passive form, meaning what we have already mentioned.

*"Wa-unẓur ilā ilāhika lladhī ẓalta ʿalayhi ʿākifan"* (And look at your god to which you remained devoted, staying constantly with it). *Ẓalta* originally was *ẓalilta*, and the first *lām* was deleted for lightness, which the Arabs do often. Al-Aʿmash read it with two *lām*s according to the original form. In the reading of Ibn Masʿud it is *ẓilta* with a *kasra* on the *ẓāʾ*. The meaning is: look at your god, to whose worship you continued and kept up. *Al-ʿākif* means the one who keeps constantly to something.

*"La-nuḥarriqannahu"* (We will surely burn it). The majority read it with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and a shadda on the *rāʾ*, from *ḥarraqahu yuḥarriquhu* (he burned it intensively). Al-Hasan read it with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*, a quiescent *ḥāʾ*, and a light *rāʾ*, from *aḥraqahu yuḥriquhu* (he burned it). ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Jaʿfar, Ibn Muhaysin, Ashhab and al-ʿUqayli read *"la-nuḥarriqannahu"* with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn*, a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ*, and a light *rāʾ*, from *ḥaraqtu l-shayʾa uḥriquhu ḥarqan*, when you file something down and rub part of it against another part; that is, we will surely file it down with files. The filer is also called *al-muḥriq*. The first reading is preferable, and its meaning is burning with fire; so too the meaning of the second reading. Some have combined these three readings by saying that he burned it, then filed it down with a file. In Ibn Masʿud's reading it is *"la-nadhbaḥannahu thumma la-nuḥriqannahu"* (we will surely slaughter it, then surely burn it). The *lām* is the one that prepares for the oath.

*"Thumma la-nansifannahu fī l-yammi nasfan"* (Then we will surely scatter it into the sea, a scattering). *Al-nasf* is shaking something so that the wind carries it away. Abu Rajaʾ read *la-nunsifannahu* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*, while the rest read it with a *kasra*; the two are dialect variants. *Al-minsaf* is that by which food is winnowed, a thing with a raised front edge, and *al-nusāfah* is what falls from it.

*"Innamā ilāhukumu llāhu lladhī lā ilāha illā huwa"* (Your god is only God, besides whom there is no god), not this calf to which you were tempted by the Samiri. *"Wasiʿa kulla shayʾin ʿilman"* (He encompasses all things in knowledge). The majority read *wasiʿa* with a *kasra* on the *sīn*, unshadded. It is transitive to one object, which is *kulla shayʾ* (everything), and *ʿilman* is in the accusative as a specifying accusative (*tamyīz*) transferred from the subject: that is, His knowledge encompassed everything. Mujahid and Qatadah read *wassaʿa* with a shadda and a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, so that it is transitive to two objects, and *ʿilman* is in the accusative as the first object even though it comes later, because it was originally the subject. The meaning is: His knowledge encompassed everything. Something similar has already passed in al-Aʿraf.

*"Kadhālika naquṣṣu ʿalayka"* (Thus We relate to you). The *kāf* is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun: that is, as We related to you the story of Musa, thus We relate to you *"min anbāʾi mā qad sabaq"* (some of the news of what has passed). That is, some of the reports of past events among the earlier nations, so that it may be a consolation for you and a proof of your truthfulness. *Min* here is partitive: that is, some of the reports of that.

*"Wa-qad ātaynāka min ladunnā dhikran"* (And We have certainly given you a reminder from Us). By *dhikr* is meant the Qur'an, and it was called *dhikr* because of what it contains that necessitates remembrance and reflection. It has also been said that *dhikr* here means honour, as in His saying: *"And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people"* [Al-Zukhruf: 44].

Then God, glorified is He, threatened those who turn away from this reminder, saying: *"Whoever turns away from it will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden"* (*man aʿraḍa ʿanhu fa-innahu yaḥmilu yawma l-qiyāmati wizran*). That is, whoever turns away from it, so that he does not believe in it nor act upon what is in it. It has also been said: whoever turns away from God, glorified is He, for whoever turns away from Him will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden: that is, a great sin and a heavy punishment because of his turning away. *"Khālidīna fīhi"* (Abiding therein): that is, in the burden. The meaning is that they will remain in its requital, and *khālidīna* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. *"Wa-sāʾa lahum yawma l-qiyāmati ḥimlan"* (And evil is the load for them on the Day of Resurrection). That is: evil is the load on the Day of Resurrection; the object of the blame is omitted, meaning: evil for them is their burden as a load. The *lām* is for explanation, as in *"hayta laka"* (come, I am at your service).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verse 92–101 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying, ﴿O Harun, what prevented you﴾ up to His saying, ﴿Have you disobeyed my command?﴾, that he said: Musa had commanded him to set things right and not follow the way of the corrupters. So part of his setting things right was to denounce the calf. He also related from him concerning His saying, ﴿and you did not observe my word﴾, that he said: you did not wait for my word, [to see] what I would do. Ibn Abbas said: "you did not observe" means you did not preserve my word.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying, ﴿Then, indeed, it is for you in the life to say, "No contact"﴾, that it was a punishment for him. ﴿And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet﴾: he said, you will not be absent from it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾, that he said: you persisted in it. ﴿We will surely burn it﴾: he said, with fire. ﴿Then we will surely scatter it into the sea﴾: he said, we will surely winnow it into the sea.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite (لَنُحْرِقَنَّهُ) with a light pronunciation (لَنُحْرِقَنَّهُ, with a single ر-less form, i.e., the verb of burning in the fourth form) and would say: gold and silver are not burned by fire; rather they are filed down with a file, then thrown into the fire, and so they become ash.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him that he said: "al-yamm" is the sea.

He also related from ʿAli that he said: "al-yamm" is the river.

He also related from Qatada concerning His saying, ﴿He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, that he said: He filled [everything]. He also related from Ibn Zayd concerning His saying, ﴿a reminder from Us﴾, that he said: it is the Qur'an. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning "wizran" (a burden) that he said: it means sin. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿and evil is it for them on the Day of Resurrection as a burden﴾, that he said: evil is what they carried.

(p-٩٢٠) The clause *qāla yā Hārūnu* (He said, "O Harun") is a resumptive sentence (*jumla mustaʾnafa*), an answer to an implied question. The meaning is: when Musa reached them, he seized his brother Harun by the hair of his head and by his beard and said, "What prevented you from following me and joining me when they fell into this misguidance and entered into this trial?"

It has also been said that the meaning of *"mā manaʿaka idh raʾaytahum ḍallū, allā tattabiʿanī"* (What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?) is: what prevented you from following me in denouncing them? It has also been said that it means: why did you not fight them, since you knew that if I had been among them I would have fought them? It has also been said that it means: why did you not separate yourself from them? The *lā* in *allā tattabiʿanī* is extra (*zāʾida*), and the phrase is in the accusative position as the second object of *manaʿa* (to prevent). That is: what prevented you, when you saw their misguidance, from following me?

The interrogative in *"afaʿaṣayta amrī"* (Did you then disobey my command?) is for denial and reproach. The *fāʾ* (then) is a conjunction joining it to an implied element, as in its counterparts. The meaning is: how did you go against my command to you, to stand up for God and to oppose those who opposed His religion, and yet you remained among those who had taken the calf as a god? It has also been said that *amrī* (my command) refers to his saying, which God related: *"Musa said to his brother Harun: 'Take my place among my people, act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters'"* [Al-Aʿraf: 142]. So when he stayed with them and did not strongly denounce them, Musa attributed to him disobedience.

*"Qāla yā-bna Umma lā taʾkhudh bi-liḥyatī wa-lā bi-raʾsī"* (He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head"). It was read with a *fatḥa* and with a *kasra* on the *mīm* (in *Umma*). This has already been discussed in the surah of Al-Aʿraf. Harun's attribution to "the mother" (*Umma*), although he was Musa's full brother (from the same father and mother), is, according to the majority of scholars, a means of appealing to Musa's compassion and softening his heart. The meaning of *"wa-lā bi-raʾsī"* (nor by my head) is: nor by the hair of my head. That is, do not treat me this way as a punishment from you to me, for I have an excuse, which is: *"I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel.'"* That is, I feared that if I left them and abandoned them, they would scatter, and you would say, "I have divided their community." This is because, if Harun had gone out, a group of them would have followed him, and others would have stayed behind with the Samiri at the calf, and this might have led to fighting among them. The meaning of *"wa-lam tarqub qawlī"* (and you did not observe my word) is: you did not act on my instruction to you concerning them. I feared that you would say, "You divided them," and say, "He did not act on my instruction to him concerning them, and did not keep it." By "my instruction" Musa meant his saying: *"Take my place among my people and act rightly."* Abu ʿUbayd said: the meaning of *"lam tarqub qawlī"* is: you did not wait for my promise and my return, because you had commanded me to be with them. So Harun here made his excuse to Musa with this, and in al-Aʿraf he made an excuse to him with what God related of him there, when he said: *"Indeed, the people oppressed me and nearly killed me."*

Then he left speaking to his brother and addressed the Samiri (the man who made the calf), so *"Qāla famā khaṭbuka yā Sāmiriyyu"* (He said, "What is your affair, O Samiri?"). That is: what is your matter, and what moved you to do what you did?

*"Qāla baṣurtu bi-mā lam yabṣurū bihi"* (He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive"). That is, the Samiri replied to Musa: I saw what they did not see, or I knew what they did not know, and I understood what they did not understand. He meant by this that he saw Gabriel (Jibril) upon the horse of life (*faras al-ḥayāh*), and it was inspired in his mind to take a handful from the trace of the Messenger; that trace does not touch anything lifeless without making it alive.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi, al-Aʿmash and Khalaf read *"bi-mā lam tabṣurū bihi"* (what you did not perceive) with a *tāʾ* (second person, addressing them). The rest read it with a *yāʾ* (third person). The latter is preferable, because it is very unlikely that he would address Musa with this and claim for himself that he knew what Musa did not know. It was also read with a *ḍamma* on the *ṣād* in both verbs, and with a *kasra* in the first and a *fatḥa* in the second. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan and Qatadah read *"faqabaṣtu qabṣatan"* (so I took a handful) with the unpointed *ṣād* (ص) in both, while the rest read it with the pointed *ḍād* (ض) in both. The difference between them is that *qabḍ* with the pointed *ḍād* means grasping with the whole palm, while with the unpointed *ṣād* it means with the fingertips. *Qubḍah* (with a *ḍamma* on the *qāf*) means the amount grasped. Al-Jawhari said: it is what you grasp of something. He said: it is sometimes with a *fatḥa*, and *qubḍatan* has also been read with a *ḍamma* and a *fatḥa* on the *qāf*. The meaning of the *fatḥa* form is one act of grasping; then it was applied to what is grasped, which is the meaning of *qubḍah* with a *ḍamma*. The meaning of *"min athari l-Rasūl"* (from the trace of the Messenger) is: from the place on which the hoof of Gabriel's horse had stepped. The meaning of *"fa-nabadhtuhā"* (so I threw it) is: I cast it into the molten jewelry cast in the shape of the calf. *"Wa-kadhālika sawwalat lī nafsī"* (And thus my soul enticed me). Al-Akhfash said: that is, it adorned (*zayyanat*): that is, similar to this enticement my soul enticed me. It has also been said that the meaning of *sawwalat lī nafsī* is: my soul suggested to me.

When Musa heard this from him, *"Qāla fa-idhhab fa-inna laka fī l-ḥayāti an taqūla lā misās"* (He said, "Go, for it is yours in life to say, 'No touching!'"). Then God, glorified is He, threatened those who turn away from this reminder, saying: *"Whoever turns away from it will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden"* (*man aʿraḍa ʿanhu fa-innahu yaḥmilu yawma l-qiyāmati wizran*). It has also been said: whoever turns away from God, glorified is He, for whoever turns away from Him will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden: that is, a great sin and a heavy punishment because of his turning away. *"Khālidīna fīhi"* (Abiding therein): that is, in the burden. The meaning is that they will remain in its requital, and *khālidīna* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. *"Wa-sāʾa lahum yawma l-qiyāmati ḥimlan"* (And evil is the load for them on the Day of Resurrection). That is: evil is the load on the Day of Resurrection; the object of the blame is omitted, meaning: evil for them is their burden as a load. The *lām* is for explanation, as in *"hayta laka"* (come, I am at your service).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 20, verse 92–101 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying, ﴿O Harun, what prevented you﴾ up to His saying, ﴿Have you disobeyed my command?﴾, that he said: Musa had commanded him to set things right and not follow the way of the corrupters. So part of his setting things right was to denounce the calf. He also related from him concerning His saying, ﴿and you did not observe my word﴾, that he said: you did not wait for my word, [to see] what I would do. Ibn Abbas said: "you did not observe" means you did not preserve my word.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying, ﴿Then, indeed, it is for you in the life to say, "No contact"﴾, that it was a punishment for him. ﴿And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet﴾: he said, you will not be absent from it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾, that he said: you persisted in it. ﴿We will surely burn it﴾: he said, with fire. ﴿Then we will surely scatter it into the sea﴾: he said, we will surely winnow it into the sea.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite (لَنُحْرِقَنَّهُ) with a light pronunciation (لَنُحْرِقَنَّهُ, with a single ر-less form, i.e., the verb of burning in the fourth form) and would say: gold and silver are not burned by fire; rather they are filed down with a file, then thrown into the fire, and so they become ash.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him that he said: "al-yamm" is the sea.

He also related from ʿAli that he said: "al-yamm" is the river.

He also related from Qatada concerning His saying, ﴿He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, that he said: He filled [everything]. He also related from Ibn Zayd concerning His saying, ﴿a reminder from Us﴾, that he said: it is the Qur'an. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning "wizran" (a burden) that he said: it means sin. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿and evil is it for them on the Day of Resurrection as a burden﴾, that he said: evil is what they carried.

(p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The rest recited it with *nūn*. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Anʿām. By "the criminals" (al-mujrimīn) are meant the polytheists and the sinners who are seized for their sins, which God has not forgiven them. By "on that day" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is meant the day of the blowing of the Trumpet.

The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

The accusative of (قاعًا) is either as a second object of (يَذَرُ) with the implication of the meaning "make," or as a *ḥāl*, and (الصَّفْصَفُ) is its adjective. The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means the sound of the gathering. It has been said: the Caller is Isrāfīl when he blows into the Trumpet. (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

(وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means the sound of the gathering. It has been said: the Caller is Isrāfīl when he blows into the Trumpet. (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

(p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The rest recited it with *nūn*. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Anʿām. By "the criminals" (al-mujrimīn) are meant the polytheists and the sinners who are seized for their sins, which God has not forgiven them. By "on that day" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is meant the day of the blowing of the Trumpet.

The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." (p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

The accusative of (قاعًا) is either as a second object of (يَذَرُ) with the implication of the meaning "make," or as a *ḥāl*, and (الصَّفْصَفُ) is its adjective. The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means the sound of the gathering. It has been said: the Caller is Isrāfīl when he blows into the Trumpet. (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

(وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." (يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means the sound of the gathering. It has been said: the Caller is Isrāfīl when he blows into the Trumpet. (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

(وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

(p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The rest recited it with *nūn*. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Anʿām. By "the criminals" (al-mujrimīn) are meant the polytheists and the sinners who are seized for their sins, which God has not forgiven them. By "on that day" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is meant the day of the blowing of the Trumpet.

The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

The accusative of (قاعًا) is either as a second object of (يَذَرُ) with the implication of the meaning "make," or as a *ḥāl*, and (الصَّفْصَفُ) is its adjective. The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive."
