Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

(p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The rest recited it with *nūn*. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Anʿām. By "the criminals" (al-mujrimīn) are meant the polytheists and the sinners who are seized for their sins, which God has not forgiven them. By "on that day" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is meant the day of the blowing of the Trumpet.

The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

The accusative of (قاعًا) is either as a second object of (يَذَرُ) with the implication of the meaning "make," or as a *ḥāl*, and (الصَّفْصَفُ) is its adjective. The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means the sound of the gathering. It has been said: the Caller is Isrāfīl when he blows into the Trumpet. (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

(وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

(وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

(p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The rest recited it with *nūn*. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Anʿām. By "the criminals" (al-mujrimīn) are meant the polytheists and the sinners who are seized for their sins, which God has not forgiven them. By "on that day" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is meant the day of the blowing of the Trumpet.

The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

The accusative of (قاعًا) is either as a second object of (يَذَرُ) with the implication of the meaning "make," or as a *ḥāl*, and (الصَّفْصَفُ) is its adjective. The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

(p-٩٢٢) The adverbial phrase "the day when the Trumpet is blown" (يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ) is connected to an implied verb, which is *udhkur* ("remember"). It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the Day of Resurrection," but the first view is preferable.

The majority of readers recited (يُنْفَخُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and in the passive voice. Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with *nūn* in the active voice. Abū ʿAmr supported this reading with the words (ونَحْشُرُ) ("and We will gather"), which begin with *nūn*. Ibn Hurmuz recited (يَنْفُخُ) with *yāʾ* in the active voice, on the basis that the agent is God, glorified is He, or Isrāfīl. Abū ʿIyāḍ recited (في الصُّوَرِ) with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, as the plural of *ṣūra*. The rest recited it with a *sukūn* on the *wāw*. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Ḥasan recited (يُحْشَرُ) with *yāʾ* in the passive voice and with *ar-mujrimīn* in the nominative, which contradicts the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. The rest recited it with *nūn*. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Anʿām. By "the criminals" (al-mujrimīn) are meant the polytheists and the sinners who are seized for their sins, which God has not forgiven them. By "on that day" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is meant the day of the blowing of the Trumpet.

The accusative of (زُرْقًا) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the criminals," meaning "blue-eyed," i.e., with the greenish-blue colour of the eye, like the eye of a cat. The Arabs regarded blueness of the eye as a bad omen. Al-Farrāʾ said that (زُرْقًا) means "blind." Al-Azharī said it means "thirsty," and this is also the view of az-Zajjāj, since the blackness of the eye changes to blueness through thirst. It has also been said that by (زُرْقًا) God meant false hope that is followed by disappointment. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for a fixed, staring gaze caused by intense greed, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Muʿakbar,
As every Ḍabbī is blue-eyed out of baseness."*

The first view is preferable. The reconciliation between this verse and His saying: *"And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf"* (17:97) is what has been said: that the Day of Resurrection has various states and stations, in which their attributes differ and their punishment varies.

The clause (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ) ("they whisper among themselves") is in the accusative place as a *ḥāl*, or it is a new sentence explaining their condition on that day. *Al-khafت* in the language means quietness, and then the one who lowers his voice is called *khafit*. The meaning is "they speak secretly to one another." (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا عَشْرًا) ("You have not remained but ten [days]") means that you have not remained in the world except for ten nights. It has been said that it refers to in the graves, and it has been said that it refers to between the two blasts. The meaning is that they will consider the duration of their stay in the world, or in the graves, or between the two blasts, to be short because of the severity of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection. It has also been said that by "ten" is meant ten hours.

Then, when they said this, God, glorified is He, said: *"We know best what they will say when their best in conduct will say: 'You remained not but a day'"* (20:104). That means: the most just of them in speech, the most complete in judgement, and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation. (إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا يَوْمًا) means you did not remain except for one day. The attribution of this statement to the best of them is because it shows more clearly the severity of the terror, not because it is closer to the truth.

(ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) means: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, saying: *"Say: 'My Lord will blow them away with a blast'"* (20:105). Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then He will turn them into sand that flows in a stream, then He will set them moving like carded wool which the winds scatter this way and that, and then like scattered dust. The *fāʾ* in His saying (فَقُلْ) is the answer to an implied condition, and the meaning is: "If they ask you, then say," or it is for hastening to oblige the questioners. The pronoun in His saying (فَيَذَرُها) refers to the mountains with regard to their places, meaning: He will leave their places, after the blowing away of what was upon them of mountains, *"as a level plain"* (20:106). Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: *al-qāʿ aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the smooth land on which there is no vegetation. Al-Jawharī said: *al-qāʿ* is the level part of the land, and its plurals are *aqwuʿ*, *aqwāʿ* and *qīʿān*. The apparent meaning in the language of the Arabs is that *al-qāʿ* is the open, exposed place, and *aṣ-ṣafṣaf* is the level and smooth. Sībawayh recited:

*"How many a *ṣafṣaf* lies beyond your house,
And dunes of sand and their ridges."*

The accusative of (قاعًا) is either as a second object of (يَذَرُ) with the implication of the meaning "make," or as a *ḥāl*, and (الصَّفْصَفُ) is its adjective. The place of (لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا) ("you will not see in it any curvature") is in the accusative as a second adjective of (قاعًا), and the pronoun refers to the mountains in that sense. *ʿIwaj* with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn* means crookedness, as Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. *Al-amt* means small hillocks. In the language *al-amt* means an elevated place. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is inclination and *al-amt* is a trace like a sandal strap. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* is a valley and *al-amt* is a mound. It has been said: they are both elevation. It has been said: *al-ʿiwaj* refers to cracks and *al-amt* to a dune. It has been said: *al-amt* is that the land is thick in one place and thin in another. Describing the places of the mountains as *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* here removes what is said: that *ʿiwaj* with a *kasra* is used for meanings and with a *fatḥa* for concrete things. The author of al-Kashshāf has overburdened himself on this point with what is unnecessary, and there is ample room elsewhere.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) ("On that day they will follow the Caller, with no deviation from him") means: on the day the mountains are blown away, people will follow God's Caller to the place of gathering. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means the sound of the gathering. It has been said: the Caller is Isrāfīl when he blows into the Trumpet. (لا عِوَجَ لَهُ) means: they have no way of deviating from his call, so they will not be able to turn away from it or swerve from it, but rather they will hasten towards it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It has also been said: there is no crookedness in his call.

(وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." (وخَشَعَتِ الأصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ) ("and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful") means they will submit to His awe. It has been said: they will be humiliated. It has been said: they will fall silent. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When the news of az-Zubayr came, the walls of Madīna and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

(فَلا تَسْمَعُ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("you will hear nothing but whispering"): *al-hams* is a faint sound. Most exegetes said: it is the sound of the feet moving to the place of gathering. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"And they walk with us in faint sound."*

He means the sound of camels' soft feet. Ruʾba described himself:

*"A lion who crushes the lion, and does not fear the elephant or the buffalo."*

It is said of lions *al-hamūs*, because it whispers in the darkness, meaning it treads lightly. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to every faint sound, whether from the foot, or from the mouth, or otherwise. This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: (فَلا يَنْطِقُونَ إلّا هَمْسًا) ("they will not speak except in a whisper").

(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ) ("On that day intercession will not benefit"), meaning: on the day what has been mentioned occurs, intercession will not benefit, from any intercessor whatsoever, *"except for him whom the Most Merciful permits"* (20:109), meaning: except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits to intercede for him, *"and whose word He approves"* (20:109), meaning: He approves his speech in intercession, or He approves the speech of the intercessor for his sake. The meaning is: intercession will only benefit the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who has a word that is approved. Similar to this verse is His saying: *"And they cannot intercede except for him whom He approves"* (21:28), and His saying: *"They shall have no power of intercession except him who has made a covenant with the Most Merciful"* (19:87), and His saying: *"So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them"* (74:48).

(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم) ("He knows what is before them and what is behind them"), meaning: what is before them of the matter of the Hour, and what is behind them of the matter of the world. Here the reference is to all creation. It has been said: the intended people are those who follow the Caller. Ibn Jarīr said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them and what is behind them. (ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا) ("and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge"), meaning: with respect to God, glorified is He. Their knowledge does not encompass His essence, nor His attributes, nor what is known of Him. It has been said: the pronoun refers to what is in the two places, for they do not know all of that.

(وعَنَتِ الوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ القَيُّومِ) ("and faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer"), meaning: they will be humiliated and submissive. This is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said. Az-Zajjāj said: the meaning of *ʿanat* in the language is "submitted." One says *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanwan* when he submits, and from this the prisoner is called *ʿānin*. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī aṣ-Ṣalt:

*"A King over the throne of the heavens, the Guardian; before His might the faces are humbled and prostrate."*

It has been said: it is from *ʿanāʾ*, meaning weariness. (وقَدْ خابَ مَن حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا) ("and he will have failed who carries injustice"), meaning: whoever carries any of injustice will have lost. It has been said: it means polytheism.

(ومَن يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصّالِحاتِ) ("And whoever does righteous deeds"), meaning: righteous deeds, *"while he is a believer in God"*, because a deed is not accepted without faith; rather, faith is a condition of acceptance. (فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْمًا) ("he will not fear injustice"), meaning he will not be afflicted with a loss of reward in the Hereafter. (ولا هَضْمًا) ("nor diminution"): *al-hadm* is loss and breaking. One says: *hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī*, meaning I reduced it and left it. *Hādhā yahḍimu aṭ-ṭaʿām*, meaning it reduces its weight. A woman with *hadīm al-kashḥ* is one with a slender belly. Ibn Kathīr and Mujāhid recited (لا يَخَفْ) with *jazm* (apocope) as an answer to His saying: *"And whoever does righteous deeds"*. The rest recited (يَخافُ) as an indicative statement.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to him and said: "I saw His saying: *'And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed'* (20:102), and another [verse] says *'blind'*." He said: "The Day of Resurrection has states: they will be in one state blue-eyed, and in another state blind." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying (يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ), that he said: "They speak secretly." Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: *"the best in conduct"* (20:104), that he said: "The one with the most understanding." In another wording he said: "The one who knows most in himself." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Quraysh said: 'How will your Lord deal with these mountains on the Day of Resurrection?' Then (ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ) was revealed, to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"so He will leave them as a level plain"* (20:106), that he said: "There is no vegetation in it." *"You will not see in it any curvature"*: he said: "A valley." *"Nor any elevation"*: he said: "A mound." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿIkrima that he was asked about His saying: *"a level plain, in which you will see no curvature nor elevation."* He said: "Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: it is the smooth land in which there is no high mound and no depression." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *ʿiwaj*, that he said: "Inclination." *Wa lā amt*: he said: "The *amt* is a trace like a sandal strap." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurẓī who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in darkness; the sky will be folded, the stars will scatter, the sun and moon will go, and a caller will call out, and the people will follow the voice, affirming it." That is God's saying: *"On that day they will follow the Caller, with no crookedness in him"* (20:108). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ regarding the verse, that he said: "No crookedness from him." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: *"And voices will be humbled"*, that he said: "They will be silent." *"You will hear nothing but whispering"*: he said: "The faint sound." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding His saying *"nothing but whispering"*, that he said: "The sound of the stepping of feet." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid who said: "The faint sound." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: "The secret of conversation and the sound of feet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding *"and faces are humbled"* that he said: "They are humiliated." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Qatāda. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid who said: "They are submissive." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliya who said: "They are subdued." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "*And faces are humbled*: the bowing and prostration." Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." ʿAbd ar-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatāda regarding *"and he has failed who carries injustice"* that he said: "Polytheism." *"He will not fear injustice or diminution"*: he said: "Injustice: that his evil deeds be increased. *Diminution*: that his good deeds be reduced." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "He will not fear that he be wronged in his evil deeds, nor that he be diminished in his good deeds." al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him, regarding *"nor diminution"*, that he said: "Usurpation."

(p-924) His saying: ﴿And thus We have sent it down﴾ is conjoined with His saying ﴿Thus We relate to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. That is, in the same manner as that sending down, We sent it down, namely the Qur'an, in a state where it is ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, that is, in the language of the Arabs, so that they may understand it. ﴿And We have varied in it some of the warning﴾: We have set forth in it various kinds of warning, as intimidation and threat. Or: We have repeated in it some of it, ﴿that perhaps they may fear﴾, that is, so that they may fear God, and so avoid His disobedience and beware of His punishment. ﴿Or it causes them to take heed﴾, that is, reflection and admonition. It was said: piety (wara'). It was said: honour (sharaf). It was said: obedience and worship, because the word dhikr (remembrance) is applied to these. Al-Hasan recited (aw nuhdithu lahum) with the letter nun. ﴿So exalted is God, the True King, above what they associate﴾: When He made clear to the servants the great magnitude of His blessing upon them in sending down the Qur'an, He declared Himself far above being likened to His creatures in any respect. That is, God is exalted above the distortion of the deviators and above what the polytheists say about His attributes, for He is the King in whose hand is reward and punishment, and He is the Truth, that is, the Possessor of Truth. ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾, that is, before its revelation to you is brought to completion.

The commentators said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would hurry ahead of Jibril and recite before Jibril finished the revelation, out of eagerness for what was being sent down to him. So God forbade him from that. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16], as will come, God willing. It was also said that the meaning is: do not convey it to the people before its interpretation comes to you. Ibn Mas'ud, Ya'qub, al-Hasan and al-A'mash recited (min qabli an naqdiya) with the letter nun, and with the accusative on waḥyahu (His revelation). ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾, that is, ask your Lord for an increase of knowledge of His Book.

﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam﴾: The lam is the lam preceding the oath (al-lam al-muwaṭṭi'ah), and the sentence that follows confirms what came before it concerning the variation of warning. That is, We had certainly commanded him and enjoined him, and the thing covenanted is omitted, namely what will come of His prohibition of eating from the tree. The meaning of ﴿from before﴾ is: from before this time. ﴿But he forgot﴾. Al-A'mash recited it with the yā' sukūn. The forgetting here means abandoning acting upon what the covenant was made concerning and refraining from it, and this is what most of the commentators said. It was said: forgetting is in its literal sense, and that he forgot what God had covenanted with him and refrain from it, and Adam was held accountable for forgetting at that time, even though forgetting is lifted from this community. The purpose of the verse, according to the first view, is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ): that is, the obedience of the children of Adam to Satan is an ancient matter, and if these contemporaries of his break the covenant, then their father Adam broke it too. Thus said Ibn Jarir and al-Qushayri. Ibn 'Atiyyah objected to this, saying that Adam's being like the disbelieving deniers of God is nothing. It was recited (fa-nussiya) with a damma on the nun and a shadda on the sin, kasra on it, in the passive voice: that is, Iblis caused him to forget. ﴿And We did not find in him determination﴾. ʿAzm (determination) in the language is the settling of the self upon an action, resolving upon it, and persisting on a belief in whatever it may be. Adam, peace be upon him, had settled his self upon not eating from the tree and was resolved upon that. But when Iblis whispered to him, his disposition softened, his resolve weakened, and the weakness of humanity overtook him. It was also said: ʿazm means patience, that is, We did not find in him patience against eating from the tree. Al-Nahhas said: That is also its meaning in the language; it is said of so-and-so that he has ʿazm, that is, patience and steadfastness in guarding against disobedience until he is safe from it, and from it is His saying: ﴿as the messengers of determination were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It was said: the meaning is that We did not find in him determination toward the sin, and this is what Ibn Kaysan said. It was said: We did not find for him a firm opinion upon which he was resolved, and this is what Ibn Qutaybah said.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to describe how his forgetting and loss of determination became manifest, and the governing element of ﴿when﴾ is implied, that is: and remember ﴿when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾. Linking the mention to the time, although the intent is to mention the events that occurred in it, is for emphasis, because when the command is related to the time, mentioning the events in it becomes necessary all the more. The explanation of this story has already been given in full in al-Baqarah. The meaning of ﴿so he would be made miserable﴾ is: so he would be tired in obtaining what is necessary for livelihood, such as ploughing and planting. He did not say ﴿so you would both be miserable﴾, because the discourse from the beginning of the story is with Adam alone.

Then He gave the reason for what this prohibition requires, by what contains complete comfort free from fatigue and concern, and said: ﴿Indeed, it is for you that you will not hunger therein or go naked﴾, that is, in Paradise. The meaning is: for you therein is enjoyment of kinds of livelihood and luxury with varieties of blessings, from delicious foods and beautiful garments. For when He negated hunger and nakedness from him, it implied the establishment of satiety and clothing for him. Likewise His saying: ﴿And that you will not thirst therein or be exposed to the sun﴾, for the negation of thirst entails the attainment of quenching and the existence of a dwelling that protects him from the hardship of exposure. It is said: ḍaḥḥā al-rajul yuḍaḥḥī ḍaḥwan, when a man comes out into the sun and its heat strikes him. Here He, glory be to Him, mentioned that He had spared him from occupying himself with the affairs of livelihood and the fatigue of toil in obtaining it. There is no doubt that the roots of hardships in this world are obtaining satiety, quenching, clothing and shelter, and what is beyond these is surplus, which one can do without. This is an announcement from God, glory be to Him, to Adam that if he obeys Him, he will have all of this in Paradise; but if he neglects His command and does not keep His covenant, He will expel him from Paradise to the world, and fatigue and toil will befall him, from which hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure must be warded off. So the intent of misery is the misery of this world, as many of the commentators said, not the misery of the Hereafter. Al-Farra' said: It is that he eats from the labour of his hands. Abu 'Amr and the Kufans, except 'Asim, recited ﴿and that you will not thirst﴾ with a fatḥah on the anna, while the rest recited it with a kasra, by coordination with ﴿Indeed, for you﴾.

﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾. Its explanation has already been given in al-A'raf in His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]: that is, he conveyed his whisper to him. The sentence ﴿he said: O Adam﴾ to its end is either a substitution for ﴿whispered﴾, or an independent sentence presupposing a question, as if it were said: what did he say to him in his whisper? ﴿The tree of eternity﴾ is the tree whoever eats from it never dies at all. ﴿And a kingdom that does not decay﴾, that is, does not pass away or end. ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them both﴾. Its explanation and what follows it have already been given in al-A'raf. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of ṭafiqā in Arabic is: they began. It was said: they both began to stick upon themselves some leaves of the fig tree. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray﴾, that is, he disobeyed Him by eating from the tree, (p-925) ﴿and went astray﴾, that is, he strayed from the right course or from his goal, which was eternity through eating from that tree. It was said: his life was spoiled by his descent to the world. It was said: he failed to know the place of his right guidance. It was said: he was overfull from eating too much. Ibn Qutaybah said: Adam ate from the tree that he had been forbidden, through the seduction and deceptions of Iblis, and his swearing to him by God that he was indeed among the sincere advisers, until he brought him down by deception. His sin was not from a prior belief or a sound intention. So we say: Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray. End of quotation. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is not permissible for anyone today to report this about Adam. I say: There is no barrier to this, since God has informed us in His Book that he disobeyed Him, just as it is said: the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near. Among what I have said on this meaning:

"The father of the world disobeyed, he whom God shaped from a clay,
And made the angels prostrate for his sake, and made Paradise his abode.
Iblis led him astray; so who am I, the poor one?
Indeed, Iblis led him astray."

﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾, that is, He selected him and brought him near. Ibn Furak said: The disobedience of Adam was before prophethood, as evidenced by this verse, for He mentioned the choosing and guidance after mentioning the disobedience, and if the disobedience was before prophethood, then sins are permissible for them in one respect. ﴿So He accepted his repentance and guided him﴾, that is, He accepted his repentance from his disobedience and guided him to steadfastness in repentance. It was said: God's acceptance of his repentance was before he and Eve repented by their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. The reason for specifying Adam for mention rather than Eve has already passed.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿or it causes them to take heed﴾, that is, the Qur'an causes them a remembrance. He said: Seriousness and piety. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾: he said: Do not hasten until We make it clear to you. Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "A man slapped his wife, and she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking retaliation. The Prophet (ﷺ) made retaliation between them. Then God sent down ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ and the verse, so the Prophet (ﷺ) paused until the verse ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 34] was revealed." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And do not hasten﴾ the verse. He said: Do not recite it to anyone until We complete it for you. Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mandah in al-Tawhid, and al-Tabarani in al-Saghir, and he authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The human being was only named insan because he was entrusted with a covenant and forgot." Abd al-Ghani and Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam﴾: that he should not approach the tree, "but he forgot, and abandoned My covenant." ﴿And We did not find in him determination﴾: he said: Retention. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted also from him: ﴿but he forgot﴾, he abandoned; ﴿and We did not find in him determination﴾ he said: We did not make for him determination. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: ﴿And that you will not thirst therein or be exposed to the sun﴾. He said: Thirst will not reach you therein, nor heat. Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree under whose shade a rider travels for a hundred years without cutting through it, and it is the tree of eternity." In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Musa debated. Musa said to him: You are the one who expelled people from Paradise by your sin and made them wretched by your disobedience. Adam said: O Musa, you are the one whom God chose with His message and His speech; do you blame me for a matter that God had written against me before He created me, or had decreed for me before He created me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "So Adam overcame Musa in the argument."

It was said: they both began to stick upon themselves some leaves of the fig tree. ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray﴾, that is, he disobeyed Him by eating from the tree, (p-925) ﴿and went astray﴾, that is, he strayed from the right course or from his goal, which was eternity through eating from that tree. He said: Seriousness and piety. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾: he said: Do not hasten until We make it clear to you. Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "A man slapped his wife, and she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking retaliation. The Prophet (ﷺ) made retaliation between them. Then God sent down ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ and the verse, so the Prophet (ﷺ) paused until the verse ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 34] was revealed." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And do not hasten﴾ the verse. He said: Do not recite it to anyone until We complete it for you. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted also from him: ﴿but he forgot﴾, he abandoned; ﴿and We did not find in him determination﴾ he said: We did not make for him determination. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: ﴿And that you will not thirst therein or be exposed to the sun﴾. He said: Thirst will not reach you therein, nor heat. Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree under whose shade a rider travels for a hundred years without cutting through it, and it is the tree of eternity." In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Musa debated. Musa said to him: You are the one who expelled people from Paradise by your sin and made them wretched by your disobedience. Adam said: O Musa, you are the one whom God chose with His message and His speech; do you blame me for a matter that God had written against me before He created me, or had decreed for me before He created me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "So Adam overcame Musa in the argument."

That is, in the same manner as that sending down, We sent it down, namely the Qur'an, in a state where it is ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, that is, in the language of the Arabs, so that they may understand it. ﴿And We have varied in it some of the warning﴾: We have set forth in it various kinds of warning, as intimidation and threat. Or: We have repeated in it some of it, ﴿that perhaps they may fear﴾, that is, so that they may fear God, and so avoid His disobedience and beware of His punishment. ﴿Or it causes them to take heed﴾, that is, reflection and admonition. It was said: piety (wara'). It was said: honour (sharaf). It was said: obedience and worship, because the word dhikr (remembrance) is applied to these. Al-Hasan recited (aw nuhdithu lahum) with the letter nun. ﴿So exalted is God, the True King, above what they associate﴾: When He made clear to the servants the great magnitude of His blessing upon them in sending down the Qur'an, He declared Himself far above being likened to His creatures in any respect. That is, God is exalted above the distortion of the deviators and above what the polytheists say about His attributes, for He is the King in whose hand is reward and punishment, and He is the Truth, that is, the Possessor of Truth. ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾, that is, before its revelation to you is brought to completion.

The commentators said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would hurry ahead of Jibril and recite before Jibril finished the revelation, out of eagerness for what was being sent down to him. He said: Seriousness and piety. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾: he said: Do not hasten until We make it clear to you. Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "A man slapped his wife, and she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking retaliation. The Prophet (ﷺ) made retaliation between them. Then God sent down ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ and the verse, so the Prophet (ﷺ) paused until the verse ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 34] was revealed." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And do not hasten﴾ the verse. He said: Do not recite it to anyone until We complete it for you. Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mandah in al-Tawhid, and al-Tabarani in al-Saghir, and he authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The human being was only named insan because he was entrusted with a covenant and forgot." Abd al-Ghani and Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam﴾: that he should not approach the tree, "but he forgot, and abandoned My covenant." ﴿And We did not find in him determination﴾: he said: Retention. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted also from him: ﴿but he forgot﴾, he abandoned; ﴿and We did not find in him determination﴾ he said: We did not make for him determination. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: ﴿And that you will not thirst therein or be exposed to the sun﴾. He said: Thirst will not reach you therein, nor heat. Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree under whose shade a rider travels for a hundred years without cutting through it, and it is the tree of eternity." In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Musa debated. Musa said to him: You are the one who expelled people from Paradise by your sin and made them wretched by your disobedience. Adam said: O Musa, you are the one whom God chose with His message and His speech; do you blame me for a matter that God had written against me before He created me, or had decreed for me before He created me?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "So Adam overcame Musa in the argument."

(p-924) His saying: ﴿And thus We have sent it down﴾ is conjoined with His saying ﴿Thus We relate to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. That is, in the same manner as that sending down, We sent it down, namely the Qur'an, in a state where it is ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, that is, in the language of the Arabs, so that they may understand it. ﴿And We have varied in it some of the warning﴾: We have set forth in it various kinds of warning, as intimidation and threat. Or: We have repeated in it some of it, ﴿that perhaps they may fear﴾, that is, so that they may fear God, and so avoid His disobedience and beware of His punishment. ﴿Or it causes them to take heed﴾, that is, reflection and admonition. It was said: piety (wara'). It was said: honour (sharaf). It was said: obedience and worship, because the word dhikr (remembrance) is applied to these. Al-Hasan recited (aw nuhdithu lahum) with the letter nun. ﴿So exalted is God, the True King, above what they associate﴾: When He made clear to the servants the great magnitude of His blessing upon them in sending down the Qur'an, He declared Himself far above being likened to His creatures in any respect. That is, God is exalted above the distortion of the deviators and above what the polytheists say about His attributes, for He is the King in whose hand is reward and punishment, and He is the Truth, that is, the Possessor of Truth. ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾, that is, before its revelation to you is brought to completion.

The commentators said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would hurry ahead of Jibril and recite before Jibril finished the revelation, out of eagerness for what was being sent down to him. So God forbade him from that. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16], as will come, God willing. It was also said that the meaning is: do not convey it to the people before its interpretation comes to you. Ibn Mas'ud, Ya'qub, al-Hasan and al-A'mash recited (min qabli an naqdiya) with the letter nun, and with the accusative on waḥyahu (His revelation). ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾, that is, ask your Lord for an increase of knowledge of His Book.
